title: Data Science in Engineering
text:
Preface
Version: 0.2
Welcome to Data Science in Engineering, a master’s course at Trier University of Applied Sciences for students of mechanical engineering, electrical engineering and industrial engineering.

title: Data Science in Engineering
text:
What this course is about
Every method in this script is introduced together with a real, publicly available engineering dataset – from power plants and gas turbines to rolling bearings, semiconductor production and jet engines. Theory and practice go hand in hand: each chapter starts with a (fictional) engineering scenario that calls for a decision, explains the methods needed to make it, applies them in Python – and returns to the scenario at the end to make the decision with the results.
The course has four parts:








Part
Topics
Chapters




A – Understanding Data
workflow, exploratory analysis, data quality
1–2


B – Statistical Inference
probability and uncertainty, hypothesis tests, regression, design of experiments
3–5


C – Prediction and Monitoring
model selection and validation, classification, ensembles, unsupervised learning
6–9


D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning
from diagnosis to prognosis: signal features, forecasting, remaining useful life with neural networks; review
10–13



Before Part A, the short lesson Getting Started with pandas introduces the Python library pandas for everyone who has not used it before.

title: Data Science in Engineering
section: What you will be able to do
text:
What you will be able to do
By the end of the course, you will be able to tackle an engineering question you have not seen before with data – on your own and from start to finish: prepare real measurement data, choose and validate suitable methods from statistics or machine learning, and derive a recommendation for a decision. A good analysis quantifies the uncertainty of its results and explains the recommendation – including the limits of data and model – so that others can follow and check it.
Engineers increasingly face exactly such questions: Is a test result strong enough to confirm a claimed improvement? Can a cheaper concrete mix be approved before any specimens exist? Is a failure alarm worth its false alarms? Which safety margin does a lifetime prediction need? The scenarios of the chapters are modelled on situations like these.
The course builds up this ability along the steps of such an analysis:

Translate the question into a data science task: target, influencing variables, type of task, and the information available at the time of the decision.
Check and prepare the data: judge whether a dataset is fit for the question, and clean it (Part A).
Quantify effects and uncertainty with statistical models: how precisely is a value known, and is an effect statistically established and practically relevant? (Part B)
Build and validate prediction and monitoring models: does a model meet the requirements of a specific use on new data? (Part C)
Respect the order in time of signals, time series and sensor sequences (Part D).
Justify a recommendation – with its uncertainty, its assumptions and the limits of data and model. Every chapter practises this in the section Back to the decision.

The first step runs through the whole course: choosing an approach requires the methods of Parts B to D, and Chapter 13 brings them together. The learning goals at the start of each chapter name the smaller steps.

title: Data Science in Engineering
text:
Prerequisites
Basic Python programming and mathematics at bachelor level (linear algebra, calculus, introductory statistics). If you have not worked with the Python library pandas before, start with the short introduction Getting Started with pandas before Chapter 1.

title: Data Science in Engineering
section: How to work with this script
text:
How to work with this script
The script is meant to be read in the browser or as a PDF. Every result in it was computed with Python, and the code is part of the script: in the HTML version, click Code above a result to show it. You can copy it into your own notebook to reproduce or vary an analysis.
During the semester, the demo code from the lectures is provided as Jupyter notebooks.

Software
You can work with any development environment you like (e.g. JupyterLab, VS Code or PyCharm), as long as it can open, run and edit Jupyter notebooks. We recommend Google Colab; a local installation is an alternative:

Google Colab (recommended): Colab runs notebooks in the browser – no installation required, on a laptop or a tablet (an external keyboard helps a lot). Sign in with a Google account and open a notebook via File → Upload notebook. Most packages used in this course are pre-installed. Files you download or upload in Colab live only as long as the session; save results you want to keep to Google Drive or download them.
Alternative – local installation: The Anaconda Distribution installs Python, Jupyter and the most important data science packages in one go – a good choice if you prefer to work offline and with files on your own computer.

Packages that are missing can be installed directly from a notebook cell with %pip install, e.g. %pip install ucimlrepo.
Optional: keep the data in Colab. The notebooks download each dataset once into a folder data in the current working directory. In Colab, this folder disappears with the session, so the data are downloaded again the next time. If you want to avoid this, run the following cell at the start of a notebook: the folder data is then created in your Google Drive and kept. The cell works only in Colab.
from google.colab import drive
drive.mount("/content/drive")                        # asks once for permission to access Drive
%mkdir -p "/content/drive/MyDrive/Data Science"      # course folder in Drive (created if missing)
%cd "/content/drive/MyDrive/Data Science"            # work there: ./data is now in Drive


Reading guide
Each chapter opens with a scenario (purple box) and closes it in a section Back to the decision. The people and situations are invented; the data are real (or, where stated, simulated).
Coloured boxes highlight what matters most:






Definitions



Blue boxes define the central concepts.








Key results



Red boxes contain theorems, key results and the takeaways at the end of each chapter.








Pitfalls



Yellow boxes warn of typical mistakes – in data science, many of them lead to results that look convincing but are wrong.








Engineering practice



Green boxes give practical advice for engineering projects.


Each chapter ends with exercises (highlighted boxes) followed by solutions, which are collapsed in the HTML version – try the exercise first, then open the solution. The lab assignments of the course build on the exercises.
Sections and exercises marked Extension go beyond the core of the course. They are optional and not required for the exam – use them to dig deeper into topics that matter for your own work.


Notation
The script uses the following conventions throughout:







Symbol
Meaning




\(x_1, \dots, x_n\)
observations (sample of size \(n\)); \(x_i\) is the \(i\)-th observation


\(\bar x\), \(s\)
sample mean and sample standard deviation


\(\tilde x\)
sample median


\(\mu\), \(\sigma\)
mean and standard deviation of the population or distribution


\(\hat\theta\)
estimate of a parameter \(\theta\) (the hat marks anything computed from data)


\(y\), \(\hat y\)
response (target) and its prediction


\(X\)
matrix of inputs: one row per observation, one column per input


\(P(A)\), \(P(A \mid B)\)
probability, conditional probability


\(E[X]\), \(\text{Var}(X)\)
expected value and variance of a random variable \(X\)


\(\ln\)
natural logarithm



The Greek alphabet is small, and the standard symbols of different fields overlap. Where a symbol has different meanings in different chapters, the meaning is stated where it is used. The most important cases: \(\beta\) is the Weibull shape parameter (Chapter 3), the probability of a type II error (Chapter 4) and a regression coefficient (Chapters 5–7); \(\eta\) is the Weibull scale parameter (Chapter 3) and the learning rate (Chapter 12); \(\sigma\) denotes a standard deviation and, in Chapters 7 and 12, an activation function.

Assessment

Lab assignments (coursework, pass/fail): four assignments during the semester.
Written exam (90 minutes, without computer): method choice, interpretation of results, justified decisions, short calculations and code reading.

Passing the lab assignments is the prerequisite for admission to the written exam.
In the exam, you may use the Python Quick Reference and the Formula Collection from the appendix. Both are handed out with the exam; your own copies or notes are not allowed.

title: Getting Started with pandas
text:
Why pandas?
Almost every chapter of this script works with tables: measurements with time stamps, test results per part, sensor values per run. In Python, such tables are handled with pandas. This lesson introduces pandas for everyone who has not used it before – and shows the typical style of pandas code, which differs from the NumPy and Matplotlib code you may know. It takes about 100 minutes; work through it before Chapter 1, run every cell yourself and change things to see what happens.
Prerequisites. Basic Python (variables, lists, dictionaries, functions, loops) and a first contact with NumPy and Matplotlib.
Learning goals. After this lesson you can
Dataset. A small, invented production log: shafts with a nominal diameter of 25 mm are turned on three machines, and one part per hour is measured; parts that deviate by more than 12 µm are scrapped. The data are created in the lesson itself, so no download is needed.
A NumPy array is fast, but it usually holds only numbers, all of the same type, addressed by position: a[3] is “the fourth value”. Real engineering tables are different:
pandas adds exactly this to NumPy: names, labels, mixed types and missing values. Underneath, the numbers are still stored in NumPy arrays, so the speed of vectorised operations remains. First the usual setup:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")             # common style for all plots, as in every chapter
pd.set_option("display.precision", 3)        # show 3 decimals in tables

Series and DataFrame
A Series is a single column: values plus labels, the index.

temps = pd.Series([21.5, 22.0, 23.1],                    # the values

                  name="spindle_temp_C")                 # an optional name

Access works by label, and arithmetic works on all values at once – as in NumPy. The labels are kept:

title: Getting Started with pandas
section: Reading a file and a first look
text:
Reading a file and a first look
In practice, tables come from files. The folded cell below creates our example file data/shafts.csv – in a real project, you would receive such a file from a measuring machine or a database export. Like many files from German software, it uses a semicolon as separator and a decimal comma.


Code
# Creates the example file data/shafts.csv (4 days, 6:00-20:00, one measured part per hour).
from pathlib import Path
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
days = pd.date_range("2025-03-03", periods=4, freq="D")                 # Monday to Thursday
time = pd.DatetimeIndex([d + pd.Timedelta(hours=h) for d in days for h in range(6, 21)])  # 6:00-20:00
n = len(time)                                                           # 60 parts
machine = np.tile(["M1", "M2", "M3"], n // 3)
offset = np.where(machine == "M3", 0.008, 0.0)                         # M3 is set too large
diameter = 25.0 + offset + rng.normal(0, 0.004, n)
warm_up = 1 - np.exp(-(time.hour.to_numpy() - 6) / 3)                  # spindle warms up after 6:00
spindle = 20 + 8 * warm_up + rng.normal(0, 0.4, n)
log = pd.DataFrame({
    "time": time.strftime("%d.%m.%Y %H:%M"),                           # German date format
    "machine": machine,
    "diameter_mm": diameter.round(4),
    "spindle_temp_C": spindle.round(1),
})
log["result"] = np.where((log["diameter_mm"] - 25).abs() > 0.012, "scrap", "OK")   # tolerance ±12 µm
log.loc[[17, 40], "spindle_temp_C"] = np.nan                            # two missing readings
Path("data").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
log.to_csv("data/shafts.csv", sep=";", decimal=",", index=False)

title: Getting Started with pandas
text:
Computing with columns
New columns are computed from existing ones – for all rows at once, without a loop:

shafts["dev_um"] = (shafts["diameter_mm"] - 25.0) * 1000      # deviation from nominal in µm
shafts[["diameter_mm", "dev_um"]].head(3)








diameter_mm
dev_um




0
24.997
-3.2


1
25.001
1.0


2
25.001
1.4







For comparison, the loop version that you would write in plain Python – it gives the same result but is longer and, for large tables, much slower:
dev = []
for value in shafts["diameter_mm"]:
    dev.append((value - 25.0) * 1000)
shafts["dev_um"] = dev
Summaries are methods of the column: s.mean(), s.median(), s.std(), s.abs(), s.max(). They skip missing values automatically:

t = shafts["spindle_temp_C"]
print("missing values:", t.isna().sum())          # isna(): True where a value is missing
print("mean:", t.mean().round(1))                 # computed from the values present
print("mean absolute deviation (µm):", shafts["dev_um"].abs().mean().round(1))

missing values: 2
mean: 26.2
mean absolute deviation (µm): 4.7


The last line shows the typical pandas style: shafts["dev_um"].abs().mean() reads from left to right – take the deviation, its absolute value, the mean. NumPy writes the same nested from the inside out, np.mean(np.abs(...)). With pandas data, prefer the methods: they skip missing values, NumPy functions often do not (see the Python reference in the appendix).

title: Getting Started with pandas
text:
Plotting from pandas
Series and DataFrames have a plot method. It calls Matplotlib, takes the x-axis from the index and returns the familiar Matplotlib axes ax, so you can continue as usual:

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.5))
shafts["spindle_temp_C"].plot(ax=axes[0], marker=".", linestyle="none")  # time series as points
axes[0].set(ylabel="Spindle temperature (°C)")
shafts.groupby("machine")["dev_um"].mean().plot.bar(ax=axes[1], rot=0)  # bar chart of a summary
axes[1].set(ylabel="Mean deviation (µm)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Every morning the spindle starts cold and warms up to about 28 °C (there is no production at night); machine M3 stands out in the bar chart. Two lines of pandas replaced the data handling that Matplotlib alone would need.

title: Getting Started with pandas
section: Three Python patterns you will meet everywhere
text:
Three Python patterns you will meet everywhere
The chapters use three pieces of plain Python again and again. They are not pandas, but you need them to read the code.
Formatted output. An f-string – a text with an f in front – inserts values in curly brackets. A format code after a colon controls how a number is shown:

d = shafts["diameter_mm"].mean()             # mean diameter in mm
m = shafts["dev_um"].mean()                  # mean deviation from nominal in µm
share = shafts["scrap"].mean()               # share of scrap parts
print(f"mean diameter: {d:.3f} mm")          # .3f: three decimals
print(f"mean deviation: {m:+.1f} µm")        # +: always show the sign
print(f"scrap: {share:.1%}")                 # .1%: as a percentage, one decimal
print(f"{12345.678:,.1f}")                   # ,: thousands separator
print(f"{'mean':8s}{m:7.2f} µm")             # 8s, 7.2f: a width of 8 or 7 characters ...
print(f"{'maximum':8s}{shafts['dev_um'].max():7.2f} µm")   # ... gives aligned columns

mean diameter: 25.002 mm
mean deviation: +2.3 µm
scrap: 8.3%
12,345.7
mean       2.30 µm
maximum   17.40 µm


List comprehensions. [expression for item in values] builds a list in one line. It is short for a loop that appends the expression for every item:

names = [f"T{i}" for i in range(1, 4)]     # the same as: names = []; for i in range(1, 4): names.append(f"T{i}")
names

['T1', 'T2', 'T3']


Tables of results. When a loop computes several numbers per case, collect each case as a dictionary in a list – one dictionary per row – and turn the list into a DataFrame at the end. The keys become the column names:

rows = []                                                  # one entry per row of the result table
for limit in [8, 10, 12]:                                  # three possible tolerance limits in µm
    within = shafts["dev_um"].abs() <= limit               # True if the part lies within ±limit
    rows.append({"limit_um": limit, "share_within": within.mean()})   # one row as a dictionary
pd.DataFrame(rows)                                         # list of rows -> table

title: Getting Started with pandas
section: The pandas style in a nutshell
text:
The pandas style in a nutshell







Principle
Example




Columns by name, not by position
df["diameter_mm"] instead of a[:, 2]


Whole columns at once, no loops
df["dev_um"] = (df["diameter_mm"] - 25) * 1000


Rows by condition
df[df["machine"] == "M3"]


Methods, read from left to right
df["dev_um"].abs().mean()


Missing values are skipped
s.mean() uses only the values present


Split – apply – combine
df.groupby("machine")["dev_um"].mean()


Methods return new objects
df.sort_values("dev_um") leaves df unchanged



The last principle makes method chaining possible: shafts.groupby("machine")["dev_um"].mean().plot.bar() is one expression of four steps. The Python quick reference in the appendix collects all functions used in this script – including the pandas functions of this lesson – and explains the design behind chaining.

title: Getting Started with pandas
text:
Summary






Key takeaways




A Series is a column with labels (index); a DataFrame is a table of Series that share one index.
Read files with pd.read_csv, stating separator and decimal mark explicitly; get an overview with shape, info(), describe(), value_counts().
Select columns by name, rows by masks (&, |, ~), both together with loc (labels) or iloc (positions).
Compute with whole columns instead of loops; summarise with methods, which skip missing values; use groupby for summaries per group.
With time stamps as index, resample and index.hour work on the time axis; .plot() draws directly from a table.
f-strings with format codes (:.1f, :.1%) print numbers readably; list comprehensions and lists of rows build lists and tables in a loop.

title: Getting Started with pandas
text:
Exercises


How many parts were measured on each machine, and how many of them are scrap? Use value_counts or groupby.
Select all parts with a diameter above 25.010 mm. On which machines were they made?
Compute the share of parts per machine whose deviation is within ±10 µm.
Compute the mean spindle temperature for each hour of the day and plot it as a line. When is the spindle warm?
Rewrite the following loop in pandas style with one line:
count = 0
for value in shafts["spindle_temp_C"]:
    if value > 27:
        count += 1
Does your line give the same result? (Hint: what happens to the two missing values?)
For the tolerance limits 5, 10, 15 and 20 µm, build a table with the share of parts whose deviation lies within ±limit, as in the last section. In the same loop, print one line per limit with an f-string, in the form ±10 µm: xx.x% within.

title: 1  The Data Science Workflow in Engineering
text:
1.1 What are data?
Engineers have always worked with data: test bench measurements, calibration curves, quality records, field failures. What has changed is the amount and the variety of data. A modern production line logs hundreds of signals per second, a wind turbine reports its state every few seconds, and simulation studies produce thousands of runs. Data science provides the methods to turn such data into decisions.
This chapter sets the stage. We clarify what data are, what makes data science in engineering special and how it relates to statistics, machine learning and AI. We introduce a process model that structures every project and get to know the Python tools we will use throughout the course. Finally, we load and inspect our first dataset and use it to answer a business question.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Course goal. This chapter contributes to step 1 of the course goals: translate the question into a data science task.
Datasets in this chapter
Before we talk about data science, we should be clear about what we mean by data. The word is used loosely – for a spreadsheet, a database, a folder of images, “the numbers”. For this course we use a sharper definition.
The four highlighted terms deserve a closer look.
Variables are what is recorded – temperature, torque, fault type. Their type determines how they can be analysed (see below).
Observational units are what the values belong to: a part, a machine, a test run, a point in time. This is not always obvious – one shaft, or one of several measurements on that shaft? The answer decides what counts as an independent observation, which will matter when data are split into training and test sets (Chapter 10). In the power plant example of this chapter, the unit is one hour of plant operation.
Observed, not specified. Data record how things actually turned out: the diameter a coordinate measuring machine found on a particular shaft, the fact that pump no. 17 failed after 3,412 hours. This distinguishes data from specifications, targets and tables computed from a formula, which state how things should be (see below). Because data record outcomes, they can contradict our expectations – this is what makes them valuable.
Context (metadata). The value 293 means nothing without its context: a temperature in kelvin? A pressure in mbar? A part number? Unit, sensor, sampling rate, time zone and the definition of each variable belong to the data. They are usually documented separately as metadata – and often lost.
crumbs: 1  The Data Science Workflow in Engineering

title: 1  The Data Science Workflow in Engineering
text:
Definition: Data



Data are recorded values of variables (characteristics such as temperature, torque or fault type), observed on observational units (parts, machines, test runs, points in time) – together with the context needed to interpret them: what was measured, how, where, when and in which unit of measurement.













Pitfall: numbers without context



In 1999 NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one software component delivered thruster impulse data in pound-force seconds while the receiving component expected newton seconds. Every number was correct – the context was not. Before analysing a dataset, make sure you know the unit and the meaning of every column.



1.1.1 Data as a table
Most methods in this course expect data as a table whose layout follows directly from the definition. This layout is called tidy data:

each row is one observation – one unit, or one unit at one point in time,
each column is one variable,
each cell holds one value.

Many real files are not tidy – a separate column for every day, two quantities in one cell – and must be reshaped first (in pandas with melt or pivot). Signals and images are data, too, even though they do not come as such a table (see below).


1.1.2 Types of variables
The type of a variable determines which summaries, plots and models make sense (Figure 1.1). A variable is either categorical – its values are labels such as “supplier B” – or numeric – its values are amounts such as 3.2 mm or 5 defects. Categorical variables are nominal (unordered) or ordinal (ordered); a nominal variable with only two categories, such as failure yes/no, is called binary. Numeric variables are discrete (countable) or continuous (any value in a range).






Figure 1.1: Types of variables with engineering examples.



For numeric variables we compute means, standard deviations and histograms; for categorical variables we count frequencies and draw bar charts. The type also decides which calculations are meaningful at all. Coding a category as a number does not make it numeric: the mean of the fault codes 1, 2 and 7 is meaningless. And even for numeric variables, not every calculation makes sense: 20 °C is 10 K warmer than 10 °C, but not “twice as warm”, because the zero of the Celsius scale is arbitrary – in kelvin, ratios are meaningful.
In the power plant data, all five variables are continuous, which is typical for process data. Two kinds of data need special treatment:

Time stamps are numeric – the difference between two time stamps is a duration – and mostly serve as the index of a time series.
Signals, images and texts consist of many values per unit, e.g. thousands of samples of a vibration recording. They are condensed into a few informative variables, so-called features (next section) – either computed by hand, such as the RMS value of a signal (Chapter 10), or learned by a neural network (Chapter 12).



1.1.3 Roles of variables: target and features
Besides its type, a variable has a role in an analysis. In the power plant example, we want to predict the electrical output from the ambient conditions and the condenser pressure:

The target is the variable we want to explain or predict – here the net electrical output (PE). It is also called output; in classification (Chapter 7), the target is usually called label.
The features are the variables used to explain or predict it – here ambient temperature, ambient pressure, relative humidity and condenser pressure (AT, AP, RH, V). They are also called inputs.

Features can be measured directly or derived from other variables – the hour of the day from a time stamp, the RMS value from a vibration signal. Constructing such features is called feature engineering; it is where engineering knowledge enters a model most directly (Chapters 10 and 11).
The role depends on the question, not on the variable: the ambient temperature is a feature when we predict the power output, but the target when we forecast the weather. And not every analysis has a target – in unsupervised learning (Chapter 9), we look for structure among the features alone.


1.1.4 Something that looks like data – but is not
Consider a table with one row per dimension of a turned shaft – diameter at bearing seat, length, roundness – and columns nominal value, upper tolerance, lower tolerance. It has rows, columns, numbers and units. Is it data?
In the sense of our definition: no. The table comes from the technical drawing and describes how the shaft should be – a specification. It contains no observation of any real shaft. Fitting a model to it would tell us something about the designer’s choices, not about the manufacturing process. The data are the values the coordinate measuring machine records on the shafts actually produced. Only by comparing them with the specification can we learn something about the process – for example its capability.
Similar cases: a table computed from a formula (a steam table) contains no information beyond the formula; a production plan is not a record of production.






Simulated data



Data generated by a simulation are observations of a model, not of reality. They are extremely useful – for training, for testing methods, when real failures are rare – but every conclusion holds for the simulated system only, and transfers to reality only as far as the simulation is valid. Two datasets in this course are simulated: the AI4I predictive maintenance data and the C-MAPSS turbofan data. We will keep this in mind when interpreting results.

title: 1  The Data Science Workflow in Engineering
section: 1.2 What is data science in engineering?
text:
1.2 What is data science in engineering?
Put briefly, data science is the systematic extraction of knowledge and decisions from data. It combines statistics (how to reason under uncertainty), computer science (how to process data and fit models efficiently) and domain knowledge (what the data mean and which questions matter). How this relates to statistics, machine learning and AI is sorted out in the next section.
The third ingredient is where engineers have a decisive advantage. A data scientist without engineering background may find that the vibration level of a pump correlates with the time of day; an engineer knows that this is because the pump runs at higher load during the day shift – and asks the right follow-up question.
Typical tasks fall into four groups:









Task
Question
Engineering example
Chapters




Description
What happened?
Distribution of tensile strength in a batch
2, 3


Inference
Is the effect real?
Did the new supplier change the scrap rate?
4, 5


Prediction
What will happen?
Remaining useful life of a bearing, tomorrow’s grid load
5–8, 11, 12


Diagnosis / detection
What is wrong?
Which fault type? Is this run abnormal?
7–10



Engineering data have some characteristic properties that we will meet again and again:

Physics behind the data. Relationships are often known in principle (energy balance, material laws). Good models use this knowledge instead of ignoring it.
Rare events. Failures and defects are – fortunately – rare. This makes them hard to learn from (Chapter 7).
Time and sequence. Sensor data are time series. Neighbouring values are not independent, which has consequences for validation (Chapter 11).
Measurement chains. Every value went through sensor, amplifier, A/D converter, logging system. Each step can introduce errors, offsets, gaps and wrong units (Chapter 2).
High cost of errors. A wrong prediction can mean an unplanned standstill or a safety issue. Uncertainty must be quantified and communicated.

title: 1  The Data Science Workflow in Engineering
section: 1.3 Statistics, machine learning, deep learning, AI: sorting the terms
text:
1.3 Statistics, machine learning, deep learning, AI: sorting the terms
You have certainly heard all of these terms – and probably noticed that they are used inconsistently. Product brochures call a linear regression “AI”, job advertisements use “data science” and “machine learning” interchangeably, and research communities draw the borders differently. There is no official definition. For this course we therefore fix working definitions: not the only possible ones, but clear enough to know what we are talking about.






Working definitions used in this course




Statistics is the science of learning from data under uncertainty: collecting data (sampling, design of experiments), describing them, and drawing conclusions with a quantified uncertainty (estimates, confidence intervals, tests). Its focus is on understanding the process that generated the data.
Machine learning (ML) is the field of algorithms that learn a task from examples instead of being explicitly programmed. Its focus is on predicting well on new, unseen data; models are judged by their performance on held-out test data.
Deep learning (DL) is the part of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. Such networks learn suitable features by themselves, directly from the raw values – the pixels of an image, the samples of a signal, the words of a text – but typically need large amounts of data and computing power.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broadest term: systems that perform tasks which would require intelligence if done by humans – perceiving, reasoning, planning, deciding. Machine learning is today the dominant approach to AI, but not the only one: rule-based expert systems or search and planning algorithms are AI without learning.
Data science is the whole process of turning data into knowledge and decisions – from the question via data acquisition, preparation, analysis and modelling to communication and deployment. It uses statistics and machine learning as tools and requires domain knowledge to ask the right questions and interpret the answers.









Figure 1.2: Working definitions used in this course. (a) Competences: data science lives where statistics, computer science and domain knowledge meet; any two of them alone fall short. (b) Methods: deep learning is part of machine learning, which is part of AI; statistics overlaps strongly with machine learning (“statistical learning”) but also covers methods outside of it, which are not AI.



Panel (a) shows the three competences that data science combines; leaving out one of them leads to typical problems – models that answer the wrong engineering question, analyses that do not scale to large data, or powerful tools used without an understanding of uncertainty. Panel (b) arranges the method families. Statistics therefore appears twice: as a competence that every analysis needs, and as a family of methods of which only one part, statistical learning, belongs to machine learning – a hypothesis test is statistics, but not AI.

1.3.1 Where statistics and machine learning differ – and where they overlap
The boundary between statistics and machine learning is the most blurred one, because both fit models to data and many methods belong to both. The difference lies mainly in the goal and the culture – the statistician Leo Breiman famously spoke of “two cultures”:









Statistics
Machine learning




Main goal
understand and explain: which factors matter, how strong, how certain?
predict accurately on new data


Typical question
“Does the coolant temperature significantly affect the tool wear?”
“Which tool will fail within the next 100 parts?”


Models
few parameters, interpretable, explicit assumptions
flexible, often many parameters, “black box” accepted


Validation
model assumptions, standard errors, tests
performance on held-out test data, cross-validation



The overlap is large: linear and logistic regression are standard tools in both communities – this common ground is often called statistical learning. In this course we use both perspectives: in Chapter 5, we interpret a regression model through its coefficients and confidence intervals (statistics); in Chapter 6, the same kind of model is judged by its prediction error on new data (machine learning). Section 5.1.5 compares the two uses of one model in detail.






How this course is positioned




Chapters 3–5 are mainly statistics: distributions, uncertainty, tests, regression, design of experiments.
Chapters 6–11 are statistical learning and machine learning: model selection, classification, ensembles, unsupervised learning, signals and time series.
Chapter 12 gives a first look at deep learning.
AI methods without learning are not covered. All chapters together follow the data science process described next.









Pitfall: buzzwords instead of methods



When a supplier advertises an “AI-based” monitoring system, ask what is behind it: a threshold rule, a regression model, a random forest or a neural network? How was it validated, on which data, with which error rates? The label says nothing about the quality – the validation does. Note also that the EU AI Act defines “AI system” broadly: even a fairly simple machine learning model in a safety-relevant product can fall under regulation.

title: 1  The Data Science Workflow in Engineering
text:
1.4 The CRISP-DM process model
Data science projects fail more often for organisational reasons than for mathematical ones: the wrong question was answered, the data did not contain the necessary information, or the model was never used. Process models help to avoid this. The most widely used is CRISP-DM.






Definition: CRISP-DM



The Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM) divides a data science project into six phases: business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modelling, evaluation and deployment. The phases are passed through iteratively, not strictly one after another.








Figure 1.3: The CRISP-DM process model. The phases form a cycle around the data; in practice, the project moves back and forth between them.



What the phases mean in engineering – in general and for the day-ahead commitment of our scenario:

Engineering understanding (business understanding in the original model). Which decision should the analysis support, and what does a wrong answer cost? Power plant: which output to commit for each hour of the next day. Every MWh of deviation costs money, so the criterion is economic: switch if the annual savings exceed the annual cost of the temperature-based procedure. At noon, only a temperature forecast for tomorrow is available.
Data understanding. Which data exist, how were they measured, and are the relevant influences measured at all? Power plant: 9,568 hourly averages at full load – hours below 420 MW were removed during cleaning, so a model is only valid for this operating state. There are no time stamps, and the temperatures are measured values, not forecasts.
Data preparation. Cleaning, merging data sources, resampling, handling missing values, constructing features – in practice usually the largest part of a project. Power plant: little to do, the table is complete and tidy. In operation, plant records would have to be merged with weather forecasts; Chapter 2 shows the pitfalls of raw weather files.
Modelling. Choosing and fitting models – always together with a simple baseline. Power plant: the baseline is the flat long-term average, the model a straight line for the output as a function of the ambient temperature.
Evaluation. Does the model answer the question, under all relevant conditions, and is it better than the baseline? Power plant: translate the deviations of both rules into annual costs and compare them (Back to the decision).
Deployment. Integration into a process, a control system or a report – including monitoring whether the model stays valid. Power plant: every day before noon, compute the commitment from the forecast and record the actual deviations.







Engineering practice: start with a baseline



Before fitting any sophisticated model, compute a trivial baseline: the mean value, yesterday’s value, or a simple physical formula. Every model must beat the baseline – otherwise its complexity is not justified. Surprisingly often, it does not.








Pitfall: answering the wrong question



A model that predicts when a machine fails is useless if maintenance can only be scheduled four weeks in advance and the model warns two days ahead. Clarify the decision and its time horizon in phase 1 – it determines which data and models make sense.

Most operations are vectorised: instead of looping over rows, we apply an operation to a whole column at once, which is shorter and much faster. If pandas is new to you, work through Getting Started with pandas first.

section: 1.6 Live coding: a first look at the power plant data
text:
1.6 Live coding: a first look at the power plant data
A combined cycle power plant (CCPP) combines a gas turbine with a steam turbine (Figure 1.4). The gas turbine draws in ambient air, compresses it, burns natural gas in it and drives a generator. Its exhaust gas is still hot enough to raise steam in a heat recovery steam generator; the steam drives a second turbine and generator. Behind the steam turbine, the steam is condensed again in a condenser cooled by water or air. The plant that supplied our dataset, located in Turkey, has a nominal capacity of 480 MW: two gas turbines of 160 MW each, two heat recovery steam generators and one steam turbine of 160 MW (Tüfekci 2014).






Figure 1.4: Simplified block diagram of a combined cycle power plant with the variables of the dataset. The features (blue) describe the ambient air and the condenser; the target (orange) is the net electrical output of gas turbine and steam turbine together.



Why does the weather matter? Warm weather reduces the output twice:

Gas turbine: warm air is less dense. The compressor draws in a smaller mass of air per second, so less fuel can be burnt and the gas turbine delivers less power.
Steam turbine: a turbine delivers the more power, the larger the pressure difference between its inlet and its outlet. Cold cooling water condenses the steam well and keeps the pressure in the condenser low. On warm days, the cooling water is warmer, the condenser pressure rises and the steam turbine delivers less power.

This is why the condenser pressure is closely linked to the ambient temperature – and why we expect the output to fall when either of them rises.
The dataset contains 9,568 hourly averages from 674 days in six years (2006–2011), all with the plant at full load. The variables are:









Column
Meaning
Unit

exhaust vacuum: pressure in the condenser behind the steam turbine
cm Hg (according to the documentation – see below)

mbar
feature

relative humidity
%
feature

net electrical output (hourly average)
MW
target



The package ucimlrepo downloads datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository directly into pandas.

from ucimlrepo import fetch_ucirepo

# Download dataset no. 294 (Combined Cycle Power Plant) from the UCI repository.
# The number is part of the address of the dataset page:
# archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/294/combined+cycle+power+plant

# ucimlrepo returns the features (AT, V, AP, RH) and the target (PE) as two
# separate tables (see "Roles of variables"). pd.concat puts them side by side
# into one DataFrame; axis=1 means "join as columns", not as rows.
df = pd.concat([ccpp.data.features, ccpp.data.targets], axis=1)

How to read describe()



Look at each column with an engineer’s eye: Are minimum and maximum physically plausible? Is the mean close to the median (50 %)? A large difference indicates a skewed distribution or outliers. Is the standard deviation large or small compared with the measurement accuracy you would expect?


For the power plant, most ranges are plausible: ambient temperatures from just above freezing to the mid-thirties, ambient pressures around 1013 mbar, and an output of roughly 420 to 500 MW. The relative humidity reaches slightly more than 100 % – physically impossible, but within the accuracy of a humidity sensor near saturation. Worth noticing, not worth correcting.
The lower limit of the output is no coincidence: according to the original publication, all hours below 420.26 MW were removed as “out of range” during data cleaning. The dataset therefore contains only hours of high output – a model fitted to it says nothing about weaker operating states.
The exhaust vacuum V does not fit, though. According to the documentation – and already the original publication – it is given in cm Hg, but a vacuum of up to 81.6 cm Hg is impossible: the atmosphere itself corresponds to only about 76 cm Hg. Moreover, V behaves like a pressure, not like a vacuum: the larger V, the lower the output (see the pair plot below). The values would fit the absolute pressure in the condenser if the unit were mm Hg – a single wrong letter – or mbar. The data alone cannot settle this. For predicting PE, the unit does not matter; for any physical interpretation, it does. This is exactly what numbers without context means.
A pair plot shows all pairwise relationships at once:


Code
# Pair plot: a scatter plot for every pair of variables, a histogram of each
# variable on the diagonal.
sns.pairplot(
    df.sample(1000, random_state=0),   # random subset of 1,000 of the 9,568 rows
                                       # (avoids overplotting); random_state=0 draws
                                       # the same rows every time the cell is run
    corner=True,                       # lower triangle only – the upper one would
                                       # show the same plots mirrored
    plot_kws={"s": 8, "alpha": 0.5},   # small (s = marker size), semi-transparent
                                       # points (alpha = 0.5), so dense regions
                                       # appear darker
)
plt.show()









Discussion. The pair plot is the most informative single figure for a small tabular dataset. Several observations stand out:

PE decreases almost linearly with ambient temperature AT – this is the strongest relationship in the data and has a clear physical explanation (air density and mass flow).
PE also decreases with the condenser pressure V, as expected from the plant (Figure 1.4).
AT and V are strongly correlated with each other – warm weather means warmer cooling water. Such correlated features (collinearity) make it hard to separate their individual effects – we will return to this in Chapter 5.
Ambient pressure and humidity show weaker, more diffuse relationships with the output.

We plotted a random sample of 1,000 points; with all 9,568 points the scatter plots would be overplotted. Sampling is a simple and legitimate trick for visual exploration – but never for computing the final statistics.

corr = df.corr()                      # Pearson correlation of every pair of columns
sns.heatmap(
    corr,
    annot=True, fmt=".2f",            # write each value into its cell, with 2 decimals
    cmap="RdBu_r",                    # diverging colour map: red = positive,
                                      # blue = negative (_r: reversed order of "RdBu")
    vmin=-1, vmax=1,                  # colour scale over the full range of r, so that
                                      # white always means r = 0
)
plt.title("Pearson correlation")
plt.show()














Definition: Pearson correlation coefficient



For two variables \(x\) and \(y\) with \(n\) observations, \[r_{xy} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \bar x)^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar y)^2}} \in [-1, 1].\] It measures the strength of a linear relationship: \(r = \pm 1\) means all points lie on a straight line, \(r = 0\) means no linear relationship.








Pitfall: correlation is not causation – and not every relationship is linear



A correlation near zero does not mean “no relationship”: \(y = x^2\) on a symmetric interval has \(r = 0\). And a strong correlation does not prove a causal effect: both variables may be driven by a third one. In the power plant, V correlates with PE partly because both depend on the ambient temperature.



1.6.1 A first simple model
To make the engineering question concrete, we fit the simplest possible model: a straight line for PE as a function of AT. We will treat regression properly in Chapter 5; here we only compare the line with the trivial baseline that always predicts the mean.

slope, intercept = np.polyfit(df["AT"], df["PE"], deg=1)   # least-squares straight line
                                                             # (polynomial of degree 1)
pred = intercept + slope * df["AT"]                          # predicted output for every hour
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((df["PE"] - pred) ** 2))              # root mean squared error
print(f"PE ≈ {intercept:.1f} MW {slope:+.2f} MW/°C · AT,   RMSE = {rmse:.1f} MW")
# The RMSE of the constant prediction "mean" is (almost exactly) the standard deviation.
print(f"Baseline 'always predict the mean': RMSE = {df['PE'].std():.1f} MW")

PE ≈ 497.0 MW -2.17 MW/°C · AT,   RMSE = 5.4 MW
Baseline 'always predict the mean': RMSE = 17.1 MW


The line explains most of the variation. Its typical error is measured by the root mean squared error (RMSE): the square root of the mean squared difference between measured and predicted output, in MW. Squaring makes large deviations count more than small ones. The RMSE of the line is a fraction of that of the trivial mean-value baseline. Each additional degree Celsius costs about two megawatts of output. Whether an error of a few MW is “good enough” is not a statistical question – it depends on the use case defined in CRISP-DM phase 1.
crumbs: 1  The Data Science Workflow in Engineering

title: 1  The Data Science Workflow in Engineering
text:
1.7 Back to the decision
In terms of CRISP-DM, this is phase 5, evaluation: we check the result against the criterion fixed in phase 1. The trading desk compares two rules for the committed output: the flat long-term average and the straight-line estimate from the ambient temperature. To turn the comparison into an economic decision, we use a deliberately simple cost model. All figures are assumptions for illustration:

Deviation cost: every MWh delivered more or less than committed costs 30 € extra. Generation and consumption in the grid must match at every moment, so the grid operator balances every deviation with short-term reserve power and settles it with the plant at the imbalance price: a shortfall has to be bought expensively, a surplus is paid poorly. (Real imbalance prices vary strongly from hour to hour and can be much higher.)
Operating hours: the plant runs at full load all 8,760 hours of a year – the data contain full-load hours only.
Cost of the new rule: a weather forecast service, implementation and maintenance cost 25,000 € per year.

The average deviation in MW – the mean absolute error (MAE) – times the number of hours gives the deviation in MWh per year, and times the price its cost. We switch if the annual savings exceed the annual cost of the new rule.

# Simple cost model – all figures are assumptions for illustration
price_dev = 30          # € per MWh of deviation (extra cost compared with an exact commitment)
hours = 8760            # full-load hours per year (simplification: the plant always runs)
cost_rule = 25_000      # € per year for the temperature-based rule: forecast service,
                        # implementation and maintenance

flat_commitment = df["PE"].mean()                                     # rule 1: long-term average
mae_flat = (df["PE"] - flat_commitment).abs().mean()                 # mean absolute error (MW)
mae_temp = (df["PE"] - (intercept + slope * df["AT"])).abs().mean()  # rule 2: straight line

# MW of deviation x hours = MWh of deviation per year; x price = cost per year
cost_flat = mae_flat * hours * price_dev
cost_temp = mae_temp * hours * price_dev
savings = cost_flat - cost_temp

print(f"Average deviation:  flat {mae_flat:5.1f} MW         temperature-based {mae_temp:5.1f} MW")
print(f"Deviation cost:     flat {cost_flat / 1e6:5.2f} M€ per year  temperature-based {cost_temp / 1e6:5.2f} M€ per year")
print(f"Savings: {savings / 1e6:.2f} M€ per year,  cost of the new rule: {cost_rule / 1e6:.3f} M€ per year")
if savings > cost_rule:                                               # criterion from phase 1
    print(f"Decision: switch to the temperature-based estimate "
          f"(net benefit {(savings - cost_rule) / 1e6:.2f} M€ per year).")
else:
    print("Decision: keep the flat commitment – the savings do not cover the costs.")

# How robust is the decision? Suppose the deviation of rule 2 doubled in operation.
savings_2x = (mae_flat - 2 * mae_temp) * hours * price_dev
print(f"Robustness: with twice the deviation, the savings would still be {savings_2x / 1e6:.2f} M€ per year.")

Average deviation:  flat  14.8 MW         temperature-based   4.3 MW
Deviation cost:     flat  3.90 M€ per year  temperature-based  1.13 M€ per year
Savings: 2.77 M€ per year,  cost of the new rule: 0.025 M€ per year
Decision: switch to the temperature-based estimate (net benefit 2.75 M€ per year).
Robustness: with twice the deviation, the savings would still be 1.65 M€ per year.


Two caveats belong in the recommendation to the team lead. First, we evaluated the rule on the same data we used to fit it; Chapter 6 shows how to evaluate on unseen data. Second, in operation the rule receives a temperature forecast, whose error adds to the error of the model. Both points make the real benefit smaller. The last line of the output shows how much room there is: even if the deviation of the temperature-based rule doubled in operation, the savings would still exceed the cost of the rule many times over. And the approach is not a textbook fiction: the plant that supplied the data uses such a model for its next-day commitment, with the temperature forecast of the national weather service as input, and reports a mean relative error below 2 % in operation (Tüfekci 2014).
The cost model is a simplification, too – Exercise 6 asks you to question it. Its value lies elsewhere: it turns “the error is smaller” into “the switch is worth this much per year”, which is the language in which the team lead has to decide.
crumbs: 1  The Data Science Workflow in Engineering

title: 1  The Data Science Workflow in Engineering
text:
1.8 Summary






Key takeaways




Data are recorded values of variables, observed on observational units, together with their context. Without unit and meaning, numbers cannot be interpreted – as the condenser pressure V shows.
Type and role of a variable determine which summaries and models make sense.
Start from the decision: every data science project starts with a precise engineering question and a clear criterion for success (CRISP-DM phase 1) – ideally expressed in money, as in the cost model of the power plant.
Know your data before you model them: info(), describe(), pair plots and correlations reveal structure and problems quickly.
Always compare a model with a simple baseline.

title: 1  The Data Science Workflow in Engineering
text:
1.9 Exercises


Which columns of the power plant data are features, which is the target? Which physical relationships between them do you expect, and which signs of the correlations follow from them?
Fit straight lines for PE against each of the four features separately and compare their RMSE. Which single feature is the best predictor? Does the ranking agree with the correlation matrix? Useful: np.polyfit(df[col], df["PE"], deg=1) in a loop over the four columns; collect the results as rows of a table (Getting Started with pandas).
Sketch the six CRISP-DM phases for a project from your own engineering background. Which phase do you expect to be the most difficult?
Place the following in Figure 1.2 (b) and justify: (a) a t-test whether a new supplier changes the scrap rate; (b) a convolutional neural network that detects cracks in X-ray images; (c) route planning for automated guided vehicles with the A* search algorithm; (d) a random forest that predicts tool breakage; (e) a straight line for power output vs. temperature with a confidence interval for the slope.
Which of the following are data in the sense of our definition? (a) The torque values logged by a screwdriving station for every screw joint; (b) the maximum torque in the screwdriver’s datasheet; (c) a table of thread friction coefficients computed with a formula from a handbook; (d) 10,000 lifetimes generated by a reliability simulation; (e) a column T with values between 280 and 320, without any further information.
Use the cost model from Back to the decision. (a) At which deviation price would the savings just cover the cost of the new rule (break-even)? (b) How large may the average deviation of the temperature-based rule become in operation before switching no longer pays off? (c) Which simplifications of the cost model would you question first, and in which direction would they change the result?



1.9.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1





The features are the ambient conditions AT, AP, RH and the condenser pressure V; the target is PE. Strictly speaking, V is not an ambient condition but a plant variable – it depends on the cooling water temperature and therefore also on the weather (Figure 1.4).
Expected signs: higher ambient temperature lowers air density and thus the mass flow and power of the gas turbine → negative correlation of AT with PE. A higher condenser pressure (worse vacuum, larger V in this dataset) reduces the pressure difference across the steam turbine → negative correlation of V with PE. Higher ambient pressure increases air density → positive correlation. Humidity has a smaller, less obvious effect. The correlation matrix confirms these signs.









Solution to Exercise 2






rows = []
for col in ["AT", "V", "AP", "RH"]:                       # one straight line per feature
    b1, b0 = np.polyfit(df[col], df["PE"], deg=1)         # slope b1, intercept b0
    rmse_col = np.sqrt(np.mean((df["PE"] - (b0 + b1 * df[col])) ** 2))
    rows.append({"feature": col, "slope": b1, "RMSE (MW)": rmse_col, "r": df[col].corr(df["PE"])})
pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("RMSE (MW)").round(3)      # best feature first

AT gives by far the smallest RMSE, followed by V. The ranking by RMSE is exactly the ranking by \(|r|\) – no coincidence: \(|r|\) measures how well a straight line describes the relationship. The closer the points lie to a line, the larger \(|r|\) and the smaller the error of the line; the sign of \(r\) only gives its direction. The original publication reports practically the same values (Tüfekci 2014).









Solution to Exercise 3





There is no single correct answer. A good sketch states a concrete decision in phase 1 (e.g. “decide weekly which tools to replace”), names the data sources and their owners in phase 2, lists expected preparation steps in phase 3 (merging, time alignment), names a baseline in phase 4, an evaluation criterion tied to the decision in phase 5 (e.g. cost of unplanned stops), and a realistic deployment path in phase 6. Many practitioners name phase 2/3 (data access and quality) or phase 6 (deployment and acceptance) as the hardest.









Solution to Exercise 4





(a) Statistics – inference about a difference with quantified uncertainty, no prediction task.
(b) Deep learning (and thus ML and AI) – a neural network learns features from raw images.
(c) AI without machine learning – A* is a search algorithm; nothing is learned from data.
(d) Machine learning – a flexible model optimised for predictive accuracy; it is not deep learning.
(e) The overlap of statistics and machine learning: the same linear model, used here in the statistical way (interpretation of the slope and its uncertainty). Used purely to predict output for the day-ahead market and validated on test data, it would be viewed as machine learning.
The examples show that the method alone does not determine the category – the purpose matters too.









Solution to Exercise 5





(a) Data – recorded observations of real screw joints (provided we know the unit and which joint each value belongs to).
(b) Not data – a specification of what the tool is designed for, not an observation.
(c) Not data about any real joint – the table only re-expresses the formula; a model fitted to it would rediscover the formula.
(d) Data about a model – valid observations of the simulation; conclusions hold for real products only as far as the simulation is valid.
(e) Not usable as data – the numbers might be temperatures in kelvin, but without unit, sensor and time stamp they cannot be interpreted. They become data once the context is recovered.









Solution to Exercise 6






# (a) price at which the savings equal the cost of the rule
price_break = cost_rule / ((mae_flat - mae_temp) * hours)
# (b) deviation of rule 2 at which the savings equal the cost of the rule
mae_break = mae_flat - cost_rule / (hours * price_dev)
print(f"(a) break-even price:     {price_break:.2f} € per MWh (assumed: {price_dev} € per MWh)")
print(f"(b) break-even deviation: {mae_break:.1f} MW (today: {mae_temp:.1f} MW, flat rule: {mae_flat:.1f} MW)")

(a) break-even price:     0.27 € per MWh (assumed: 30 € per MWh)
(b) break-even deviation: 14.7 MW (today: 4.3 MW, flat rule: 14.8 MW)


(a) Even a deviation price far below 1 € per MWh would cover the cost of the rule – real prices are much higher.
(b) The rule pays off as long as it is even slightly better than the flat commitment: the break-even deviation lies only about 0.1 MW below that of the flat rule. With well over 100,000 MWh of deviation per year, even small improvements are worth a lot of money.
(c) For example:

The two directions are not equally expensive. The plant runs at full load, and its output depends on the weather. If it is cooler than expected and the plant could deliver more than committed, it simply throttles its output or sells the surplus in short-term trading – it loses revenue but pays no penalty. If it is warmer than expected and the plant delivers less, it cannot ramp up: the missing energy has to be bought at the imbalance price. A shortfall therefore usually costs more than a surplus, and the best commitment lies deliberately somewhat below the forecast – a safety margin. Chapter 12 meets the same idea when predicting the remaining useful life of engines.
The imbalance price depends on the state of the grid and varies from hour to hour.
The plant does not run at full load in every hour (maintenance, partial load), so fewer hours mean smaller savings.
The forecast error of the temperature increases the deviation of the new rule.
The cost of the new rule may be underestimated (staff time, IT).

None of these is likely to reverse the decision here – but in a project with a smaller margin, each of them could.

title: 2  Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Quality
text:
2.1 Reading raw data
Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the systematic first look at a dataset before any model is built. Its purpose is twofold: to understand the structure of the data – distributions, relationships, patterns over time – and to find problems – gaps, outliers, implausible values, inconsistencies. In engineering, many failed data science projects can be traced back to data problems that a careful EDA would have revealed.
The statistician John Tukey, who coined the term, put it this way: EDA is detective work. We look for clues without knowing in advance what we will find. The tools are simple – summary statistics and plots – but using them well requires domain knowledge.
In terms of the CRISP-DM process from Chapter 1, EDA is the core of phase 2, data understanding. The original CRISP-DM model names four tasks for this phase, and this chapter follows them: collect the data (Section 2.1), describe them (Section 2.2), explore them (Section 2.3) and verify their quality (Section 2.4 and Section 2.5). The findings determine what happens in phase 3, data preparation – which outliers to keep, how to fill gaps, which sensors to drop. And they often lead back to phase 1: can the question be answered with these data at all? The scenario of this chapter is exactly such a decision.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Course goal. This chapter contributes to step 2 of the course goals: check and prepare the data.
Datasets in this chapter
Before data can be described, they have to be read – and read correctly. Real measurement data rarely come as a ready-made table: they arrive as text files with their own separators, codes for missing values and time formats. This section reads a sensor dataset with an unusual time format; Exercise 1 reads a raw file from a weather service, with a code for missing values and time stamps in UTC. First, the usual setup:
# Setup (as in every chapter): install packages that are not pre-installed in
# Google Colab or Anaconda, then import the standard data stack.
import importlib.util, subprocess, sys
for pkg in ["ucimlrepo"]:
    if importlib.util.find_spec(pkg) is None:        # package not found?
        subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", pkg], check=True)

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")                     # common style for all plots

title: 2  Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Quality
text:
2.1.1 Live coding: the energy data of a house
Our first dataset accompanies us through the next three sections. It was recorded in a low-energy house in Belgium. A wireless sensor network measured temperature and humidity at nine places – in eight rooms and outside the building – as 10-minute averages for about 4.5 months; the electricity consumption of the appliances was logged by an energy meter, and outdoor weather was taken from a nearby airport. Key columns:








Column
Meaning
Unit




Appliances
energy use of appliances in the 10-minute interval
Wh


lights
energy use of light fixtures
Wh


T1 … T9, RH_1 … RH_9
temperature and relative humidity in the rooms; T6, RH_6 outside the building (north side)
°C, %


T_out, RH_out, Windspeed, …
outdoor weather
various


rv1, rv2
random numbers, added deliberately by the authors as a test
–



The columns rv1 and rv2 were not measured: the authors added random numbers on purpose, to test their models. The idea: a variable that a model rates no better than random numbers is probably useless. A careful analysis should therefore find that rv1 and rv2 carry no information about the energy use (Exercise 3).

from ucimlrepo import fetch_ucirepo

appl = fetch_ucirepo(id=374)                       # Appliances Energy Prediction (UCI)
energy = appl.data.original.copy()                 # whole table incl. time, as a copy

raw = energy["date"].astype(str).str.strip()       # look at the raw time stamps first ...
print("Raw time stamps:", raw.head(3).tolist())    # first three, as a plain list
# ... then parse them with the matching format. In the version served by UCI, date and
# time are glued together without a blank: "2016-01-1117:00:00" = 11 January 2016, 17:00.
# If the output above shows a blank between date and time, use "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S".
energy["date"] = pd.to_datetime(raw, format="%Y-%m-%d%H:%M:%S")
# Two steps in one line ("method chaining"): set_index() returns a new table,
# and sort_index() is applied directly to it (more in the Python reference, appendix).
energy = energy.set_index("date").sort_index()     # time as index, in chronological order

# rows and columns, first and last time stamp:
print(energy.shape, energy.index.min(), "to", energy.index.max())
# isna() gives True where a value is missing; True counts as 1, so sum() counts
# the missing values per column, and the second sum() adds up all columns:
print("Missing values:", energy.isna().sum().sum())
# Regular grid? A complete 10-minute grid from the first to the last time stamp has this
# many time stamps; if the table had fewer rows, some time steps would be missing.
full_grid = pd.date_range(energy.index.min(), energy.index.max(), freq="10min")
print("Rows:", len(energy), "| complete 10-min grid:", len(full_grid), "time stamps")

Raw time stamps: ['2016-01-1117:00:00', '2016-01-1117:10:00', '2016-01-1117:20:00']
(19735, 28) 2016-01-11 17:00:00 to 2016-05-27 18:00:00
Missing values: 0
Rows: 19735 | complete 10-min grid: 19735 time stamps








Pitfall: letting the software guess date formats



Is 03/04/2016 the 3rd of April or the 4th of March? If you let pandas guess, it may parse some time stamps one way and others the other way – or fail on a single unusual entry. Always look at the raw strings and give the format explicitly. If a column mixes several formats, as in the SECOM data below, state at least the order of day and month (dayfirst=True) and check the range of the result. An explicit format has a second advantage: if it does not fit even a single time stamp, pandas stops with an error message that shows this time stamp – much better than a date that is silently read the wrong way.


The time stamps of this dataset are a real-world surprise: in the version served by the UCI repository, date and time are glued together without a blank. pandas cannot guess this format – but the explicit format %Y-%m-%d%H:%M:%S reads it without problems.
Checking that the time index is regular is a quick but important test. Gaps in the time grid are “hidden” missing values: df.isna() does not see them because the rows do not exist at all.






Good practice: downloading and reading raw files




Keep the raw file untouched. Never correct values by hand in the file. Every step from the raw file to the clean table is code – so anyone can repeat it, including you next semester.
Download once, keep a copy – e.g. with the helper download() in the solution to Exercise 1. Check that the download succeeded (raise_for_status()); otherwise an error page may be stored as “data”.
Note source and version: URL, download date, version. Many sources are updated: the DWD weather data of Exercise 1 cover roughly the last 500 days and change daily, so the same code can give slightly different results next month.
Read the documentation first: separator, decimal mark, missing value code, units, time format and time zone. Weather services usually deliver UTC, production data are often in local time with daylight saving time – a common source of one-hour shifts.
State everything explicitly instead of letting pandas guess: sep=";", decimal="," (numbers with a decimal comma, common in German files), na_values=[-999], format= for time stamps.
Check right after reading: df.head(), df.info(), df.describe(). A numeric column of type str (object in pandas versions before 3.0) contains at least one text entry; a table with only one column or unexpectedly many missing values points to a wrong separator or code.









Engineering practice: data from databases



In companies, engineering data often come from databases rather than files – process data from a historian, quality and order data from a manufacturing execution system. They are read with SQL: a few commands such as SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY and JOIN cover most needs, and pd.read_sql loads the result directly into pandas. The questions of this section remain the same: units, missing values (in SQL: NULL) and time zones. Appendix C gives a short introduction.
