title: 2  Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Quality
text:
2.2 Describing distributions
Which description fits a single variable depends on its type (Chapter 1):

A categorical variable is described by the frequencies of its categories – counts or shares – and shown in a bar chart. The most frequent category is called the mode. For an ordinal variable, the median is meaningful as well (quality class M lies in the middle), the mean is not.
A numeric variable is described by its location (where are the values?), its spread (how much do they vary?) and its shape (symmetric, skewed, multimodal?).

Engineering data are mostly numeric, and so is the rest of this section. A categorical example – the pass/fail label of this chapter’s scenario – follows in Section 2.5.






Definition: Location and spread



For numeric observations \(x_1, \dots, x_n\):

Mean \(\bar x = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i\) and median (the middle value of the sorted data).
Sample standard deviation \(s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}\).
Quantiles: the \(p\)-quantile is the value below which a share \(p\) of the sorted data lies. The median is the 50 % quantile; the quartiles \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) are the 25 % and 75 % quantiles. Together with the median, they divide the data into four parts with 25 % of the values each. The interquartile range \(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\) is the width of the middle half of the data.
Median absolute deviation: with the median \(\tilde x = \operatorname{median}(x_1, \dots, x_n)\), \[\text{MAD} = \operatorname{median}\big(|x_1 - \tilde x|, \dots, |x_n - \tilde x|\big),\] i.e. the median of the absolute deviations from the median.



Mean and standard deviation are sensitive to extreme values: a single wrong reading of \(10^6\) can dominate both. Median, IQR and MAD are robust: they barely change if a few values are wrong. For engineering data, where sensor glitches are common, it pays to look at both and compare them.
Reading a histogram. A histogram divides the range of values into intervals of equal width (bins) and shows how many values fall into each; tall bars mark frequent values (Figure 2.1, top). The number of bins changes the picture: too few hide details, too many make it noisy – trying two or three settings is worthwhile.
Reading a box plot. Figure 2.1 shows how the quartiles divide a skewed dataset and how a box plot summarises it. The box spans the middle half of the data from \(Q_1\) to \(Q_3\) – its width is the IQR – and the line inside marks the median. The whiskers reach to the smallest and largest values that lie no more than 1.5 IQR outside the box; values beyond are drawn individually as candidates for outliers (Section 2.4). The skewness is visible at a glance: the right part of the box and the right whisker are longer than the left ones. A box plot hides details of the shape – two peaks, for example, are invisible – but it is compact and ideal for comparing several groups side by side. In pandas, describe() reports the quartiles as 25%, 50% and 75%.






Figure 2.1: Quartiles divide the data into four parts with 25 % of the values each (top); the box plot summarises the same data (bottom).









Which plot for which question?




Frequencies of a categorical variable: bar chart – sorted by frequency, or in the natural order of an ordinal variable.
Distribution of a numeric variable: histogram (shape) or box plot (compact, good for comparing groups).
Relationship between two variables: scatter plot; with many points use transparency or a random sample (Chapter 1).
Development over time: line plot, possibly with a rolling mean (Section 2.3).
Patterns over two time scales (hour of day × weekday): heatmap.
Many variables at once: correlation heatmap, pair plot of a subset.




2.2.1 Live coding: appliance energy use
The target variable of the energy dataset is the energy use of the appliances. Histogram and box plot show its distribution:


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))         # two plots side by side
sns.histplot(energy["Appliances"], bins=60, ax=axes[0])  # histogram with 60 bins (left)
axes[0].set(xlabel="Appliances (Wh per 10 min)")
sns.boxplot(x=energy["Appliances"], ax=axes[1])          # box plot (right); x= draws it horizontally
axes[1].set(xlabel="Appliances (Wh per 10 min)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()                           # tight_layout: avoid overlapping labels
energy["Appliances"].describe().round(1)                 # the same distribution in numbers









count    19735.0
mean        97.7
std        102.5
min         10.0
25%         50.0
50%         60.0
75%        100.0
max       1080.0
Name: Appliances, dtype: float64


Discussion. The distribution is strongly right-skewed: most of the time the consumption is low (base load from fridge, standby), but occasionally it rises sharply (cooking, washing machine). Consequently, the mean is clearly larger than the median, and the box plot flags many points as “outliers” (Section 2.4). Here these are not measurement errors but real usage events – deleting them would remove the most interesting part of the data.
For skewed, positive quantities a log transformation often helps: it makes the distribution more symmetric and turns multiplicative effects into additive ones.
crumbs: 2  Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Quality

title: 2  Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Quality
text:
2.3 Patterns over time
Engineering data are mostly time series. Besides the distribution of each variable, its development over time matters: trends, cycles, sudden steps. Two tools help to see them in noisy data. A rolling mean (moving average) replaces every value by the mean of a window of neighbouring values – below, the preceding 24 hours. Short peaks are averaged out, the level remains, and every time stamp keeps its own value. At the start of the series, fewer than 24 hours are available; pandas then averages over the values it has, so the first hours are smoothed less. Resampling instead combines all values of an interval into one value, e.g. from 10 minutes to hours. Figure 2.2 shows the difference on a small example.






Figure 2.2: Resampling and rolling mean on the same small time series: resample forms fixed intervals and returns one value per interval; rolling moves a window along the time axis and returns one value per time stamp.









resample or rolling?



Rule of thumb: one value per period → resample; same time stamps, but smoother → rolling.

resample when the question needs a coarser time grid: daily energy, monthly maximum, hourly load. It is also the tool to bring series with different time steps onto a common grid – e.g. hourly electricity load and hourly weather data as daily values (Chapter 11) – and to reduce large datasets. Choose the summary per variable: sum for energies and counts, mean for temperatures (Exercise 2).
rolling when every time stamp should be kept, but short fluctuations hide the level or trend: smoothing a plot, or monitoring – “has the mean of the last hour exceeded the limit?”. Because the window only looks back, the rolling mean at each time uses only past values and can be computed in real time; rolling means of the past are also common inputs for forecasting models.




2.3.1 Live coding: daily and weekly profiles
First the whole measurement period: the 10-minute values of the appliance energy use with a 24-hour rolling mean, and the indoor and outdoor temperature as hourly means – temperatures change slowly, so hourly values keep the daily cycle and make the plot lighter:


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 6), sharex=True)   # two plots, one time axis
# top: 10-minute values (thin, transparent line) and their 24-hour rolling mean
energy["Appliances"].plot(ax=axes[0], lw=0.3, alpha=0.6, label="10 min")
# rolling("1D") defines a window of one day that slides along the time axis; mean() then
# computes the mean of each window - one smoothed value per time stamp. Same pattern as
# resample(): first define the windows, then summarise them.
smooth = energy["Appliances"].rolling("1D").mean()
smooth.plot(ax=axes[0], color="k", label="24 h rolling mean")
axes[0].set(ylabel="Appliances (Wh)"); axes[0].legend()
# bottom: indoor and outdoor temperature, resampled from 10 minutes to hourly means
energy[["T1", "T_out"]].resample("h").mean().plot(ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set(ylabel="Temperature (°C)")
plt.show()









The rolling mean reveals the level of consumption over time. Indoor temperature T1 is much more stable than the outdoor temperature – as expected for a well-insulated building.
Consumption depends on human behaviour, so we expect patterns over the hour of the day and the day of the week. This needs a different kind of grouping than resample: not consecutive days, but all Mondays together and all values at 8 a.m. together – no matter in which week. This is what groupby() does (Getting Started with pandas), here with two keys at once: hour and weekday. pivot_table combines this grouping with arranging the result as a table – one row per hour, one column per weekday, one mean per cell. A heatmap then shows the table:


Code
# pivot_table groups by two keys and arranges the means as a table:
# 24 hours (rows) x 7 weekdays (columns) = 168 groups, one mean consumption each.
hour = energy.index.hour.rename("hour")                  # 0, ..., 23
weekday = energy.index.dayofweek.rename("weekday")       # 0 = Monday, ..., 6 = Sunday
profile = energy.pivot_table(values="Appliances",        # mean consumption ...
                             index=hour,                 # ... with one row per hour
                             columns=weekday,            # ... and one column per weekday
                             aggfunc="mean")
sns.heatmap(profile, cmap="viridis",                      # colour = mean consumption
            cbar_kws={"label": "mean Appliances (Wh)"})   # label of the colour bar
plt.xlabel("Day of week (0 = Monday)"); plt.ylabel("Hour of day")
plt.show()









Discussion. Low consumption at night and a peak in the early evening (about 17–19 h) on every day – a typical residential profile. The heatmap also shows how the two time scales work together: between about 10 and 16 h, consumption is high on Monday, Friday and Saturday, lower on Sunday and lowest from Tuesday to Thursday – apparently the house is empty on these days. The effect of the hour of day thus depends on the weekday, an interaction. A model that simply adds a daily profile and a weekday effect would miss it. Be careful, though: the dataset covers only 4.5 months, so each cell is the mean of only about 20 days, and a single day with unusual use – a laundry day, a party – can shape a cell. Patterns that extend over several hours and days are more trustworthy than a single bright cell. Hour of day and weekday – and their interaction – are strong features for forecasting (Chapter 11).

title: 2  Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Quality
text:
2.4 Data quality and outliers
Measured data pass through a long chain – sensor, signal conditioning, A/D conversion, data logger, database, export – and every link can introduce errors. Typical problems:








Problem
Typical cause
How to detect




Missing values
sensor dropout, logging gap, value not measured for every product
df.isna(), gaps in the time index (Section 2.5)


Outliers
real rare event or measurement error
box plot, IQR rule, robust z-score


Implausible values
sensor fault, wrong scaling
physical limits (e.g. humidity > 100 %)


Frozen values
sensor stuck, communication lost
long runs of identical values


Coarse resolution
A/D converter or logger rounds values (e.g. to 0.1 K)
many identical values, gaps in the histogram


Wrong units / time stamps
°C vs. K, local time vs. UTC
domain knowledge, comparison of sources (Section 2.1)


Drift and offsets
sensor ageing, recalibration
trends, steps in the time series



Two of these problems need more than a quick check: outliers, treated in this section, and missing values (Section 2.5).






Definition: Outlier rules




IQR rule (Tukey): a value is flagged if it lies below \(Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR}\) or above \(Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}\). These limits determine the whiskers of the box plot (Figure 2.1): values beyond them are drawn individually.
Robust z-score: \(z_i = \dfrac{x_i - \tilde x}{1.4826 \cdot \text{MAD}}\), flag if \(|z_i| > 3.5\), where \(\tilde x\) is the median. The factor 1.4826 makes MAD comparable to the standard deviation for normally distributed data.



For normally distributed data, the two rules set their limits at different distances from the centre (Figure 2.3): the IQR rule at about 2.7 standard deviations, the robust z-score at 3.5. Even data in which every value is valid therefore contain “outliers” – 0.7 % with the IQR rule, 0.05 % with the robust z-score. Flagged does not mean wrong.






Figure 2.3: Limits of the two outlier rules for normally distributed data. Left: density and box plot – the whiskers end exactly at the IQR limits. Right: the right tail, enlarged; the coloured areas are the shares flagged on this side.









Extension: where does the factor 1.4826 come from?





The robust z-score should measure distances in the same unit as the ordinary z-score – the standard deviation \(\sigma\) – but without being disturbed by outliers. The MAD is robust, but for normally distributed data it is smaller than \(\sigma\): half of all values lie within \(\pm 0.6745\,\sigma\) of the median (these are the quartiles, Figure 2.1), so the median of the absolute deviations is \(\text{MAD} = 0.6745\,\sigma\). Dividing by 0.6745, i.e. multiplying by \(1/0.6745 = 1.4826\), turns the MAD into an estimate of \(\sigma\): \(\sigma \approx 1.4826 \cdot \text{MAD}\). For normal data, \(|z| > 3.5\) therefore means “more than 3.5 standard deviations from the median”.



The ordinary z-score \((x_i - \bar x)/s\) is less suitable for outlier detection: the outliers themselves inflate \(\bar x\) and \(s\) and can hide each other (masking).






Pitfall: deleting “outliers” automatically



An outlier is a value that is unusual with respect to a model of the data – it is not automatically an error. The rare high current peaks of a motor may be exactly the events that announce a failure. Never delete data before you understand why they are extreme, and always document what you removed.



2.4.1 Live coding: outliers in the energy data
We apply both rules to the appliance energy use and to three variables with roughly symmetric distributions:

def iqr_outliers(x, k=1.5):
    """IQR rule: True for values more than k * IQR below Q1 or above Q3."""
    q1, q3 = x.quantile([0.25, 0.75])                # first and third quartile
    iqr = q3 - q1                                    # interquartile range
    return (x < q1 - k * iqr) | (x > q3 + k * iqr)

def robust_z_outliers(x, limit=3.5):
    """Robust z-score rule: True for values with |z| > limit."""
    mad = (x - x.median()).abs().median()            # median absolute deviation
    z = (x - x.median()) / (1.4826 * mad)            # robust z-score of every value
    return z.abs() > limit

for col in ["Appliances", "T1", "T_out", "RH_1"]:
    x = energy[col]
    share_iqr = iqr_outliers(x).mean()               # mean of True/False = share of flagged values
    share_z = robust_z_outliers(x).mean()
    print(f"{col:11s} IQR rule: {share_iqr:6.1%}   |robust z| > 3.5: {share_z:6.1%}")

Appliances  IQR rule:  10.8%   |robust z| > 3.5:  11.2%
T1          IQR rule:   2.6%   |robust z| > 3.5:   0.2%
T_out       IQR rule:   2.2%   |robust z| > 3.5:   0.3%
RH_1        IQR rule:   0.7%   |robust z| > 3.5:   0.2%


Discussion. Both rules flag about 11 % of Appliances, but for the temperatures the IQR rule flags far more than the robust z-score – for T1, 2.6 % instead of 0.2 %. Its limits lie closer to the centre (Figure 2.3), and real data with heavier tails than the normal distribution – like the room temperature – raise both shares, the IQR rule’s more. How many values count as “outliers” is therefore partly a choice of rule and threshold.
The decisive question is what the flagged values are. When do the flagged values of Appliances occur?


Code
flag = iqr_outliers(energy["Appliances"])                # True for flagged values
share = flag.groupby(energy.index.hour).mean()           # share of flagged values per hour of day
ax = share.plot.bar(rot=0, xlabel="Hour of day", ylabel="Share flagged by IQR rule")
plt.show()









Between midnight and 6:00, almost no value is flagged; during the day, about 15–20 % of the values are, and at 18:00 a third of them – the same pattern as in the heatmap (Section 2.3). They are cooking, washing, ironing: real usage, not measurement errors. Decision: keep them. Deleting them would remove exactly the events a forecast of the energy use has to predict. The skewness that makes them look extreme is better handled by a log transformation (Exercise 4).
Two general hints. For strongly skewed data, transform first and then apply a rule. For multimodal data – e.g. a machine with an idle and a full-load mode – apply the rule separately for each mode (groupby): a global rule judges every value against a mixture of modes, so a faulty value in the idle mode can look perfectly normal. In the end, the flags tell us where to look; the engineer decides what the values mean.






Engineering practice: removing values that are errors



If a value is clearly an error – physically impossible, or caused by a known sensor fault – remove it in code, never in the raw file (Section 2.1), and document what you removed:
bad = (df["RH_1"] < 0) | (df["RH_1"] > 100)       # physically impossible values
print(bad.sum(), "values removed")                 # always document what was removed
df["RH_1"] = df["RH_1"].mask(bad)                  # set these values to NaN, keep the rows
Dropping the rows instead (df[~bad]) is simple, but it also removes the valid values of the other columns and leaves holes in the time grid. For time series, mask is usually better: the row stays, only the wrong value becomes a missing value – to be treated like any other gap (Section 2.5).

title: 2  Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Quality
text:
2.5 Missing data
Almost every real dataset has gaps. How to treat them depends less on how many values are missing than on why they are missing. Statisticians distinguish three mechanisms. Because the names are notoriously confusing, we explain them with one running example.
Example: a hardening furnace. A thermocouple measures the furnace temperature once per minute; the target is about 850 °C. The actual temperature depends on the load: a fully loaded furnace runs hotter than a nearly empty one. The load is logged reliably by the control system. Now suppose that some temperature values are missing. Three different reasons are possible:

The radio link drops messages at random. About 10 % of the readings are lost, regardless of load, temperature or time of day. Whether a value is missing has nothing to do with the process.
The logger runs in an energy-saving mode at low load. When the furnace is nearly empty, only every fifth reading is stored. Missing values are therefore much more frequent at low load – and since low load means lower temperatures, the missing values tend to be the lower ones. But the reason for the gap (low load) is itself recorded in the data.
The amplifier saturates above 900 °C. Whenever the furnace gets too hot, the measurement fails and nothing is stored. The values are missing because they are high. The load gives a hint – very hot readings occur at high load – but it cannot tell us which readings actually exceeded 900 °C.







Definition: Missing data mechanisms



Let \(R\) indicate whether a value is missing.

MCAR (missing completely at random): \(R\) does not depend on any variable, observed or unobserved. Case 1 – random radio losses.
MAR (missing at random): \(R\) depends only on observed variables. Once we know those (here: the load), the missingness tells us nothing more about the missing value: at a given load, the missing temperatures do not differ from the recorded ones. Case 2 – energy-saving mode at low load.
MNAR (missing not at random): \(R\) depends on the missing value itself (or on other unobserved quantities), even after accounting for everything observed. Case 3 – saturation at high temperatures.









Pitfall: “missing at random” is not random



The name MAR is misleading: in case 2 the values are not missing randomly – low temperatures are missing much more often. “At random” only means “random once we take the observed variables into account”. Do not read MAR as “harmless”.


Whether gaps are MAR or MNAR depends on what is recorded: had the load not been logged, case 2 would be MNAR. It therefore pays to log quantities that may explain gaps – operating mode, load, sensor status.
What the mechanism means in practice:








Mechanism
Mean of the remaining values
What helps




MCAR
unbiased – we just have fewer values
deleting incomplete rows is acceptable – only the sample gets smaller; filling gaps with the mean keeps the mean unbiased, but makes the spread look too small


MAR
biased (case 2: too high, because low values are missing)
use the observed variable that explains the gaps – e.g. impute temperature from load with a regression, or average per load level


MNAR
biased (case 3: too low, because high values are missing)
the data alone cannot fix it; we need knowledge of the mechanism – e.g. “missing means above 900 °C”: such a value is censored, known only to lie beyond a limit – or a better sensor



Exercise 5 simulates the furnace and shows these effects in numbers. Beyond the table, common strategies in practice:

drop variables with a very high share of missing values,
for time series: interpolate short gaps, but not long ones,
add an indicator variable “value was missing” – missingness itself can be informative,
above all: find out why the values are missing – ask the people who run the process.


2.5.1 Live coding: gaps in semiconductor data
The dataset of the scenario, SECOM, contains data from a semiconductor manufacturing process: 1,567 production runs, each described by 590 sensor and process measurements, a time stamp and a label pass (−1) or fail (1). The sensor names are anonymised. Many signals have gaps. A small obstacle on the way: the repository’s metadata do not say which column is the label – its variable list is empty, another example of incomplete metadata. A look at the table shows two special columns, timestamp and class; we name them in the code ourselves.

secom = fetch_ucirepo(id=179).data.original          # all columns of the dataset
# Besides the 590 measurements, the table has two special columns: "timestamp" (time
# of the run) and "class" (the label: -1 = pass, 1 = fail). We name them explicitly.
y = secom["class"].astype(int)                       # the label, as whole numbers
X = secom.drop(columns=["timestamp", "class"])       # all other columns: measurements

missing = X.isna().mean().sort_values(ascending=False)   # share of missing values per feature
print(f"Runs: {len(X)}, failed runs: {(y == 1).sum()}")
print(f"Features: {X.shape[1]}, with any missing value: {(missing > 0).sum()}, "
      f"more than 50 % missing: {(missing > 0.5).sum()}")
missing.plot.hist(bins=40, xlabel="Share of missing values per feature")   # how are the shares distributed?
plt.show()

Runs: 1567, failed runs: 104
Features: 590, with any missing value: 538, more than 50 % missing: 28









The label is a categorical – more precisely, a binary – variable. As explained in Section 2.2, it is described by the frequencies of its two categories:

label = y.map({-1: "pass", 1: "fail"})        # readable category names instead of codes
counts = label.value_counts()                 # frequency of each category
print(counts.to_string())
print(f"Share of failed runs: {counts['fail'] / counts.sum():.1%}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))        # a small figure of its own
counts.plot.bar(ax=ax, rot=0, ylabel="number of runs")   # bar chart; rot=0: horizontal labels
plt.show()

class
pass    1463
fail     104
Share of failed runs: 6.6%









Only about one run in fifteen failed. For the decision, this share matters more than the number of sensors: a model can only learn what a failure looks like from the failed runs, and rare events are hard to learn from (Chapter 7).


Code
# Is the missingness itself related to the outcome?
miss_rate = X.isna().mean(axis=1)                  # axis=1: share of missing values per run (row)
print(miss_rate.groupby(y).describe().round(3))    # compare passed (-1) and failed (1) runs

# Constant features carry no information
n_constant = (X.nunique(dropna=True) <= 1).sum()   # at most one different value (gaps ignored)
print("Constant features:", n_constant)


        count   mean    std    min    25%    50%    75%    max
class                                                         
-1     1463.0  0.046  0.023  0.007  0.034  0.041  0.054  0.258
 1      104.0  0.043  0.017  0.014  0.034  0.041  0.047  0.108
Constant features: 116


Discussion. Most features are complete or nearly complete, but a group of features has a large share of missing values – often entire sensors that were only recorded for part of the runs. In addition, a considerable number of features are constant and can be removed without loss. Comparing the share of missing values between passed and failed runs is a quick check of whether missingness could be informative: if the shares differ, the gaps are not MCAR. Here they are similar – no sign that the gaps carry information about the outcome, although this does not prove MCAR.

title: 2  Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Quality
text:
2.6 Back to the decision
In CRISP-DM terms, this is the step back from phase 2 to phase 1: what we learned about the data decides whether and how the project continues. For a go/no-go recommendation, three questions matter: Are enough features usable? Are there enough examples of the event we want to predict? And are the gaps understood? We fix simple, transparent criteria before looking at the result: at least half of the features should be usable, and there should be at least 50 failed runs to learn from. A feature counts as usable if the middle half of its values is not identical – its IQR is larger than zero (Section 2.2) – and if at most 20 % of its values are missing. These thresholds are not general rules but a judgement for this question; another project may need others. What matters is to state them openly and to check whether the decision depends on them.
Before applying these criteria, one more check that uses the time stamps of the runs: is the failure rate stable over the recording period?

# The time stamps come in two formats: "19/07/2008 11:55:00" and, later, "1/8/2008 2:02"
# (no leading zeros, no seconds) - both with the day first. No single format fits both, so
# format="mixed" reads each time stamp on its own; dayfirst=True fixes the order of day and month.
time = pd.to_datetime(secom["timestamp"], format="mixed", dayfirst=True)
print("Period:", time.min(), "to", time.max())       # check: plausible range?

runs = pd.DataFrame({"time": time, "fail": y == 1}).set_index("time")   # one row per run
weekly = runs["fail"].resample("W").agg(["mean", "count"])   # failure rate and runs per week
print(weekly.round(3).to_string())
ax = weekly["mean"].plot(marker="o", ylabel="Share of failed runs per week")
plt.show()

Period: 2008-07-19 11:55:00 to 2008-10-17 06:07:00
             mean  count
time                    
2008-07-20  0.231     13
2008-07-27  0.095     21
2008-08-03  0.208     48
2008-08-10  0.130    108
2008-08-17  0.137     51
2008-08-24  0.106    208
2008-08-31  0.041    169
2008-09-07  0.015    133
2008-09-14  0.042     95
2008-09-21  0.032    154
2008-09-28  0.024    166
2008-10-05  0.089    169
2008-10-12  0.058    138
2008-10-19  0.011     94









The failure rate is not stable: in July and August, 10–20 % of the runs failed, from September on mostly only 1–4 %. The process has obviously changed during the recording – perhaps it was improved. A model could therefore learn when failures happened instead of why, and it must be tested on runs that are later than those it was trained on (Chapter 11). Note also the number of runs per week: the first two weeks contain only 13 and 21 runs, so their rates are uncertain.
All findings of this chapter, sorted by the four tasks of CRISP-DM phase 2:








Task
Finding
Consequence




Collect
metadata incomplete: label column not documented, sensor names anonymised; time stamps in two formats
clarify meaning and units of the sensors with the fab


Describe
104 failed runs (6.6 %)
few examples of the event: keep models simple, evaluate carefully (Chapter 7)


Explore
failure rate falls from 10–20 % (July, August) to 1–4 % (from September)
ask the fab what changed; train on earlier, test on later runs (Chapter 11)


Verify quality
116 constant and further nearly constant features, 28 with more than 50 % gaps; similar share of gaps in passed and failed runs
remove these features; clarify the cause of the gaps with the process engineers



Outliers are deliberately not part of this check. With 590 anonymised sensors, nobody can say whether an extreme value is a measurement error or a real process state (Section 2.4), and an automatic rule would flag many values that no one can judge. This becomes possible only once the sensors have names and units – one more reason for the first consequence.
The two criteria from above, in code:

# A feature is usable if its IQR is larger than zero and at most 20 % of its values are missing.
iqr = X.quantile(0.75) - X.quantile(0.25)          # interquartile range of every feature
usable = (iqr > 0) & (X.isna().mean() <= 0.2)
n_fail = int((y == 1).sum())                       # number of failed runs
print(f"Usable features: {usable.sum()} of {X.shape[1]} ({usable.mean():.0%})")
print(f"Failed runs: {n_fail} of {len(y)} ({n_fail / len(y):.1%})")
if usable.mean() >= 0.5 and n_fail >= 50:          # the two criteria from the text
    print("Decision: GO – with a data-quality work package in the first project phase.")
else:
    print("Decision: NO-GO for now – improve data acquisition first.")

Usable features: 432 of 590 (73%)
Failed runs: 104 of 1567 (6.6%)
Decision: GO – with a data-quality work package in the first project phase.


The result hardly depends on the thresholds: with more lenient criteria (not constant, at most 50 % missing – Exercise 6), 446 features would count as usable instead of 432. Whatever the code prints, the recommendation should name the conditions: the sensor names are anonymised, so no process engineer can yet judge which signals are physically relevant; the missing values must be explained (are they MAR or MNAR?); the drop of the failure rate in September must be explained; and roughly one hundred failures is a small number for a problem with hundreds of candidate features. Whether the usable features are also informative about failures is a different question: it belongs to the modelling phase and needs careful validation (Chapters 6 and 9). With 590 features and only 104 failures, some features will look informative by pure chance. Chapter 9 will show how hard the prediction actually is. These conditions are at the same time the tasks for the next round of the CRISP-DM cycle: with better-understood data, phases 2 and 3 are passed through again.






EDA toolbox



The functions used most in this chapter – all of them, with examples, in the Python quick reference (Appendix A):

overview: df.info(), df.describe(), df.head(), df.nunique()
missing values: df.isna().sum(), df.fillna(...)
time stamps: pd.to_datetime(..., format=...), df.set_index(...), s.resample(...), s.rolling(...)
groups and summaries: df.groupby(...).mean(), s.median(), s.quantile(...)
masks and selection: df[m], &, |, ~
plots: sns.histplot, sns.boxplot, sns.heatmap

title: 2  Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Quality
text:
2.7 Summary






Key takeaways




Read raw files deliberately: separator, missing value code, time format, units and time zone are documented in the metadata.
Describe distributions by location, spread and shape; compare classical (mean, s) and robust (median, IQR, MAD) statistics.
Know your data before you model them: check data quality systematically – missing values, gaps in time, implausible values, frozen sensors, outliers.
Outlier rules flag candidates – domain knowledge decides whether they are errors or important events.
The treatment of missing data depends on the mechanism (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) – and whether gaps are MAR or MNAR depends on what else is measured.

title: 2  Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Quality
text:
2.8 Exercises


Reading a raw weather file. The German Weather Service (DWD) publishes hourly air temperatures as raw files: a zip archive with metadata files and a semicolon-separated data file whose name starts with produkt. Missing values are coded as -999, and the time stamps are integers such as 2025041113 (year, month, day, hour) in UTC. Load the data of station Trier-Petrisberg from https://opendata.dwd.de/climate_environment/CDC/observations_germany/climate/hourly/air_temperature/recent/stundenwerte_TU_05100_akt.zip.

Read the data file with the correct separator and missing value code, convert the time stamps and count the missing values.
Determine type and role (Chapter 1) of each column of the raw file for the question “How does the air temperature in Trier vary over the day?”.
Compute the mean temperature per hour of the day. At which hour is it warmest – and does the result change if you convert the time stamps from UTC to German local time?

Useful: pd.read_csv(f, sep=";", na_values=[-999]), pd.to_datetime(s.astype(str), format="%Y%m%d%H"), df.tz_localize("UTC").tz_convert("Europe/Berlin"). To use a station near your home town, look it up in the station list.
Resample the energy data to hourly values. Which aggregation (mean, sum, max, last) is correct for Appliances, which for the temperatures? Explain. Useful: df.resample("h").agg({column: summary, ...}) applies one summary per column.
Show that the random columns rv1 and rv2 carry no information about Appliances. Compare their correlation with that of the outdoor temperature. Useful: df[cols].corrwith(s) correlates several columns with one series.
Compare the IQR rule and the robust z-score for Appliances after a log transformation, np.log(energy["Appliances"]). How many values are flagged now? What does this tell you about the “outliers” in the original scale? Useful: the functions iqr_outliers and robust_z_outliers from the live coding.
How missing values bias a mean. Simulate the hardening furnace of Section 2.5: 10,000 readings, the load uniformly distributed between 0 and 1, the temperature \(820 + 80 \cdot \text{load}\) °C plus normally distributed noise with a standard deviation of 15 K. Delete values according to the three mechanisms – MCAR: 10 % at random; MAR: with probability \(0.8\,(1 - \text{load})\); MNAR: all values above 900 °C – and compare mean and standard deviation with the truth after three treatments: dropping the gaps, filling them with the median of the remaining values, and filling them from the load with a straight line fitted on the complete rows. Which treatment works for which mechanism? Useful: rng = np.random.default_rng(0), rng.uniform(0, 1, n), rng.normal(0, 15, n), np.where(m, a, b), np.polyfit(x, y, deg=1).
(Extension) For SECOM: propose a strategy for features with 0–5 %, 5–50 % and more than 50 % missing values. Then implement a simple preparation: remove constant features, remove features with more than 50 % missing values and impute the remaining gaps with the median. How many features remain? Useful: X.loc[:, m] keeps the columns where the mask m is True; X.fillna(X.median()).



2.8.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1






A small helper function downloads the archive on the first run and keeps a copy in the folder data; every later run reads this copy. The data file is the one whose name starts with produkt:


from pathlib import Path
import requests

DATA = Path("data")
DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)                         # create the folder ./data if it does not exist

def download(url, fname=None):
    """Download a file once and cache it in ./data."""
    if fname is None:                             # no file name given:
        fname = url.split("/")[-1]                # use the last part of the URL
    path = DATA / fname                           # "/" joins folder and file name
    if not path.exists():                         # download only if not cached yet
        r = requests.get(url, timeout=120)        # give up after 120 s without response
        r.raise_for_status()                      # stop with an error if the download failed
        path.write_bytes(r.content)               # open, write and close the file in one step
    return path


import zipfile

# The URL is long; we build it from three parts with "+":
server  = "https://opendata.dwd.de/climate_environment/CDC/observations_germany/"
product = "climate/hourly/air_temperature/recent/"   # hourly air temperature, recent data
fname   = "stundenwerte_TU_05100_akt.zip"           # 05100 = station ID of Trier-Petrisberg
url = server + product + fname

with zipfile.ZipFile(download(url)) as z:       # open the archive (closed after the block)
    print(z.namelist())                         # what is inside?
    # The data file is the one whose name starts with "produkt". Its full name contains
    # the dates of the measurement period and changes daily, so we search for it:
    for n in z.namelist():
        if n.startswith("produkt"):
            name = n
            break                               # found: stop searching
    dwd = pd.read_csv(z.open(name),             # read the file directly from the archive
                      sep=";",                  # columns are separated by semicolons

                      skipinitialspace=True)    # ignore blanks after each separator

dwd.columns = dwd.columns.str.strip()           # remove blanks around the column names

The raw table has cryptic column names (TT_TU = air temperature in °C, RF_TU = relative humidity in %, QN_9 = quality level). STATIONS_ID and QN_9 are stored as numbers but are codes, i.e. categorical variables (Chapter 1). The second cell turns MESS_DATUM into real time stamps, uses them as the index and gives the columns meaningful names (format codes such as %Y: Appendix A).
The output reports a few missing hours – the former -999 codes, now NaN. The metadata file Metadaten_Fehldaten_… in the archive lists every gap with its start, end and number of missing hours. This is useful in two ways. First, it is a check: if our count of NaN agrees with the official count, we have read the file correctly. Second, it shows the structure of the gaps – at the time of writing, one isolated hour and one block of 18 consecutive hours. A single hour can be interpolated safely, a long block cannot (Section 2.5). What the file does not tell is why the values are missing: its column for a description is empty. To find out, one would have to ask the data provider.




STATIONS_ID: categorical (nominal) – a code, although stored as a number; constant within the file.
MESS_DATUM: time stamp – numeric (differences are durations); after conversion, the index of the time series.
QN_9: categorical – a code for the quality level of the record. Whether the levels are ordered must be looked up in the DWD documentation; computing a mean is meaningless either way.
TT_TU: continuous (°C) – the variable of interest for this question; there is no target, because nothing is predicted.
RF_TU: continuous (%) – not needed for this question.
eor: not a variable at all – a marker for “end of record” in each line of the file.


The DWD time stamps are in UTC (stated in the metadata file Metadaten_Parameter_…). Declare this with tz_localize, then convert to German time:

cycle = pd.DataFrame({                                    # mean temperature per hour of day
    "UTC": weather.groupby(weather.index.hour)["temp_C"].mean(),
    "local time": local.groupby(local.index.hour)["temp_C"].mean(),
})
ax = cycle.plot(marker="o")

The maximum typically occurs in the early or mid afternoon. In local time the curve is shifted by one hour in winter and two hours in summer, so the hour of the maximum changes accordingly. This is exactly the kind of shift that causes errors when weather data are merged with production data recorded in local time.
Another station: Open the station list in a browser or read it with pandas, find your station and replace 05100 in the file name. The file name of the recent product always has the form stundenwerte_TU_<ID>_akt.zip, where <ID> is the five-digit station ID with leading zeros. Not all stations measure all variables – if the file does not exist, choose a neighbouring station.

After the log transformation, fewer values are flagged – 6.5 % instead of 10.8 % with the IQR rule – but still many, almost all of them on the high side: the usage peaks remain unusual even on the log scale. Part of the “outliers” on the original scale was simply the long right tail of a skewed distribution, the rest are real usage events. Outlier rules implicitly assume a roughly symmetric distribution – applying them to skewed data without transformation flags normal behaviour.









Solution to Exercise 5






# --- 1. Simulate the "true" furnace data ------------------------------------------
# A random number generator with a fixed start value (seed = 0): every run produces
# the same random numbers, so the results in the script are reproducible.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

n = 10_000                                   # number of readings (_ only for readability)
load = rng.uniform(0, 1, n)                  # load between 0 (empty) and 1 (full); always recorded
noise = rng.normal(0, 15, n)                 # random scatter, standard deviation 15 K
temp = 820 + 80 * load + noise               # true temperature: 820 °C empty, 900 °C full

# --- 2. Delete values according to the three mechanisms ---------------------------
# Each mask is an array of n truth values: True means "this reading is missing".
# rng.random(n) draws n numbers between 0 and 1; "< p" is True with probability p.
missing = {
    "MCAR": rng.random(n) < 0.10,               # random radio losses: always 10 %
    "MAR":  rng.random(n) < 0.8 * (1 - load),   # energy-saving mode: 80 % if empty, 0 % if full
    "MNAR": temp > 900,                         # saturation: missing because hot
}

# --- 3. Treat the gaps in three ways and compare with the truth --------------------
rows = []
for name, m in missing.items():              # name = mechanism, m = mask of missing values
    obs = ~m                                 # ~ negates the mask: True means "value observed"
    # straight line temperature vs. load, fitted on the observed readings only
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(load[obs], temp[obs], deg=1)
    # np.where(m, a, b): where a value is missing (m is True) take a, otherwise b
    filled_median = np.where(m, np.median(temp[obs]), temp)            # fill with the median
    filled_line = np.where(m, intercept + slope * load, temp)          # fill from the load
    for treatment, values in [("drop gaps", temp[obs]),
                              ("median", filled_median),
                              ("regression", filled_line)]:
        rows.append({"mechanism": name, "treatment": treatment,
                     "mean (°C)": values.mean(),
                     "std (K)": values.std(ddof=1)})   # ddof=1: divide by n - 1, as for s

print(f"Truth: mean {temp.mean():.1f} °C, standard deviation {temp.std(ddof=1):.1f} K")
print("Share missing:", ", ".join(f"{name} {m.mean():.0%}" for name, m in missing.items()))
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(1)

Read the table treatment by treatment:

Dropping the gaps keeps the mean unbiased only under MCAR. Under MAR it is too high, because the cooler low-load readings are under-represented; under MNAR it is too low, because the hottest readings are missing.
Filling with the median of the remaining values looks like a repair, but it is none. It hardly changes the mean (filling with the mean would not change it at all), so the bias under MAR and MNAR remains completely. On top of that, the spread shrinks, because all gaps receive the same value: under MAR, the standard deviation drops from 27.5 K to 20.2 K. Every later analysis would consider the process more stable than it is.
Regression imputation uses the load, which explains why values are missing. Under MAR, it repairs the mean completely and almost restores the spread. Under MNAR, it removes only part of the bias: the line was fitted on readings below 900 °C and cannot know what happens above the saturation limit.

Even regression imputation slightly underestimates the spread, because the filled-in values lie exactly on the line, without the scatter of real readings. A few degrees may not sound like much – but for a heat treatment with a tolerance of ±10 °C, they can decide whether a batch is released.

Strategy: 0–5 % missing → median imputation (little influence on results); 5–50 % → median or model-based imputation plus an indicator variable “was missing”; more than 50 % → remove the feature, unless domain experts know that it is important (then investigate why it is missing). In a real project the imputation would be fitted on the training data only (Chapter 6).

title: 3  Probability and Uncertainty
text:
3.1 Random variables and distributions
No two measurements are identical, no two components have the same lifetime, and every estimate computed from a sample would come out slightly differently with another sample. Engineers deal with this variability every day – in tolerances, safety factors, reliability targets and maintenance plans. Probability theory provides the language to describe it, and statistics provides the tools to quantify how certain our estimates are.
In this chapter we model the lifetimes of jet engines with a probability distribution, derive reliability figures such as the B10 life, and quantify the uncertainty of our estimates with confidence intervals – computed both with a classical formula and with the bootstrap. Finally, Bayes’ theorem shows how a probability changes when new information arrives.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Course goal. This chapter contributes to step 3 of the course goals: quantify effects and uncertainty.
Datasets in this chapter
In SciPy, every distribution offers these functions as methods:
ppf (percent point function) is SciPy’s name for the quantile function – it reverses cdf. We will use it often: the B10 life is ppf(0.10) of a lifetime distribution, and Q–Q plots compare the data with ppf values.
In reliability engineering, \(X\) is the lifetime of a component, and the variable of the CDF is written \(t\) for time. The same CDF, \(F(t) = P(X \le t)\), is then the probability that the component has failed by time \(t\), and the reliability (survival function) \(R(t) = 1 - F(t) = P(X > t)\) is the probability that it is still working.
Choosing a distribution is a modelling decision, guided by physics and by the data:
Figure 3.1 shows their typical shapes. The Weibull distribution – probably the least familiar of them, but the most important one for lifetimes – is explained in detail in the next section.
The prominence of the normal distribution is explained by one of the most important results of probability theory:
Two consequences matter for engineers. First, the uncertainty of a mean decreases with \(1/\sqrt{n}\) – four times as many measurements halve the uncertainty.
Second, the theorem explains why so many measured quantities are approximately normal. A machined diameter results from many small, independent effects – tool wear, temperature, clamping, material. Their sum is approximately normal even if the effects are not identically distributed, as long as none of them dominates. If a single large effect dominates – a worn tool, two different machine settings – the distribution takes on its shape and can be skewed or have two peaks.

title: 3  Probability and Uncertainty
text:
Definition: Random variable, CDF, PDF and quantile function



A random variable \(X\) assigns a number to the outcome of a random experiment, e.g. the lifetime of a component. For a continuous random variable,

the cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(F(x) = P(X \le x)\) gives the probability of a value up to \(x\),
the probability density function (PDF) \(f(x) = F'(x)\) describes how probability is distributed,
the probability of an interval follows from either of them: \[P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx.\] For a continuous random variable, a single value has probability 0, so it does not matter whether the limits are included,
the quantile function \(F^{-1}(p)\) gives the value below which a share \(p\) of the distribution lies – the counterpart of the sample quantiles in Chapter 2; \(F^{-1}(0.5)\) is the median.

The expected value \(E[X] = \int x\,f(x)\,dx\) is the long-run average, the variance \(\text{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]\) measures the spread.
A discrete random variable – a count such as the number of defects – takes only separate values \(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) Instead of a density, it has probabilities \(P(X = k)\), and sums replace the integrals; the CDF is defined in the same way.

Theorem: Central limit theorem



Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be independent random variables with the same distribution, mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\). Then the distribution of the sample mean \(\bar X_n\) approaches a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) as \(n\) grows – whatever the distribution of the \(X_i\).





3.1.1 Live coding: sums and products of many effects
Two simulated quantities make the difference visible. Both result from the same ten small, independent effects, which are uniformly distributed – flat, not bell-shaped – and of different size, none of them dominating. For the diameter of a turned shaft, the effects are added to the nominal value of 25 mm as a few micrometres each. For the fatigue life of a component, the same effects act as factors between about 0.6 and 1.4 on a nominal life of 100,000 cycles.

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)                         # random generator with fixed seed
n_parts = 100_000                                      # number of simulated parts
# Ten independent effects per part: uniformly distributed between -1 and 1 (not normal!).
u = rng.uniform(-1, 1, size=(n_parts, 10))             # rows = parts, columns = effects
width = np.linspace(1, 5, 10)                          # different sizes of the effects, none dominates

diameter = 25.0 + (0.001 * width * u).sum(axis=1)      # additive: 25 mm PLUS effects of 1-5 µm
life = 1e5 * (1 + 0.08 * width * u).prod(axis=1)       # multiplicative: 100,000 cycles TIMES factors
print(f"Fatigue life: mean {life.mean():,.0f}, median {np.median(life):,.0f} cycles")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.5))      # three histograms side by side
sns.histplot(diameter, bins=80, ax=axes[0])            # sum of the effects
axes[0].set(title="Sum: diameter (mm)")
sns.histplot(life / 1000, bins=80, ax=axes[1])         # product of the effects, in thousands of cycles
axes[1].set(title="Product: fatigue life (1,000 cycles)")
sns.histplot(np.log(life), bins=80, ax=axes[2])        # the same product on a log scale
axes[2].set(title="Product on a log scale: ln(life)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Fatigue life: mean 99,960, median 89,547 cycles









Discussion. Although every single effect is flat, the sum of ten of them is practically normal: the diameter scatters symmetrically by a few micrometres around 25 mm. The same effects, applied as factors, give a right-skewed fatigue life: half of the components reach between about 64,000 and 125,000 cycles, a few far more, and the mean lies clearly above the median. On a logarithmic scale, the product becomes a sum again, \(\ln X = \ln Z_1 + \dots + \ln Z_n\), and the histogram is normal: the life is lognormally distributed.
In practice, the question is therefore whether the effects shift a quantity by a fixed amount or change it by a percentage. Machining errors add micrometres; surface quality or stress level shorten a fatigue life by a factor, and each grinding step breaks a particle into a random fraction of its size. Multiplicative quantities are always positive and right-skewed, and their spread is relative (“±30 %”): large values scatter more than small ones. On a logarithmic scale they become normal – this is why the log transformation helped for the skewed energy data in Chapter 2.

title: 3  Probability and Uncertainty
text:
3.2 The Weibull distribution for lifetimes
Here the random variable \(X\) is the lifetime of a unit: the operating time until it fails – measured in hours, or as a count such as load cycles or, for our engines, flight cycles. \(F(t) = P(X \le t)\) is the probability that a unit has failed by time \(t\); in a large fleet, it is the share of units that have failed by then.
The two-parameter Weibull distribution has the CDF and the hazard rate – the instantaneous failure rate of the survivors, in reliability engineering also simply called the failure rate –
\[F(t) = 1 - \exp\left[-\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^{\beta}\right], \qquad h(t) = \frac{f(t)}{R(t)} = \frac{\beta}{\eta}\left(\frac{t}{\eta}\right)^{\beta - 1}.\]
Where does \(h(t)\) come from? Of the units still working at time \(t\), a share
\[P(t < X \le t + \Delta t \mid X > t) = \frac{F(t + \Delta t) - F(t)}{R(t)} \approx \frac{f(t)\,\Delta t}{R(t)}\]
fails in a short interval \(\Delta t\). Per unit of time, this is \(h(t) = f(t)/R(t)\). Both count the same failures in the interval, but relate them to different groups: \(f(t)\,\Delta t\) is the failing share of all units put into service, \(h(t)\,\Delta t\) the failing share of the units still running at \(t\). Example: of 1,000 lamps, 800 still work after 100 hours, and 5 fail in the next hour. Then \(f \approx 5/1000 = 0.5\,\%\) per hour, but \(h \approx 5/800 \approx 0.63\,\%\) per hour. For maintenance, \(h\) is the relevant quantity: it tells how risky the next hour is for a unit that is still running.
The scale parameter \(\eta\) is the characteristic life: by \(t = \eta\), 63.2 % of all units have failed, regardless of \(\beta\). The shape parameter \(\beta\) determines how the failure rate changes over time:






Interpretation of the Weibull shape parameter




\(\beta < 1\): decreasing failure rate – early failures (manufacturing defects, infant mortality).
\(\beta = 1\): constant failure rate – random failures; the Weibull becomes the exponential distribution.
\(\beta > 1\): increasing failure rate – wear-out (fatigue, corrosion, abrasion). For \(\beta \approx 3.5\), the density is nearly symmetric (Figure 3.1), although the hazard rate keeps increasing.

Together, the three regimes form the well-known bathtub curve of a product’s life.








Figure 3.2: Left: Weibull hazard rate for different shape parameters. Right: the bathtub curve of a product’s life as the superposition of early failures, random failures and wear-out.



The shape parameter has direct consequences for maintenance: preventive replacement only makes sense if the failure rate increases (\(\beta > 1\)). With \(\beta \le 1\), a new part is not more reliable than an old one, and replacing it early wastes money.
A frequently used reliability figure is the B10 life: the time by which 10 % of the units have failed, i.e. \(F(B_{10}) = 0.1\). Solving the Weibull CDF gives
\[B_{10} = \eta\,\left(-\ln 0.9\right)^{1/\beta}.\]

3.2.1 Estimating parameters: maximum likelihood






Definition: Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)



Given independent observations \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) and a model with density \(f(x;\theta)\), the likelihood \(L(\theta) = \prod_i f(x_i;\theta)\) measures how plausible the observed data are for a parameter value \(\theta\). For discrete data, the probabilities \(P(X = x_i;\theta)\) take the place of the density. The maximum likelihood estimate \(\hat\theta\) maximises \(L\), in practice its logarithm \(\ell(\theta) = \sum_i \ln f(x_i;\theta)\) – the logarithm turns the product into a sum and does not move the maximum.


The likelihood is a function of the parameter; the data are fixed. A small example: five parts of a batch are inspected, and the second and the fifth are defective. If \(p\) is the unknown defect probability, a single part is defective with probability \(p\) and OK with probability \(1 - p\) – a Bernoulli distribution. Both cases fit into one formula, \(P(Y = y) = p^{\,y}(1-p)^{1-y}\), with \(y = 1\) for defective and \(y = 0\) for OK. The likelihood of the five results is \[L(p) = (1-p) \cdot p \cdot (1-p) \cdot (1-p) \cdot p = p^2\,(1-p)^3.\]



\(p\)
0.2
0.3

0.6




\(L(p)\)
0.020
0.031
