0.023



\(L\) is largest at \(p = 0.4\): the maximum likelihood estimate is the observed share of defective parts, 2 of 5. Chapter 7 fits a classifier with the same likelihood.
For the normal distribution, MLE gives the familiar mean, \(\hat\mu = \bar x\). Its estimate of the standard deviation divides by \(n\) instead of \(n - 1\) and is therefore slightly smaller than the sample standard deviation \(s\) of Chapter 2 – a difference without practical consequences. For the Weibull distribution, there is no closed-form solution; scipy.stats.weibull_min.fit maximises the likelihood numerically.
To check whether the fitted distribution describes the data, we use a probability plot, also called a Q–Q plot (quantile–quantile plot). It compares the data with the model point by point, in three steps:

Sort the \(n\) observations. The \(i\)-th smallest value has a share of about \(p_i = (i - 0.5)/n\) of the data below it – every observation is an empirical quantile. (The \(-0.5\) places each value in the middle of its share \(1/n\) and avoids \(p = 1\), whose model quantile would be infinite.)
For the same shares, compute the quantiles of the fitted distribution, \(F^{-1}(p_i)\) – in SciPy with ppf.
Plot each pair: the model quantile on the x-axis, the observed value on the y-axis.

If the model fits, every observed quantile is close to the model quantile, and the points lie on the diagonal \(y = x\). Typical deviations have typical shapes (Figure 3.3). They matter most at the ends: a histogram shows the tails only vaguely, the Q–Q plot shows every single value – and the lower tail is exactly where reliability figures such as the B10 life are decided.






Figure 3.3: Idealised Q–Q plots for typical deviations between data and a normal model. A point above the diagonal means: at this share, the data are larger than the model expects; below: smaller.

title: 3  Probability and Uncertainty
section: 3.3 Live coding: lifetimes of turbofan engines
text:
3.3 Live coding: lifetimes of turbofan engines
C-MAPSS (Commercial Modular Aero-Propulsion System Simulation) is a NASA simulation of a large turbofan engine. The dataset contains run-to-failure trajectories of a fleet of engines with different initial wear and manufacturing variation. In the training file train_FD001.txt, every one of the 100 engines runs until failure, so the last recorded cycle of each engine is its lifetime (in flight cycles). We will use the sensor data of the same file in Chapter 12.
Data access. The cell below downloads CMAPSSData.zip (about 12 MB) from the NASA Open Data Portal once and reads train_FD001.txt directly from the archive. The file has one row per engine and flight cycle, with the columns separated by blanks and no header line. The helper function download() – the same as in the solution to Exercise 1 of Chapter 2 – fetches the file on the first run and keeps a copy in the folder data; every later run reads this copy, and the other chapters use the same helper.

# Download helper: fetch a file once and keep a copy in the folder ./data
from pathlib import Path
import requests

DATA = Path("data")
DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)                         # create the folder ./data if it does not exist

def download(url, fname=None):
    """Download a file once and cache it in ./data."""
    if fname is None:                             # no file name given:
        fname = url.split("/")[-1]                # use the last part of the URL
    path = DATA / fname                           # "/" joins folder and file name
    if not path.exists():                         # download only if not cached yet
        r = requests.get(url, timeout=300)        # give up after 300 s without response
        r.raise_for_status()                      # stop with an error if the download failed
        path.write_bytes(r.content)               # open, write and close the file in one step
    return path


import zipfile

url = "https://data.nasa.gov/docs/legacy/CMAPSSData.zip"
# Column names: engine number, cycle, three operating settings, 21 sensors
cols = ["unit", "cycle", "op1", "op2", "op3"] + [f"s{i}" for i in range(1, 22)]

with zipfile.ZipFile(download(url)) as z:         # open the archive (closed after the block)
    train = pd.read_csv(z.open("train_FD001.txt"),  # read the file directly from the archive
                        sep=r"\s+",               # columns are separated by blanks
                        header=None, names=cols)  # the file has no header line

lifetimes = train.groupby("unit")["cycle"].max()  # last cycle of each engine = its lifetime
lifetimes.describe().round(1)

count    100.0
mean     206.3
std       46.3
min      128.0
25%      177.0
50%      199.0
75%      229.2
max      362.0
Name: cycle, dtype: float64


Fitting in SciPy. Every SciPy distribution has a location loc, which shifts it along the axis, and a scale scale, which stretches it. Most distributions have an additional shape parameter. For the normal distribution, loc and scale are simply \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\). For the Weibull distribution, the shape is \(\beta\), scale is \(\eta\), and loc is a failure-free time \(t_0\): the distribution then starts at \(t_0\) instead of 0 (formula in the model decision below). SciPy calls the Weibull distribution weibull_min: it describes the minimum of many independent lifetimes – the weakest link. fit() estimates all parameters by default; floc=0 fixes the location at 0 (f for fixed). This gives the two-parameter Weibull distribution introduced above.

# fit() returns shape, location and scale; floc=0 fixes the location at 0
beta, loc, eta = stats.weibull_min.fit(lifetimes, floc=0)
print(f"Weibull fit: shape beta = {beta:.2f}, scale eta = {eta:.1f} cycles")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))       # left: histogram, right: probability plot
t = np.linspace(0, lifetimes.max() * 1.1, 300)        # time axis for the fitted density
axes[0].hist(lifetimes, bins=15, density=True, alpha=0.6, label="data")  # density=True: same scale as the pdf
axes[0].plot(t, stats.weibull_min.pdf(t, beta, scale=eta), label="Weibull fit")  # fitted density
axes[0].set(xlabel="Lifetime (cycles)", ylabel="Density"); axes[0].legend()
# Probability plot in three steps
n = len(lifetimes)
p = (np.arange(1, n + 1) - 0.5) / n                   # 1. share below the i-th smallest value
model_q = stats.weibull_min.ppf(p, beta, scale=eta)   # 2. quantiles of the fitted Weibull distribution
axes[1].scatter(model_q, np.sort(lifetimes), s=12)    # 3. model quantile vs. observed lifetime
axes[1].axline((0, 0), slope=1, color="k", lw=1)      # diagonal y = x: perfect fit
axes[1].set(xlim=(50, 380), ylim=(50, 380))           # same range on both axes
axes[1].set(xlabel="Weibull quantile (cycles)", ylabel="Observed lifetime (cycles)",
            title="Probability plot (Weibull)")
plt.show()

Weibull fit: shape beta = 4.41, scale eta = 225.0 cycles









Discussion. We fixed the location parameter at zero (floc=0), i.e. we use the two-parameter Weibull distribution. The estimated shape parameter is clearly larger than 1 – the engines show wear-out behaviour, as expected for a degradation simulation. In the probability plot, the points follow the diagonal in the middle. At the lower end, they lie clearly above it: the shortest observed lifetime is 128 cycles, whereas the fitted model expects about 68 cycles for the shortest of 100 engines. The data contain fewer early failures than the Weibull model – in the lower tail, which determines the B10 life, the model is on the safe side. At the upper end, the points lie above the diagonal, too: a few engines live longer than the nearly symmetric Weibull distribution (\(\beta \approx 4.4\)) allows.
Note that no engine fails very early: the shortest lifetime is well above zero. A three-parameter Weibull distribution with a failure-free time (location parameter \(t_0 > 0\)) could describe this better – the next section compares it with other candidates.

b10 = stats.weibull_min.ppf(0.10, beta, scale=eta)   # B10 = 10 % quantile: the time by which 10 % have failed
print(f"B10 life from the fit:    {b10:.0f} cycles")
print(f"B10 from the formula:     {eta * (-np.log(0.9)) ** (1 / beta):.0f} cycles")  # eta (-ln 0.9)^(1/beta)
print(f"Empirical 10 % quantile:  {lifetimes.quantile(0.10):.0f} cycles")           # directly from the data

B10 life from the fit:    135 cycles
B10 from the formula:     135 cycles
Empirical 10 % quantile:  155 cycles



3.3.1 Which distribution? A model decision
The B10 life of the fitted model, 135 cycles, is clearly lower than the empirical 10 % quantile of 155 cycles – the consequence of the misfit in the lower tail. Since the B10 life decides the overhaul interval, the choice of the distribution matters. We compare four candidates: the two-parameter Weibull distribution from above, the lognormal and the normal distribution, and a three-parameter Weibull distribution with a failure-free time \(t_0\). Its CDF is the two-parameter CDF shifted by \(t_0\) – \(t\) is simply replaced by \(t - t_0\): \[F(t) = \begin{cases} 0, & t \le t_0, \\ 1 - \exp\left[-\left(\dfrac{t - t_0}{\eta}\right)^{\beta}\right], & t > t_0. \end{cases}\] No unit fails before \(t_0\); after \(t_0\), \(\beta\) and \(\eta\) play the same role as before, with time measured from \(t_0\) instead of from 0.
Besides the Q–Q plots, we compare the candidates with a single number:






Definition: Akaike information criterion (AIC)



A model with more parameters can adapt more closely to the data, so its maximised log-likelihood \(\ell(\hat\theta)\) is almost always higher – even if the extra parameter only fits noise. The AIC therefore adds a penalty for each of the \(k\) fitted parameters: \[\mathrm{AIC} = 2k - 2\,\ell(\hat\theta).\] Smaller is better, and only differences between models fitted to the same data are meaningful. Rule of thumb (Burnham and Anderson): models less than 2 above the best AIC are about equally well supported, models more than 10 above have essentially no support. The same idea – goodness of fit minus a penalty for complexity – returns as the adjusted \(R^2\) in Chapter 5.
AIC only ranks the candidates; it does not show that any of them fits. Always look at the Q–Q plot, too.



# Four candidate models, each fitted by maximum likelihood. fit() returns the parameters
# as a tuple; *params passes them on to ppf one by one. The last entry is the number k of
# fitted parameters for the AIC (a location fixed with floc=0 is not fitted, so it does not count).
candidates = [
    ("Weibull (2 parameters)", stats.weibull_min, stats.weibull_min.fit(lifetimes, floc=0), 2),
    ("Weibull (3 parameters)", stats.weibull_min, stats.weibull_min.fit(lifetimes), 3),  # free t0
    ("lognormal", stats.lognorm, stats.lognorm.fit(lifetimes, floc=0), 2),
    ("normal", stats.norm, stats.norm.fit(lifetimes), 2),
]
n = len(lifetimes)
p = (np.arange(1, n + 1) - 0.5) / n                     # shares, as in the probability plot above
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 4))         # one Q–Q plot per candidate
for ax, (name, dist, params, k) in zip(axes, candidates):
    ax.scatter(dist.ppf(p, *params), np.sort(lifetimes), s=10)   # model quantile vs. observed
    ax.axline((0, 0), slope=1, color="k", lw=1)                 # diagonal y = x
    ax.set(xlim=(50, 380), ylim=(50, 380), title=name, xlabel="model quantile (cycles)")
    loglik = dist.logpdf(lifetimes, *params).sum()              # maximised log-likelihood
    print(f"{name:23s} B10 = {dist.ppf(0.10, *params):3.0f} cycles   AIC = {2 * k - 2 * loglik:6.1f}")
axes[0].set_ylabel("observed lifetime (cycles)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"Empirical 10 % quantile: {lifetimes.quantile(0.10):.0f} cycles")   # for comparison
beta3, t0, eta3 = candidates[1][2]                      # parameters of the 3-parameter Weibull
print(f"3-parameter Weibull: shape {beta3:.2f}, failure-free time t0 = {t0:.0f}, scale {eta3:.0f} cycles")

Weibull (2 parameters)  B10 = 135 cycles   AIC = 1065.5
Weibull (3 parameters)  B10 = 152 cycles   AIC = 1039.0
lognormal               B10 = 154 cycles   AIC = 1038.9
normal                  B10 = 147 cycles   AIC = 1054.0









Empirical 10 % quantile: 155 cycles
3-parameter Weibull: shape 1.83, failure-free time t0 = 125, scale 91 cycles


Discussion. Three criteria lead to a decision:

Fit where it matters. The B10 life is decided in the lower tail. There, the two-parameter Weibull and, to a lesser extent, the normal distribution deviate from the diagonal. The three-parameter Weibull and the lognormal distribution follow the data closely, and their B10 lives (152 and 154 cycles) agree with the empirical 10 % quantile (155 cycles). The AIC confirms the picture: the three-parameter Weibull and the lognormal distribution are practically tied (1039.0 and 1038.9), the normal distribution (1054.0) and the two-parameter Weibull distribution (1065.5) are far behind. Between the two good candidates, statistics cannot decide.
Physics. In C-MAPSS, the engines degrade gradually from a small initial wear; a failure needs time to develop. A failure-free time is therefore plausible: the three-parameter Weibull distribution estimates \(t_0 \approx 125\) cycles, and indeed no engine failed before cycle 128. Its shape parameter, \(\beta \approx 1.8\), still indicates wear-out after \(t_0\).
Consequences. The choice is worth about 17 cycles of B10 – more than 10 % of the overhaul interval. That two well-fitting models agree gives confidence; the poorly fitting two-parameter model would be needlessly conservative.

We therefore use the three-parameter Weibull distribution from now on. A model with one more parameter always fits at least as well. Here the extra parameter is justified: the gain in likelihood is far larger than the AIC penalty, the parameter has a physical meaning, and it changes the result substantially.

title: 3  Probability and Uncertainty
text:
3.4 Confidence intervals
The mean lifetime we computed is an estimate from 100 engines. Another fleet of 100 engines would give a somewhat different value. A confidence interval quantifies this sampling uncertainty.






Definition: Confidence interval



A 95 % confidence interval is computed from the data by a procedure that, if the experiment were repeated many times, would contain the true parameter in 95 % of the repetitions.


For the mean, the central limit theorem provides such a procedure. The sample mean \(\bar X\) is approximately normal around the true mean \(\mu\), with standard deviation \(\sigma/\sqrt n\) – the standard error of the mean. In general, the standard error of an estimate is the standard deviation with which the estimate would vary from sample to sample if the experiment were repeated with new data. For a normal distribution, 95 % of the values lie within \(\pm 1.96\) standard deviations of the mean (1.96 is the 97.5 % quantile computed above). So in 95 % of all samples, \(\bar x\) lies within \(\pm 1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt n\) of \(\mu\). Turned around: in 95 % of all samples, the interval \(\bar x \pm 1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt n\) contains \(\mu\).
In practice, \(\sigma\) is unknown and replaced by the sample standard deviation \(s\). This adds uncertainty: in a small sample, \(s\) may by chance come out too small, and the interval would be too narrow. The t-distribution accounts for this. It was published in 1908 by W. S. Gosset, a chemist at the Guinness brewery, under the pseudonym “Student”. For normal data, the standardised mean \((\bar X - \mu)/(s/\sqrt n)\) follows a t-distribution: bell-shaped like the standard normal distribution, but with heavier tails. Its shape is controlled by the degrees of freedom \(n - 1\) – one less than \(n\), because \(s\) measures the spread around the mean estimated from the same data (the reason why pandas’ std() divides by \(n - 1\)). With growing \(n\), the t-distribution approaches the standard normal distribution:



sample size \(n\)
5
10
30
100
\(\infty\)




97.5 % quantile \(t_{n-1,\,0.975}\)
2.78
2.26
2.05
1.98
1.96









Confidence interval for the mean



\[\bar x \pm t_{n-1,\,0.975}\,\frac{s}{\sqrt n}\] The interval is exact for normally distributed data. For other distributions it is approximately valid if \(n\) is large enough for the central limit theorem – the more skewed the data, the larger \(n\) must be.








Figure 3.4: Twenty simulated repetitions of the same experiment – 25 engines each, true mean 200 cycles – each with its own 95 % confidence interval for the mean. On average, 19 of 20 intervals contain the true mean; here two miss it (red). For a single computed interval we never know whether it is one of the lucky ones.









Pitfall: what a confidence interval does not say



A computed interval, say [197.1, 215.5] cycles, does not contain the true mean “with 95 % probability” – in the classical view, the true mean is fixed and either inside or not. The 95 % refers to the reliability of the method. A correct statement is: “The interval [197.1, 215.5] cycles was computed with a method that captures the true mean in 95 % of all samples.” A probability statement about the parameter itself requires a Bayesian analysis with a prior distribution for the parameter (Bayes’ theorem, end of this chapter); we do not use it for confidence intervals. Also, a confidence interval for the mean says nothing about the spread of individual lifetimes: most single engines lie far outside it.


For many quantities – the B10 life, a median, a ratio – there is no simple formula for the interval. The bootstrap solves this by simulation:






Definition: Bootstrap



Draw \(B\) (e.g. 10,000) samples of size \(n\) with replacement from the observed data and compute the statistic of interest for each. The distribution of these bootstrap replicates approximates the sampling distribution of the statistic – the bootstrap simulates the repetitions that define the standard error, and the standard deviation of the replicates estimates it; its 2.5 % and 97.5 % quantiles give an approximate 95 % confidence interval (percentile method; by default, SciPy uses a refined variant that corrects the limits slightly for skewness).



n = len(lifetimes)                                  # number of engines
x_bar = lifetimes.mean()                            # sample mean
se = lifetimes.std() / np.sqrt(n)                   # standard error s / sqrt(n); std() uses n - 1
t_q = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=n - 1)                  # 97.5 % quantile of the t-distribution
ci_t = (x_bar - t_q * se, x_bar + t_q * se)         # shortcut: stats.t.interval(0.95, df=n - 1, loc=x_bar, scale=se)
# Bootstrap interval for comparison
boot = stats.bootstrap((lifetimes.values,),         # the data, as a tuple of samples (here: one)
                       np.mean,                     # statistic computed for every resample
                       confidence_level=0.95,
                       rng=0)                       # fixed seed: same resamples in every run
print(f"Mean lifetime: {x_bar:.1f} cycles, standard error: {se:.2f} cycles, t-quantile: {t_q:.3f}")
print("t-interval:        ", np.round(ci_t, 1))
print("bootstrap interval:", np.round(boot.confidence_interval, 1))

Mean lifetime: 206.3 cycles, standard error: 4.63 cycles, t-quantile: 1.984
t-interval:         [197.1 215.5]
bootstrap interval: [198.  216.3]


Discussion. For the mean of 100 observations both methods give almost the same interval – the central limit theorem makes the t-interval reliable here. The bootstrap becomes valuable for statistics without a known formula (Exercise 2) and for small or strongly skewed samples.






Extension: the bootstrap by hand





stats.bootstrap hides a simple loop. Written by hand, with the percentile method from the definition above:

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)                            # random generator with fixed seed
boot_means = [rng.choice(lifetimes.values, size=n, replace=True).mean()  # n engines, drawn with replacement
              for _ in range(9999)]                       # ... in 9999 bootstrap samples
lo_b, hi_b = np.percentile(boot_means, [2.5, 97.5])       # middle 95 % of the 9999 means
print(f"Bootstrap interval by hand: [{lo_b:.1f}, {hi_b:.1f}]")
print(f"Spread of the 9999 means: {np.std(boot_means, ddof=1):.2f} cycles, standard error s/sqrt(n): {se:.2f} cycles")

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3))
plt.hist(boot_means, bins=50)                             # the bootstrap distribution of the mean
for v in (lo_b, hi_b):
    plt.axvline(v, color="k", ls="--")                    # dashed lines at the interval limits
plt.xlabel("Mean lifetime of a bootstrap sample (cycles)"); plt.ylabel("Count")
plt.show()

Bootstrap interval by hand: [197.4, 215.5]
Spread of the 9999 means: 4.60 cycles, standard error s/sqrt(n): 4.63 cycles









The histogram shows the bootstrap distribution of the mean. It is bell-shaped, as the central limit theorem predicts, and its standard deviation matches the standard error \(s/\sqrt n\). The interval practically agrees with the t-interval; stats.bootstrap with method="percentile" gives practically the same result, its default refined variant shifts the limits slightly.

title: 3  Probability and Uncertainty
text:
3.5 Bayes’ theorem: updating a probability
New information changes probabilities. A conditional probability \(P(F \mid A)\) is the probability of an event \(F\) when we know that the event \(A\) has occurred. Bayes’ theorem computes it from the reverse conditional probability \(P(A \mid F)\):






Theorem: Bayes’ theorem



For events \(F\) and \(A\) with \(P(A) > 0\): \[\begin{aligned} P(F \mid A) &= \frac{P(A \mid F)\,P(F)}{P(A)} \\ &= \frac{P(A \mid F)\,P(F)}{P(A \mid F)\,P(F) + P(A \mid \bar F)\,P(\bar F)}. \end{aligned}\] \(\bar F\) is the event “not \(F\)”. \(P(F)\) is the prior probability – before we know about \(A\). \(P(A \mid F)\) is the likelihood of the observation \(A\) if \(F\) holds – the same idea as the likelihood in maximum likelihood estimation. \(P(F \mid A)\) is the posterior probability after observing \(A\). The denominator \(P(A)\) only makes the probabilities add up to 1; in short: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.


Example: besides the planned overhaul, the airline monitors its engines with a health monitoring system. It raises an alarm \(A\) for a developing fault \(F\) with probability \(P(A \mid F) = 0.95\), and a false alarm for a healthy engine with probability \(P(A \mid \bar F) = 0.05\). Only 1 % of the monitored engines actually have such a fault. If the system raises an alarm, how likely is a real fault?
\[P(F \mid A) = \frac{0.95 \cdot 0.01}{0.95 \cdot 0.01 + 0.05 \cdot 0.99} \approx 0.16\]
Five out of six alarms are false – not because the system is bad, but because faults are rare. Chapter 7 returns to this base rate effect for classifiers. The same rule holds for probability densities instead of events: the posterior density is proportional to likelihood × prior density. Chapter 6 uses it to predict with Gaussian processes.

title: 3  Probability and Uncertainty
text:
3.6 Back to the decision
The requirement “at most 10 % failures with 95 % confidence” has two parts. The 10 % defines the B10 life. The 95 % confidence means that we must not use the point estimate of B10 but a value that is, with 95 % confidence, below the true B10 – the lower bound of a one-sided 95 % confidence interval, which we obtain with the bootstrap, using the three-parameter Weibull model chosen above. And preventive overhaul only makes sense if the failure rate increases with age, i.e. \(\beta > 1\).

def b10_of(x):
    """B10 life of a three-parameter Weibull distribution fitted to the lifetimes x."""
    c, loc, scale = stats.weibull_min.fit(x)                     # fit all three parameters (free t0)
    return stats.weibull_min.ppf(0.10, c, loc=loc, scale=scale)  # 10 % quantile of the fitted model

b10_3p = b10_of(lifetimes.values)                  # point estimate from all 100 engines
boot_b10 = stats.bootstrap((lifetimes.values,),    # the data, as a tuple of samples (here: one)
                           b10_of,                 # statistic: refit the model to every resample
                           n_resamples=1000,       # 1,000 refits are enough here and take a few seconds
                           confidence_level=0.90,  # two-sided 90 %: its lower end is a one-sided 95 % bound
                           method="percentile",    # limits = quantiles of the replicates, as in the definition
                           rng=1)                  # fixed seed: same resamples in every run
b10_lower = boot_b10.confidence_interval.low       # 95 % lower confidence bound of B10

if beta3 > 1:                                      # failure rate increases after t0?
    print(f"Weibull shape beta = {beta3:.2f} > 1: wear-out, preventive overhaul is sensible")
else:
    print(f"Weibull shape beta = {beta3:.2f} <= 1: no wear-out, preventive overhaul does not help")
print(f"B10 point estimate: {b10_3p:.0f} cycles, 95 % lower confidence bound: {b10_lower:.1f} cycles")
print(f"Decision: overhaul after {int(np.floor(b10_lower))} flight cycles at the latest.")  # rounded down: safe side

Weibull shape beta = 1.83 > 1: wear-out, preventive overhaul is sensible
B10 point estimate: 152 cycles, 95 % lower confidence bound: 147.7 cycles
Decision: overhaul after 147 flight cycles at the latest.


The difference between the point estimate (152 cycles) and the lower bound (147.7 cycles) is the price of having data from only 100 engines. More data would make the confidence interval narrower, move the lower bound closer to the point estimate and thus allow a longer overhaul interval. The model decision was worth even more: with the two-parameter Weibull model, the same procedure gives a bound of only about 128 cycles. In the real world, the decision would also consider that C-MAPSS is a simulation: before an interval is approved, the model would have to be validated against field data of real engines.






Recommendation to the fleet manager




Recommendation: overhaul the engines preventively after 147 flight cycles at the latest.
Uncertainty: the B10 life is estimated at 152 cycles; 147.7 cycles is its 95 % lower confidence bound from 100 engines.
Assumptions: the three-parameter Weibull distribution describes the lifetimes, and the 100 engines are representative of the fleet. The lognormal model, which fits equally well, gives practically the same bound (Exercise 1).
Limits: C-MAPSS is a simulation – the model must be validated against field data before the interval is approved.

title: 3  Probability and Uncertainty
text:
3.7 Summary






Key takeaways




Every model rests on assumptions: a distribution is a modelling choice; physics (sum, product, weakest link) guides it, probability plots and the AIC check it – and the choice can change the decision.
The Weibull shape parameter distinguishes early failures, random failures and wear-out – and decides whether preventive maintenance makes sense.
Every estimate has an uncertainty: confidence intervals quantify it, and the bootstrap provides them for almost any statistic.
Bayes’ theorem updates a prior probability with new information: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.

title: 3  Probability and Uncertainty
text:
3.8 Exercises


Repeat the decision of Back to the decision with the lognormal model: compute its B10 life and the 95 % lower confidence bound. How much does the overhaul interval depend on the choice between the two well-fitting models? Useful: stats.lognorm.fit(x, floc=0) returns shape, location and scale; stats.lognorm.ppf(0.10, ...) gives the 10 % quantile; bootstrap settings as in Back to the decision.
Use the bootstrap to compute a 95 % confidence interval for the B10 life. Why is it wider (relative to the estimate) than the interval for the mean? Useful: stats.bootstrap with the function b10_of from Back to the decision.
How does the width of the confidence interval of the mean change if only 20 engines are available? Simulate it by drawing many random subsamples of 20 engines. Useful: rng.choice(x, size=20, replace=False) draws 20 different engines; stats.t.interval(0.95, df=19, loc=x_bar, scale=se) returns the limits of the t-interval; stats.sem(x) computes the standard error \(s/\sqrt n\).
Interpret the shape parameter for the maintenance strategy: does preventive replacement make sense? At which age would you replace an engine if at most 5 % of the engines may fail before replacement? Useful: stats.weibull_min.ppf(0.05, beta3, loc=t0, scale=eta3) with the parameters of the three-parameter model.
An ultrasonic test detects 90 % of the cracked parts and flags 2 % of the intact parts by mistake; 5 % of the parts are cracked. What is the probability that a flagged part is cracked – and that a part that was not flagged is cracked? What do the two results mean for the handling of flagged and unflagged parts?



3.8.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1






def b10_lognormal(x):
    """B10 life of a lognormal distribution fitted to the lifetimes x."""
    s, loc, scale = stats.lognorm.fit(x, floc=0)                 # two-parameter lognormal (loc fixed at 0)
    return stats.lognorm.ppf(0.10, s, loc=loc, scale=scale)      # 10 % quantile of the fitted model

boot_ln = stats.bootstrap((lifetimes.values,), b10_lognormal, n_resamples=1000, confidence_level=0.90,
                          method="percentile", rng=1)            # same settings as for the Weibull model
print(f"lognormal:   B10 {b10_lognormal(lifetimes.values):.0f} cycles, 95 % lower bound {boot_ln.confidence_interval.low:.0f} cycles")
print(f"3-p Weibull: B10 {b10_3p:.0f} cycles, 95 % lower bound {b10_lower:.0f} cycles")

lognormal:   B10 154 cycles, 95 % lower bound 148 cycles
3-p Weibull: B10 152 cycles, 95 % lower bound 148 cycles


Both well-fitting models give practically the same B10 life (152 and 154 cycles) and the same lower bound of about 148 cycles: here the decision does not depend on the choice between them – only on avoiding the poorly fitting two-parameter model. If two plausible models led to clearly different intervals, the more conservative one would be the safer choice, and the difference should be reported as model uncertainty.









Solution to Exercise 2






# b10_of (three-parameter Weibull) is defined in "Back to the decision"
boot_95 = stats.bootstrap((lifetimes.values,), b10_of, n_resamples=1000,
                          method="percentile", rng=0)            # two-sided 95 % interval (default level)
lo, hi = boot_95.confidence_interval                             # its limits
print(f"B10 = {b10_3p:.0f} cycles, 95 % CI [{lo:.0f}, {hi:.0f}]  (relative width {(hi - lo) / b10_3p:.0%})")
print(f"Mean: relative width {(ci_t[1] - ci_t[0]) / lifetimes.mean():.0%}")   # width / estimate

B10 = 152 cycles, 95 % CI [147, 164]  (relative width 11%)
Mean: relative width 9%


The B10 life is a statement about the lower tail of the distribution, where only about 10 of the 100 engines contribute information. In addition, it depends on three estimated parameters, and the shape parameter enters as an exponent. The mean uses all observations equally. Reliability figures in the tails are therefore more uncertain than averages – the further out in the tail (B1 instead of B10), the more so. This is one reason for safety factors.









Solution to Exercise 3






rng = np.random.default_rng(0)                      # random generator with fixed seed
widths = []                                         # interval widths of all subsamples
for _ in range(2000):                               # 2000 random fleets of 20 engines
    sub = rng.choice(lifetimes.values, size=20, replace=False)   # 20 different engines
    lo_, hi_ = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=19, loc=sub.mean(), scale=stats.sem(sub))  # sem = s / sqrt(n)
    widths.append(hi_ - lo_)
print(f"n = 100: width {ci_t[1] - ci_t[0]:.1f} cycles")
print(f"n = 20:  mean width {np.mean(widths):.1f} cycles (ratio {np.mean(widths) / (ci_t[1] - ci_t[0]):.2f})")

n = 100: width 18.4 cycles
n = 20:  mean width 42.6 cycles (ratio 2.32)


The width scales approximately with \(1/\sqrt{n}\), so going from 100 to 20 engines should make the interval about \(\sqrt{5} \approx 2.2\) times wider; the t-quantile for 19 degrees of freedom (2.09 instead of 1.98) adds a little more. (Subsampling without replacement from only 100 engines slightly reduces the spread, so the simulated ratio can be a bit smaller.)









Solution to Exercise 4






t05 = stats.weibull_min.ppf(0.05, beta3, loc=t0, scale=eta3)   # 5 % quantile of the chosen model
print(f"beta = {beta3:.2f} > 1 -> wear-out; replacement age for 5 % failures: {t05:.0f} cycles")

beta = 1.83 > 1 -> wear-out; replacement age for 5 % failures: 143 cycles


Since \(\beta > 1\), the failure rate increases with age after the failure-free time, so preventive replacement reduces failures. The replacement age for at most 5 % failures is the 5 % quantile of the chosen model, \(B_5 = t_0 + \eta(-\ln 0.95)^{1/\beta}\). Given the large uncertainty of tail estimates (Exercise 2), one would in practice use the lower confidence bound of \(B_5\) rather than the point estimate. Whether replacement is economical depends additionally on the cost ratio of planned replacement and unplanned failure.









Solution to Exercise 5





With \(F\) = “cracked” and \(A\) = “flagged”: \(P(F) = 0.05\), \(P(A \mid F) = 0.90\), \(P(A \mid \bar F) = 0.02\). \[P(F \mid A) = \frac{0.90 \cdot 0.05}{0.90 \cdot 0.05 + 0.02 \cdot 0.95} = \frac{0.045}{0.064} \approx 0.70.\] For a part that was not flagged, the probabilities of no alarm enter: \(P(\bar A \mid F) = 0.10\) and \(P(\bar A \mid \bar F) = 0.98\): \[P(F \mid \bar A) = \frac{0.10 \cdot 0.05}{0.10 \cdot 0.05 + 0.98 \cdot 0.95} = \frac{0.005}{0.936} \approx 0.005.\] A flagged part is cracked with a probability of about 70 % – it should be inspected again rather than scrapped automatically, because 3 of 10 flagged parts are intact. An unflagged part is cracked with only 0.5 %, ten times less than before the test, but not zero: about 5 of 1,000 unflagged parts are still cracked. Whether that is acceptable depends on the consequences of a crack.

title: 4  Statistical Testing
text:
4.1 The logic of a hypothesis test
A process engineer changes the supplier of a raw material, and the mean scrap rate in the following week is slightly lower. Is the new material better – or was it a good week by chance? Questions like this are everyday engineering questions, and statistical hypothesis tests are the standard tool to answer them. They provide a disciplined way to decide whether an observed difference is larger than what random variation alone would plausibly produce.
Tests are also among the most misunderstood tools of statistics. A small p-value does not mean that an effect is large or important, and a large p-value does not prove that there is no effect. With the big datasets of modern production, almost every difference becomes “significant”. This chapter therefore puts as much weight on effect sizes and practical relevance as on p-values.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Course goal. This chapter contributes to step 3 of the course goals: quantify effects and uncertainty.
Datasets in this chapter
A hypothesis test is a proof by contradiction with uncertainty. We assume that there is no effect and check whether the data are compatible with this assumption.
Two kinds of wrong decisions are possible:
The significance level controls the false alarm rate. The power depends on the size of the effect, the noise level and the sample size – small samples often have too little power to detect relevant effects.

title: 4  Statistical Testing
text:
Definition: Elements of a hypothesis test




Null hypothesis \(H_0\): the “nothing special” statement, e.g. \(\mu_1 = \mu_2\) (both suppliers give the same mean).
Alternative hypothesis \(H_1\): what we want to detect, e.g. \(\mu_1 \neq \mu_2\).
Test statistic \(T\): a number computed from the data that measures the deviation from \(H_0\).
p-value: the probability of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one, assuming \(H_0\) is true.
Significance level \(\alpha\) (often 0.05): \(H_0\) is rejected if \(p < \alpha\).













\(H_0\) true (no effect)
\(H_0\) false (effect exists)




\(H_0\) rejected
type I error (false alarm), probability \(\alpha\)
correct decision, probability \(1 - \beta\) = power


\(H_0\) not rejected
correct decision
type II error (missed effect), probability \(\beta\)









Figure 4.1: Left: the p-value is the probability, computed under the null hypothesis, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one (two-sided test). Right: the two error types. The critical value is set such that the false alarm probability α is 5 %; the probability β of missing a real effect depends on the effect size and the sample size.










Pitfall: what the p-value is not




It is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true.
\(p \ge 0.05\) does not prove that there is no effect – maybe the sample was just too small (“absence of evidence is not evidence of absence”).
\(p < 0.05\) says nothing about the size or the importance of the effect.

title: 4  Statistical Testing
text:
4.2 Comparing two groups: the t-test
For two independent samples with means \(\bar x_1, \bar x_2\), standard deviations \(s_1, s_2\) and sizes \(n_1, n_2\), the Welch t-test uses
\[t = \frac{\bar x_1 - \bar x_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2}}.\]
Under \(H_0\), \(t\) follows approximately a t-distribution (introduced with the confidence interval for the mean in Chapter 3) with
\[\nu = \frac{\left(s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2\right)^2}{\dfrac{(s_1^2/n_1)^2}{n_1 - 1} + \dfrac{(s_2^2/n_2)^2}{n_2 - 1}}\]
degrees of freedom. \(\nu\) is usually not an integer; it lies between the smaller of \(n_1 - 1\) and \(n_2 - 1\) and \(n_1 + n_2 - 2\). SciPy computes it automatically. For large samples, the t-distribution is practically the standard normal distribution (table in Chapter 3), so \(\nu\) hardly matters. Welch’s version does not assume equal variances and should be the default (the classical Student t-test assumes them).






Tests and confidence intervals are two sides of one coin



A two-sided test at level \(\alpha = 0.05\) rejects \(H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0\) exactly when the 95 % confidence interval for \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) does not contain 0. The interval is more informative: it shows not only whether there is a difference but also how large it plausibly is. Report intervals whenever possible.

title: 4  Statistical Testing
section: 4.3 More than two groups, categories and non-normal data
text:
4.3 More than two groups, categories and non-normal data








Question
Test (data approx. normal)
Rank-based alternative (no normality assumption, also for ordinal data)




Do two independent groups differ?
Welch t-test, ttest_ind(equal_var=False)
Mann–Whitney U, mannwhitneyu


Paired measurements (before/after on the same parts)
paired t-test, ttest_rel
Wilcoxon signed-rank, wilcoxon


Do \(k\) groups differ?
one-way ANOVA, f_oneway
Kruskal–Wallis, kruskal


Are two categorical variables related?
chi-squared test, chi2_contingency
–



The rank-based tests do not compare means: they check whether the values of one group tend to be larger than those of another (Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis), or whether paired differences are centred at zero (Wilcoxon). They are robust against outliers and skewed data; if the data are approximately normal, the t-test and ANOVA detect a difference slightly more often.






Pitfall: check the assumptions



All tests in the table assume independent observations – each value carries its own information. Values measured in time order (hourly values, consecutive parts of one machine) usually violate this: the p-value comes out too small and the interval too narrow.

t-test and ANOVA: approximately normal data, or large samples (central limit theorem). The classical ANOVA also assumes equal variances; f_oneway(..., equal_var=False) gives Welch’s version.
Rank-based tests: no distribution assumed, but the values must at least be ordered (ordinal).
Chi-squared test: an expected count of at least 5 in every cell.



The one-way ANOVA (analysis of variance) compares the variation between group means with the variation within the groups:
\[\begin{aligned} F &= \frac{\text{variance between groups}}{\text{variance within groups}} \\ &= \frac{\sum_j n_j(\bar x_j - \bar x)^2/(k-1)}{\sum_j \sum_i (x_{ij} - \bar x_j)^2/(N-k)}. \end{aligned}\]
Here \(x_{ij}\) is observation \(i\) in group \(j\), \(\bar x_j\) the mean of group \(j\) with \(n_j\) observations, \(\bar x\) the overall mean, \(k\) the number of groups and \(N\) the total number of observations. A large \(F\) indicates that at least one group mean differs. ANOVA does not say which one – this requires pairwise comparisons, and with them many tests at once:






Pitfall: many tests, many false alarms



If we perform 20 independent tests at \(\alpha = 0.05\) and no effect exists anywhere, we still expect one “significant” result by chance; the probability of at least one false alarm is \(1 - 0.95^{20} \approx 64\,\%\). Decide before looking at the data which comparisons you will test, and correct the significance level. The simplest correction, Bonferroni, uses \(\alpha/m\) for each of \(m\) tests. It is strict and misses real effects more often than necessary; the Holm method gives the same protection with less strict thresholds. Both are available in statsmodels.stats.multitest.multipletests.


The chi-squared test compares the observed counts \(O\) in a contingency table with the counts \(E\) expected if the variables were independent: \(\chi^2 = \sum (O - E)^2/E\). The expected count of a cell is \(E = \text{row total} \cdot \text{column total} / \text{total count}\).

title: 4  Statistical Testing
text:
4.4 Effect size and practical relevance






Definition: Cohen’s d



The standardised mean difference \[d = \frac{\bar x_1 - \bar x_2}{s_p}, \qquad s_p = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2 + s_2^2}{2}},\] expresses a difference in units of the standard deviation. Rough conventions: \(|d| \approx 0.2\) small, \(0.5\) medium, \(0.8\) large.


In engineering, the most meaningful effect size is often the raw difference in physical units, compared with a tolerance or a requirement: “the mean diameter differs by 0.2 µm, the tolerance is ±20 µm”.






Pitfall: significance with large samples



The standard error shrinks with \(1/\sqrt{n}\). With thousands of observations, differences far too small to matter become highly significant. With big data, always ask: Is the difference large enough to matter for the process?



# Setup: works locally and in Google Colab

for pkg in ["ucimlrepo"]:                       # package that is not pre-installed everywhere

        subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", pkg], check=True)  # install it

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")


# Download helper, as in Chapter 3
from pathlib import Path
import requests

DATA = Path("data")
DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)                         # create the folder ./data if it does not exist

def download(url, fname=None):
    """Download a file once and cache it in ./data."""
    if fname is None:                             # no file name given:
        fname = url.split("/")[-1]                # use the last part of the URL
    path = DATA / fname                           # "/" joins folder and file name
    if not path.exists():                         # download only if not cached yet
        r = requests.get(url, timeout=120)        # give up after 120 s without response
        r.raise_for_status()                      # stop with an error if the download failed
        path.write_bytes(r.content)               # open, write and close the file in one step
    return path

title: 4  Statistical Testing
text:
4.5 Live coding: NOx emissions 2011–2015
The dataset contains 36,733 hourly sensor values of a gas turbine in north-western Turkey, recorded over five years, with one CSV file per year. Besides ambient conditions and turbine process variables, it contains the emissions of carbon monoxide (CO) and nitrogen oxides (NOX), both in mg/m³. Emission limits make NOx a relevant quantity for plant operators and authorities.

import zipfile

url = "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/551/gas+turbine+co+and+nox+emission+data+set.zip"
frames = []                                                   # one table per year
with zipfile.ZipFile(download(url, "gas_turbine.zip")) as z:  # open the archive (closed after the block)
    for year in range(2011, 2016):                            # it contains gt_2011.csv ... gt_2015.csv
        df = pd.read_csv(z.open(f"gt_{year}.csv"))            # read this year's file from the archive
        df["YEAR"] = year                                     # add the year as a column
        frames.append(df)
gt = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)                     # stack the five tables, rows numbered anew

sns.boxplot(data=gt, x="YEAR", y="NOX")   # one box per year
plt.ylabel("NOx (mg/m³)")

The box plots show the distribution of NOx per year. Before testing, look at the size of the differences between the medians compared with the spread within each year – this is what the tests will formalise. With five years, the first question is whether they differ at all – the job of the ANOVA, with Kruskal–Wallis as a cross-check without normality assumption. The contract itself compares only two years, 2011 and 2015 – the job of the t-test. Because this one comparison is fixed in advance, no correction for multiple tests is needed.

def p_text(p):
    """p-value as text; values below 1e-300 are rounded to 0 by the computer."""
    return f"p = {p:.2g}" if p >= 1e-300 else "p < 1e-300"

# One sample per year (all its hourly values); * passes the five samples to a test one by one
nox_samples = [gt.loc[gt.YEAR == year, "NOX"] for year in range(2011, 2016)]
anova = stats.f_oneway(*nox_samples)                       # one-way ANOVA: do the five means differ?
kw = stats.kruskal(*nox_samples)                           # Kruskal-Wallis: the same question, based on ranks
print(f"ANOVA:          F = {anova.statistic:.0f}, {p_text(anova.pvalue)}")
print(f"Kruskal-Wallis: {p_text(kw.pvalue)}")

nox_2011 = gt.loc[gt.YEAR == 2011, "NOX"]                  # NOx values of 2011
nox_2015 = gt.loc[gt.YEAR == 2015, "NOX"]                  # NOx values of 2015
res = stats.ttest_ind(nox_2011, nox_2015, equal_var=False) # Welch t-test (no equal variances assumed)
ci = res.confidence_interval(0.95)                         # 95 % CI of mean(2011) - mean(2015)
diff = nox_2011.mean() - nox_2015.mean()                   # difference of the means
cohens_d = diff / np.sqrt((nox_2011.var() + nox_2015.var()) / 2)  # difference in units of s_p
print(f"Welch t-test 2011 vs 2015: t = {res.statistic:.1f}, {p_text(res.pvalue)}")
print(f"difference = {diff:.1f} mg/m³, 95 % CI [{ci.low:.1f}, {ci.high:.1f}], "
      f"Cohen's d = {cohens_d:.2f}")

ANOVA:          F = 1496, p < 1e-300
Kruskal-Wallis: p < 1e-300
Welch t-test 2011 vs 2015: t = 42.8, p < 1e-300
difference = 7.7 mg/m³, 95 % CI [7.3, 8.0], Cohen's d = 0.70


Discussion. With several thousand hourly values per year, the p-values are astronomically small – too small for the computer to store, which would round them to 0. The code therefore reports them as an upper bound, \(p < 10^{-300}\). Any systematic difference between years is detected. The t statistic is more telling: the difference between 2011 and 2015 is about 43 standard errors away from 0. The informative numbers are the difference in mg/m³ with its confidence interval and Cohen’s d. Whether the change matters depends on the distance to the emission limit and on the cause.
And here an engineering caution is needed: the hourly values are not independent – consecutive hours are strongly correlated, so the effective sample size – the number of independent values that would carry the same information – is much smaller than the number of rows, and the p-values are too optimistic. Moreover, differences between years can be caused by different ambient conditions (a hot year), different load profiles or maintenance work. A test can establish that the years differ, not why. To attribute the change to a cause we would need a model that accounts for these influences (Chapter 5).

title: 4  Statistical Testing
section: 4.6 How many measurements do we need?
text:
4.6 How many measurements do we need?
Planning comes before testing. If a difference of \(\delta\) is relevant, how many samples are needed to detect it with a power of, say, 80 %? For the two-sample t-test, the required number per group is approximately
\[n \approx \frac{2\,(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2}{d^2}, \qquad d = \delta/\sigma,\]
where \(\delta\) is the smallest relevant difference, \(\sigma\) the standard deviation and \(z_q\) the \(q\)-quantile of the standard normal distribution. This gives about \(16/d^2\) for \(\alpha = 0.05\) and power 0.8. Halving the detectable effect requires four times as many samples.

from statsmodels.stats.power import TTestIndPower

power_analysis = TTestIndPower()                   # power calculations for the two-sample t-test
for d in [0.2, 0.5, 0.8]:                          # small, medium and large effect (Cohen's d)
    n = power_analysis.solve_power(effect_size=d, alpha=0.05, power=0.8)  # solve for n per group
    print(f"d = {d}: n = {np.ceil(n):.0f} per group")                      # round up to whole samples

d = 0.2: n = 394 per group
d = 0.5: n = 64 per group
d = 0.8: n = 26 per group

title: 4  Statistical Testing
text:
4.7 Back to the decision
The contract requires two things: the reduction must be demonstrable (larger than random variation) and relevant (at least 5 % of the 2011 mean). At first sight, a small p-value settles the first part; for the second part we need the confidence interval of the difference: the bonus is justified only if the whole interval lies above the relevance threshold.

# res and ci: the Welch t-test 2011 vs 2015 and its 95 % CI from the live coding
threshold = 0.05 * nox_2011.mean()                 # contract: "relevant" = at least 5 % of the 2011 mean
print(f"Reduction 2011 -> 2015: {diff:.1f} mg/m³, "
      f"95 % CI [{ci.low:.1f}, {ci.high:.1f}], relevance threshold {threshold:.1f} mg/m³")
if ci.low > threshold:                             # the whole interval lies above the threshold
    print("Decision: claim confirmed – the reduction is demonstrable and relevant.")
elif ci.low > 0:                                   # above 0, but not entirely above the threshold
    print("Decision: reduction demonstrable, but not demonstrably relevant – no bonus under the contract.")
else:                                              # the interval contains 0
    print("Decision: no demonstrable reduction – claim rejected.")

Reduction 2011 -> 2015: 7.7 mg/m³, 95 % CI [7.3, 8.0], relevance threshold 3.4 mg/m³
Decision: claim confirmed – the reduction is demonstrable and relevant.


The whole interval lies far above the threshold. But what does the tiny p-value contribute to this result? The same test for 2011 against 2012 – two years before NOx dropped – gives:

nox_2012 = gt.loc[gt.YEAR == 2012, "NOX"]
res_12 = stats.ttest_ind(nox_2011, nox_2012, equal_var=False)  # the same Welch t-test for 2011 vs 2012
print(f"Change 2011 -> 2012: {nox_2012.mean() - nox_2011.mean():+.1f} mg/m³ "
      f"({(nox_2012.mean() / nox_2011.mean() - 1) * 100:+.1f} %), {p_text(res_12.pvalue)}")

Change 2011 -> 2012: +1.2 mg/m³ (+1.8 %), p = 1.2e-12


An increase of less than 2 % – irrelevant, and part of the ordinary variation from year to year – is just as “highly significant”. The test compares a difference with the scatter of the individual hours; it does not know how much a whole year varies without any intervention. With thousands of hourly values, it calls every difference between two years significant, so the p-value cannot distinguish a real improvement from ordinary variation. What carries the decision is the size of the reduction: 7.7 mg/m³ is more than twice the relevance threshold and more than three times the largest difference between 2011, 2012 and 2013 (2.4 mg/m³, table above). And the lower level was reached in 2014 and held in 2015.
Even a confirmed reduction does not prove that the consultant caused it: different weather, load profiles or maintenance could have the same effect. NOx dropped abruptly between 2013 and 2014 rather than gradually; the plant should find out what changed at that time. A fair contract would have specified how such influences are accounted for – a lesson for the next one.






Recommendation to the plant management




Recommendation: confirm the claim – the contract conditions for the bonus are met. The argument is the size of the reduction, not the p-value.
Uncertainty: NOx fell by 7.7 mg/m³ from 2011 to 2015 (95 % CI 7.3 to 8.0 mg/m³). The interval is too narrow because consecutive hours are dependent, but the reduction is more than twice the relevance threshold of 3.4 mg/m³ and more than three times the variation between 2011 and 2013; the lower level held in 2014 and 2015.
Assumptions: the NOx values of both years were measured in the same way (same measuring system and calibration), and the contract judges the reduction, not its cause.
Limits: the analysis does not show that the consultant caused the reduction.

title: 4  Statistical Testing
text:
4.8 Summary






Key takeaways




A test checks whether data are compatible with “no effect”; the p-value is a probability under \(H_0\), not of \(H_0\).
Significant is not the same as relevant: report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not just p-values, and judge relevance in physical units.
Large samples make tiny effects significant; small samples miss relevant effects – plan the sample size.
Many tests produce false alarms; correct (Bonferroni, Holm) and plan comparisons in advance.
Every model rests on assumptions: tests assume independent observations – time series data violate this.

title: 4  Statistical Testing
text:
4.9 Exercises


Check the normality assumption for NOx per year with Q–Q plots. Does a violation matter for the ANOVA with these sample sizes? Useful: stats.probplot(x, dist="norm", plot=ax) draws a normal Q–Q plot into the subplot ax.
Draw a random sample of 30 hourly values per year and repeat the ANOVA and the 2011 vs. 2015 t-test. What changes and why? Repeat the sampling a few times. Useful: gt.groupby("YEAR").sample(30, random_state=0) draws 30 random rows per year.
Consecutive hourly values are strongly dependent. Compute the correlation between consecutive values (.autocorr()) of the NOx values of 2011 – for the hourly values, for daily means (blocks of 24 hours) and for weekly means (blocks of 168 hours). Does averaging make the values independent? Why not? Useful: x.groupby(np.arange(len(x)) // 24).mean() averages blocks of 24 consecutive values.
Run pairwise Welch t-tests between all years. How many comparisons are there? Apply a Bonferroni and a Holm correction. Useful: itertools.combinations(years, 2) lists all pairs; multipletests(pvals, method="holm")[1] from statsmodels.stats.multitest returns the corrected p-values.
The AI4I dataset is a synthetic dataset modelled on a real milling process. Each of its 10,000 records belongs to a product of quality variant L (low, 50 % of products), M (medium, 30 %) or H (high, 20 %). Is the failure rate independent of the variant? Load the data with fetch_ucirepo(id=601) from the package ucimlrepo, build the contingency table of Type and Machine failure and apply the chi-squared test. Is its condition met, and is the difference in failure rates relevant? Useful: pd.crosstab(a, b) counts all combinations of the values of two columns.
A new coating is supposed to reduce the wear of a tool by 10 µm. From previous tests the standard deviation of the wear is 25 µm. How many tools must be tested per variant to detect the improvement with 80 % power (\(\alpha = 0.05\))?
Formulate an engineering conclusion from the NOx analysis in two or three sentences – for a plant manager, not for a statistician.



4.9.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1






years = sorted(gt["YEAR"].unique())                          # 2011 ... 2015
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(years), figsize=(16, 3.5))   # one panel per year
for ax, yr in zip(axes, years):
    stats.probplot(gt.loc[gt.YEAR == yr, "NOX"], dist="norm", plot=ax)  # normal Q–Q plot
    ax.set_title(str(yr))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Deviations from the straight line at the ends indicate heavier or lighter tails than the normal distribution, curvature indicates skewness. With thousands of observations per group, the central limit theorem makes the group means approximately normal, so the ANOVA is robust against moderate non-normality. The variances differ only moderately between years (standard deviations 10.0 to 12.0 mg/m³), which the ANOVA tolerates with almost equal group sizes. More critical is the dependence of consecutive hourly values. The Kruskal–Wallis test, which does not assume normality, serves as a cross-check.









Solution to Exercise 2






for seed in range(3):                                        # three different random samples
    small = gt.groupby("YEAR").sample(30, random_state=seed)       # 30 random hours per year
    samples_s = [small.loc[small.YEAR == year, "NOX"] for year in range(2011, 2016)]  # one sample per year
    a_s = small.loc[small.YEAR == 2011, "NOX"]; b_s = small.loc[small.YEAR == 2015, "NOX"]
    res_s = stats.ttest_ind(a_s, b_s, equal_var=False)       # Welch t-test 2011 vs 2015
    ci_s = res_s.confidence_interval(0.95)                    # 95 % CI of the difference
    print(f"seed {seed}: ANOVA {p_text(stats.f_oneway(*samples_s).pvalue)}, t-test {p_text(res_s.pvalue)}, "
          f"difference = {a_s.mean() - b_s.mean():.1f} mg/m³, 95 % CI [{ci_s.low:.1f}, {ci_s.high:.1f}]")

seed 0: ANOVA p = 0.00046, t-test p = 0.2, difference = 4.5 mg/m³, 95 % CI [-2.5, 11.6]
seed 1: ANOVA p = 5.7e-07, t-test p = 0.00012, difference = 8.8 mg/m³, 95 % CI [4.5, 13.0]
seed 2: ANOVA p = 7.3e-06, t-test p = 0.024, difference = 7.0 mg/m³, 95 % CI [1.0, 13.1]


The estimated differences stay of similar size, but the p-values are much larger and vary from sample to sample: with 30 values per year, the standard error is roughly \(\sqrt{7000/30} \approx 15\) times larger. Small differences that were “highly significant” with all data may no longer be detectable. The effect did not change – only the power of the test. With seed 0, the t-test does not reject \(H_0\) (\(p = 0.2\)), although the difference is real: the interval from −2.5 to 11.6 mg/m³ contains 0 but also large reductions. The result is inconclusive – not a proof of “no effect”.









Solution to Exercise 3






for hours, label in [(1, "hourly values"), (24, "daily means"), (168, "weekly means")]:

Averaging hardly reduces the correlation: consecutive weeks are about as strongly correlated as consecutive hours. The dependence does not come from short-term noise, which averaging would remove, but from slow changes – seasons, ambient temperature, operating mode – that affect many hours, days and weeks in a row. Averaging therefore does not create independent observations. Time series need their own methods (Chapter 11).

The failure rate is 2.1 % for variant H, 2.8 % for M and 3.9 % for L, and the test rejects independence (\(p = 0.001\)). The effect size is \(d = 10/25 = 0.4\), which requires about 100 tools per variant. If that is too expensive, options are: reduce the noise (more homogeneous test conditions, paired design with both coatings on the same machine), accept a lower power, or test for a larger minimum effect.









Solution to Exercise 7





A good answer states the size of the change in physical units, relates it to a meaningful reference and names the limits of the analysis, for example: “The mean NOx emission in 2015 was 7.7 mg/m³ lower than in 2011, about 11 % of the 2011 level. This is more than three times the usual variation from one year to the next. The data alone do not show whether the change was caused by maintenance, different operation or different weather; to find out, we should model the emissions as a function of load and ambient conditions.” Avoid statistical jargon such as “p < 0.001” without explanation.

title: 5  Linear and Nonlinear Regression
text:
5.1 The linear model
Regression is the workhorse of engineering data analysis. Calibration curves, empirical material laws, characteristic maps of engines and process models are all regression models: they describe how a quantity of interest – the response – depends on one or more influencing quantities – the inputs, factors or features. A regression model can be used to understand a process (which factors matter, how strongly?) and to predict the response for new input values. The two purposes ask different questions of the same model; Section 5.1.5 compares them.
This chapter starts with the multiple linear regression model, its estimation by least squares and the statistical tools to interpret and check it. We then fit nonlinear models with physical meaning, which are common in engineering. Finally, we show how a designed experiment avoids correlated inputs from the start.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Course goal. This chapter contributes to step 3 of the course goals: quantify effects and uncertainty.
Datasets in this chapter
“Linear” refers to the parameters, not to the inputs. Models like \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln x + \beta_2 x^2\) or \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 x_2\) are linear models, because they are linear in \(\beta\). This makes the linear model much more flexible than its name suggests.

title: 5  Linear and Nonlinear Regression
text:
Definition: Multiple linear regression



The response \(y\) is modelled as a linear function of \(p\) inputs plus a random error: \[\begin{gathered} y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \dots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \varepsilon_i, \\ \varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ independent}. \end{gathered}\] In matrix form, \(y = X\beta + \varepsilon\), where the design matrix \(X\) has a first column of ones for the intercept.




5.1.1 Estimation by least squares
The coefficients are chosen to minimise the sum of squared residuals \(\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\). If the errors are normally distributed, this is exactly the maximum likelihood estimate (Chapter 3): apart from constants, the negative log-likelihood of normal errors is the sum of squared residuals. Setting the derivatives to zero gives the solution:






Least squares estimate and its uncertainty



The minimisation gives the coefficients – without any assumption about the errors: \[\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y.\] If the errors are independent and have the same variance \(\sigma^2\) everywhere, the uncertainty of the coefficients follows as \[\begin{aligned} \widehat{\text{Cov}}(\hat\beta) &= \hat\sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}, \\ \hat\sigma^2 &= \frac{1}{n - p - 1}\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2. \end{aligned}\] \(\hat\sigma^2\) estimates the scatter of the data around the model from the residuals. The divisor \(n - p - 1\) takes into account that the \(p + 1\) coefficients were estimated from the same data – just as the standard deviation \(s\) divides by \(n - 1\) because the mean was estimated (Chapter 3).


The covariance matrix \(\widehat{\text{Cov}}(\hat\beta)\) collects the uncertainty of all coefficients: its diagonal contains their variances, i.e. the squared standard errors – how much each coefficient would vary with new data (Chapter 3); an off-diagonal entry describes how strongly two estimates vary together. Divided by the two standard errors, it gives their correlation – between −1 and 1, as in Chapter 1.
You will not compute these formulas by hand – statsmodels does. What they show: the standard errors grow with the scatter \(\hat\sigma\) of the data around the model and with the correlation between the inputs (through \((X^\top X)^{-1}\), see Collinearity below), and they shrink as \(n\) grows. And while the coefficients need no assumptions, their standard errors – and with them confidence intervals and p-values – are valid only if the errors are independent with constant variance. This is what the residual analysis below checks.


5.1.2 Interpreting the output

Coefficient \(\hat\beta_j\): expected change of \(y\) when \(x_j\) increases by one unit and all other inputs stay constant. The last part is crucial – and often unrealistic when inputs are correlated.
Standard error, t-value, p-value: the t-value \(t_j = \hat\beta_j / \text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)\) states how many standard errors the coefficient lies away from 0 – the same idea as the t-statistic in Chapter 4. It tests \(H_0: \beta_j = 0\), i.e. whether \(x_j\) has any effect when the other inputs are in the model. Under \(H_0\), it follows a t-distribution with \(n - p - 1\) degrees of freedom, which gives the p-value (column P>|t|). The 95 % confidence interval is \(\hat\beta_j \pm t_{n-p-1,\,0.975}\,\text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)\), with the t-distribution from Chapter 3.
Coefficient of determination \(R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2}{\sum (y_i - \bar y)^2}\): share of the variance of \(y\) explained by the model. It never decreases when another input \(x_j\) is added to the model – even a column of random numbers, like rv1 in Chapter 2, raises it slightly. The adjusted \(R^2\), \(1 - (1 - R^2)\,\frac{n - 1}{n - p - 1}\), corrects for this: every additional input costs a degree of freedom, so the adjusted \(R^2\) rises only if the new input improves the fit noticeably.







Pitfall: R² measures fit, not validity



A high \(R^2\) does not mean that the model is correct, that it predicts well on new data or that the relationships are causal. Conversely, a low \(R^2\) can be perfectly acceptable if the process is inherently noisy. Always look at the residuals – and, for prediction, at the error on test data (Chapter 6).




5.1.3 Model assumptions and residual analysis
The statistical statements (standard errors, p-values, intervals) rely on assumptions about the errors. The residuals \(e_i = y_i - \hat y_i\) are our window to check them:









Assumption
Check
Typical violation in engineering data
If violated




Linearity (correct functional form)
residuals vs. fitted values and vs. each input: no pattern
saturation, threshold effects
coefficients and predictions are biased


Constant variance
spread of residuals constant
relative errors: spread grows with the response
standard errors and prediction intervals are wrong


Independence
residuals vs. time / order
time series, batches, repeated measurements on the same part
standard errors too small, p-values too optimistic


Normality
Q–Q plot of residuals
outliers, skewed responses
prediction intervals for single values are wrong; in small samples also confidence intervals and p-values









Engineering practice: transformations



Many engineering relationships are multiplicative or saturating. A log transformation of the response or of an input often linearises the relationship and stabilises the variance at the same time. Physical knowledge tells you which transformation makes sense: for concrete, strength grows quickly at first and then levels off, which suggests \(\ln(\text{age})\).




5.1.4 Collinearity
When inputs are strongly correlated, their individual effects cannot be separated well: the coefficients get large standard errors, can have implausible signs and change strongly when another input is added. The variance inflation factor \(\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)\) quantifies this. \(R_j^2\) is the \(R^2\) of an auxiliary regression that predicts \(x_j\) from all other inputs – how well \(x_j\) is already explained by them. The VIF states by which factor the squared standard error of \(\hat\beta_j\) is larger than it would be for uncorrelated inputs; values above about 5–10 indicate problematic collinearity. Collinearity does not harm predictions within the range of the data, but it ruins the interpretation of individual coefficients.


5.1.5 Understanding or predicting?
The last point shows that it matters what a model is used for. The same fitted model can serve two purposes, and each purpose asks different questions of it:






Two uses of the same model












Inference (this chapter)
Prediction (from Chapter 6)




Question
Which inputs matter, how strongly, and how certain is that?
How accurately is the response predicted for new inputs?


What we look at
coefficients with standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values
the error on data that were not used for fitting (test data, cross-validation)


What must hold
the model form is correct and the errors meet the assumptions – checked with the residuals
new data come from the same process and range as the training data


Collinearity
serious: individual coefficients cannot be interpreted
harmless, as long as new inputs combine like those in the training data


Suitable models
simple and interpretable
any model that predicts well, including very flexible ones (Chapters 6–8, 12)





Many engineering questions need both. The release decision at the end of this chapter is a prediction – the strength of a new mix – but it is made with the statistical tools of this chapter: a prediction interval that is valid only if the model assumptions hold. Chapter 6 shows how to check the quality of predictions directly on data the model has not seen.

The other fields are formal tests of the model and the residuals, and numbers for comparing models. You can skip them here – the residual plots below show the same more clearly. Not knowing every number of an output is normal; knowing which numbers answer your question is the skill.
What the values say:

The model explains about 82 % of the variation in strength.
Coefficients: each value is the change in MPa per additional kg/m³ of the component (or per unit of \(\ln\) age), holding all other components constant. Cement, slag and fly ash act as binders and should have positive coefficients; water should have a negative one.
Holding constant is tricky here: the components add up to roughly the volume of one cubic metre. If we add more cement, something else must be reduced. This built-in dependence causes collinearity – hence the warning about the large condition number (VIF values below) –, so the coefficients of the aggregates in particular cannot be interpreted on their own.

Discussion. Look for patterns: a curved band in the residuals vs. fitted values indicates a missing nonlinearity; a funnel shape indicates non-constant variance; structure in the residuals vs. age shows that the \(\ln\) transformation captures the age effect only approximately. Systematic patterns tell us that the linear model is an approximation – which is fine for interpretation of the main effects but limits its predictive accuracy. Flexible models in Chapters 6 and 8 will do better.

# VIF from its definition: regress each input on all other inputs (auxiliary regression)
data = conc.assign(log_age=np.log(conc["age"]))           # ln(age) as a column of its own
inputs = ["cement", "slag", "fly_ash", "water", "superplasticizer",
          "coarse_agg", "fine_agg", "log_age"]
vif = {}
for col in inputs:
    others = " + ".join(c for c in inputs if c != col)    # e.g. "slag + fly_ash + ... + log_age"
    r2 = smf.ols(f"{col} ~ {others}", data=data).fit().rsquared   # R_j²: col explained by the others
    vif[col] = 1 / (1 - r2)                               # VIF_j = 1 / (1 - R_j²)
vif = pd.Series(vif, name="VIF")
vif.round(1)

water               7.0
superplasticizer    3.0
coarse_agg          5.1
fine_agg            7.0
log_age             1.1
Name: VIF, dtype: float64


Discussion. All mix components have VIF values between 3 and 7.5: their standard errors are 1.7 to 2.7 times larger than they would be for uncorrelated inputs. The cause is the fixed volume – the components add up to about one cubic metre, so each of them is largely determined by the others; for cement, the other inputs explain about 87 % of its variation (\(1 - 1/7.5\)). The age, in contrast, varies independently of the mix (VIF 1.1). This is the collinearity behind the large condition number in the summary. Thanks to more than 1,000 tests, most coefficients are still significant, but the coefficients of the components should not be read as the effect of one component with “all else constant” (Exercise 3).

5.2.1 Confidence vs. prediction intervals
A regression model gives two different kinds of intervals for a new input \(x_0\):






Definition: Confidence interval vs. prediction interval



Both intervals are centred on the predicted value \(\hat y_0 = x_0^\top \hat\beta\); they differ in what they describe.

The confidence interval for the mean response \(E[y \mid x_0]\) reflects only the uncertainty of the estimated coefficients, expressed by the standard error \(\text{SE}(\hat y_0)\) of the predicted value: \[\hat y_0 \pm t_{n-p-1,\,0.975}\,\text{SE}(\hat y_0).\] This standard error shrinks towards zero as \(n\) grows.
The prediction interval for a single new observation \(y_0\) additionally contains the scatter \(\sigma\) of individual observations around the mean: \[\hat y_0 \pm t_{n-p-1,\,0.975}\,\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2 + \text{SE}(\hat y_0)^2}.\] Even for very large \(n\), it never becomes narrower than about \(\pm 2\hat\sigma\).



\(\text{SE}(\hat y_0)\) follows from the covariance matrix of the coefficients (formula in Appendix B). It grows with the distance of \(x_0\) from the centre of the data – this is why both bands in Figure 5.1 widen towards the edges.






Figure 5.1: Confidence band of the regression line (mean response) and prediction band for single new observations. Both widen with distance from the centre of the data – and in the extrapolation region, neither is supported by data.



For an engineer who needs to know the strength of the next concrete batch, the prediction interval is the relevant one.

new_mix = pd.DataFrame({"cement": [350], "slag": [0], "fly_ash": [0], "water": [180],
                        "superplasticizer": [5],
                        "coarse_agg": [1000], "fine_agg": [780],  # aggregates: typical values (assumed)
                        "age": [28]})                             # the mix of the scenario at 28 days
model.get_prediction(new_mix).summary_frame(alpha=0.05).round(1)  # mean, confidence and prediction interval

The columns contain everything from the definition box: mean is the predicted value \(\hat y_0\), mean_se its standard error \(\text{SE}(\hat y_0)\), mean_ci_lower/upper the confidence interval of the mean strength of such mixes at 28 days and obs_ci_lower/upper the prediction interval for a single specimen. With 1,030 tests, the mean is known to within about ±1 MPa, but individual tests scatter by \(\hat\sigma \approx 7\) MPa around the model – so the prediction interval is more than ten times wider than the confidence interval.






Pitfall: extrapolation



Regression models are only supported by data within the range of the inputs – and, with correlated inputs, only within the region where input combinations were observed. A mix with an unusual combination of components may lie within every single input range and still be far from the data.

title: 5  Linear and Nonlinear Regression
text:
5.3 Nonlinear curve fitting
Many engineering models are nonlinear in their parameters: hardening and creep curves, exponential decay, saturation curves, characteristic curves of components. They cannot be written as a linear model, but their parameters can still be estimated by least squares – numerically, by iteration:
\[\hat\theta = \arg\min_{\theta} \sum_i \left(y_i - f(x_i; \theta)\right)^2.\]
Unlike for the linear model, there is no formula for the solution. scipy.optimize.curve_fit begins with starting values and improves the parameters step by step until the sum of squared deviations no longer decreases.






Engineering practice: fitting physical models




Starting values: poor starting values can lead to a wrong result or to none at all. Derive them from physics or read them off the data.
Parameter uncertainty: curve_fit returns the fitted parameters popt and their covariance matrix pcov (p for parameters), as for linear regression; the square roots of its diagonal are the standard errors. They are approximations – computed from the curvature of the sum of squares at the optimum – valid for approximately normal, independent errors.
Plausibility: physically meaningful parameters – unlike the coefficients of a polynomial – can be checked against experience. If the data do not determine a parameter, e.g. the final strength of a mix tested only at early ages, its standard error becomes large and its value implausible.



As an example we model the strength development of one concrete mix over time with the hyperbolic model
\[f_c(t) = f_\infty \, \frac{t}{a + t},\]
with the final strength \(f_\infty\) (MPa) and the time \(a\) (days) at which half of it is reached. Physically it describes a hydration process that slows down over time. We use the mix with 500 kg cement and 200 kg water per m³ (w/c = 0.4), which was tested at eight ages:

from scipy.optimize import curve_fit

mix = conc[(conc["cement"] == 500) & (conc["water"] == 200)]   # all tests of this mix

The strength rises steeply in the first week and then ever more slowly. The starting values can be read off the table: the highest measured value for \(f_\infty\), and about 3 days for \(a\), since half of it (about 28 MPa) is reached after about 3 days.

def strength_model(t, f_inf, a):
    """Hyperbolic strength development: f_inf * t / (a + t)."""
    return f_inf * t / (a + t)

p0 = [mix["strength"].max(), 3]                          # starting values read off the table
popt, pcov = curve_fit(strength_model, mix["age"], mix["strength"], p0=p0)  # least squares fit
perr = np.sqrt(np.diag(pcov))                            # standard errors of the two parameters
print(f"f_inf = {popt[0]:.1f} ± {perr[0]:.1f} MPa,  a = {popt[1]:.1f} ± {perr[1]:.1f} days  (± standard error)")
