plt.plot(t, strength_model(t, f_inf, a), label="fitted model")
plt.axhline(f_inf, ls=":", c="k", lw=1, label="final strength f_inf")
plt.plot(a, f_inf / 2, "ko", label="half of f_inf, reached after a days")
plt.xscale("log")                                        # logarithmic age axis: the first days become visible
plt.xticks(mix["age"], mix["age"])                       # label the axis with the test ages
plt.xlabel("Age (days, log scale)"); plt.ylabel("Compressive strength (MPa)"); plt.legend()
plt.show()








Discussion. The two parameters have a direct engineering meaning: according to the model, this mix approaches a final strength of about 51 MPa and reaches half of it after less than four days. Such parameters can be compared between mixes – Exercise 4 relates the final strength to the water/cement ratio.
The plot also shows the limits of the model. The deviations are systematic: between 14 and 90 days the measurements lie below the curve, at 270 days even above the fitted final strength – the real strength keeps growing slowly. The standard errors assume random deviations and are therefore too optimistic. A model with two parameters is a compromise; whether it is good enough depends on the question (Exercise 5 compares it with a logarithmic model).

title: 5  Linear and Nonlinear Regression
text:
5.4 Designed experiments
The concrete data are observational: the mixes were not chosen to separate the effects of the components, so the inputs are correlated – the collinearity problem described above. Such data show which quantities move together, but not which one causes what. In a designed experiment, we set the factors ourselves, uncorrelated with each other; a difference between the levels of a factor can then be attributed to that factor.






Definition: Full factorial design



In a \(2^k\) full factorial design, each of \(k\) factors is set to a low and a high level, coded as −1 and +1, and all \(2^k\) combinations are run. In every pair of columns, all four combinations of levels occur equally often – so the factors are uncorrelated.


Suppose the plant of our scenario wants to tune the new mix with trial batches and varies three factors – cement, water and superplasticizer – each at two levels. A full factorial design needs \(2^3 = 8\) batches:

In the laboratory data, mixes with more superplasticizer contain clearly less water (r = −0.66): superplasticizer is used to save water, so the effects of the two are entangled. In the design, all correlations are zero – and therefore all VIF values equal 1. The effect of a factor is simply the mean strength of the four batches at its high level minus the mean of the four batches at its low level. Both halves contain the same settings of the other factors, so their influences cancel out.
Three additions make a real experiment reliable:

Replicates – running every combination at least twice – estimate the scatter of the results; without them there are no standard errors.
Randomising the order of the runs protects against drifts, e.g. a change in the raw materials during the test series.
Interactions: the effect of one factor can depend on the level of another – superplasticizer, for instance, may help more at low water content. A full factorial design can estimate such interactions, too; how to plan and analyse them is the subject of the literature on design of experiments.

title: 5  Linear and Nonlinear Regression
text:
5.5 Back to the decision
A strength promise concerns individual elements, not the average of many – so the relevant interval is the prediction interval. To be on the safe side, we require that the lower end of the 95 % prediction interval reaches 35 MPa. We check 28 days and, if necessary, search for the earliest age at which the requirement is met.

required = 35.0                                            # MPa
ages = np.arange(1, 366)                                   # every age from 1 day to one year
candidates = pd.concat([new_mix.drop(columns="age")] * len(ages),
                       ignore_index=True).assign(age=ages)  # the new mix at every age
pi_low = model.get_prediction(candidates).summary_frame(alpha=0.05)["obs_ci_lower"].values  # lower 95 % prediction bound
low_28 = pi_low[ages == 28][0]                             # ... at 28 days
print(f"Lower 95 % prediction bound at 28 days: {low_28:.1f} MPa")
if low_28 >= required:
    print("Decision: approve the mix for the 28-day promise.")
elif (pi_low >= required).any():                           # argmax finds the first age that meets the requirement
    print(f"Decision: no promise at 28 days – the model reaches a safe bound only after "
          f"{ages[np.argmax(pi_low >= required)]} days.")
else:
    print("Decision: the model cannot guarantee 35 MPa within a year – adjust the mix (e.g. lower w/c ratio).")

Lower 95 % prediction bound at 28 days: 19.9 MPa
Decision: no promise at 28 days – the model reaches a safe bound only after 158 days.


Not even the mean strength at 28 days reaches the requirement: the model predicts 34.0 MPa, and a single element can fall far below that. A safe promise would only be possible after about five months – a date that relies entirely on the simple \(\ln(\text{age})\) trend of the model and that no customer would accept. In practice, no plant would release a new mix on the basis of a regression model alone. But the model tells us that trial batches of this mix are expected to reach only about 34 MPa at 28 days, and that the mix needs a lower water/cement ratio if 35 MPa are required at that age.






Recommendation to the production manager




Recommendation: do not promise 35 MPa after 28 days. If the customer needs 35 MPa at 28 days, lower the water/cement ratio (currently 180/350 ≈ 0.51) and confirm the strength with trial batches before any promise.
Uncertainty: the model predicts a mean 28-day strength of 34.0 MPa (95 % CI 32.9 to 35.0 MPa) – even the average strength does not reliably reach 35 MPa. For a single element, the 95 % prediction interval reaches down to 19.9 MPa.
Assumptions: the linear model with \(\ln(\text{age})\) describes the new mix, the assumed aggregate contents are close to the real ones, and the laboratory specimens are representative of the plant’s production.
Limits: the residual analysis showed systematic deviations from the model, and many mixes were tested at several ages, so the tests are not fully independent. The prediction for a single new mix is therefore more uncertain than the stated intervals suggest.

title: 5  Linear and Nonlinear Regression
text:
5.6 Summary






Key takeaways




Linear regression is linear in the parameters; transformations of inputs and response make it flexible.
Coefficients mean “change per unit, all else constant” – collinearity makes this hard to interpret.
Every model rests on assumptions: check them with the residuals; R² alone does not validate a model.
Use prediction intervals for single new observations; beware of extrapolation.
Nonlinear models with physically meaningful parameters are fitted with curve_fit; good starting values and a plausibility check of the parameters are essential.
Associations are not causes: observational data show which inputs move together. Where you can choose the settings, a factorial design makes the inputs uncorrelated, so their effects can be separated cleanly.

5.7 Exercises


Replace np.log(age) by age in the linear model. How do R² and the residual plot change? Explain physically why the log transform helps. Useful: replace np.log(age) by age in the formula of smf.ols; model.rsquared, model.resid.
Compute the water/cement ratio and use it as an input instead of water and cement. Compare R² and interpretability with the original model. Useful: conc["wc"] = conc["water"] / conc["cement"] adds the ratio as a column.
Which coefficients of the concrete model are statistically significant? Are the signs plausible from a materials point of view? Relate your answer to the VIF values. Useful: model.params, model.pvalues and the series vif from the live coding.
Fit the strength model \(f_\infty\,t/(a+t)\) to five mixes without slag, fly ash and superplasticizer, each tested at six or more ages. Their cement and water contents in kg/m³ are 540/173, 525/189, 500/200, 475/228 and 339/197. How does the final strength \(f_\infty\) depend on the water/cement ratio? Are all fitted parameters plausible? Useful: select each mix with a mask, as in Nonlinear curve fitting; collect the results as rows of a table (Getting Started with pandas).
Compare the hyperbolic model with a logarithmic model \(f(t) = c_0 + c_1 \ln t\) for the selected mix. Which one extrapolates more plausibly to 1000 days, and why is extrapolation risky anyway? Useful: np.polyfit(np.log(mix["age"]), mix["strength"], deg=1) fits \(c_0 + c_1 \ln t\).
The plant wants to study four factors at two levels each in trial batches. (a) How many batches does a full factorial design need, and how many with two replicates? (b) Why can the design answer the question “What does more superplasticizer do at constant water content?” more reliably than the 1,030 laboratory tests?



5.7.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1






model_lin_age = smf.ols("strength ~ cement + slag + fly_ash + water + superplasticizer"
                        " + coarse_agg + fine_agg + age", data=conc).fit()  # age instead of ln(age)
print(f"R² with log(age): {model.rsquared:.3f},  with age: {model_lin_age.rsquared:.3f}")

Physically, hydration of cement is fast in the first days and slows down later – the strength gain per day decreases with age. \(\ln(\text{age})\) captures this diminishing return.

Solution to Exercise 6






\(2^4 = 16\) batches, 32 with two replicates.
In the design, superplasticizer and water are uncorrelated: half of the batches with much superplasticizer have a high water content, half a low one. The difference of the means therefore shows the effect of superplasticizer alone. In the laboratory data, more superplasticizer usually goes with less water (r = −0.66). The regression has to separate the two effects using the few mixes in which they vary independently – this is why the superplasticizer coefficient is not significant (Exercise 3), although superplasticizer is known to increase strength.

title: 6  Model Selection, Regularisation and Gaussian Processes
text:
6.1 Training error, test error and overfitting
In Chapter 5, we used regression to understand a process: which inputs matter, how strongly, and how certain are we? From this chapter on, the main goal is to predict – and that changes how a model is judged (Section 5.1.5). A model that reproduces its training data perfectly is usually useless. Given enough parameters, any model can pass through every data point – including the noise. What we really want is a model that generalises: that predicts well for new operating points, new parts, next week’s data. This chapter introduces the central idea of machine learning: models must be judged on data they have not seen during fitting.
We study how model complexity affects the prediction error, learn to estimate this error honestly with cross-validation, and meet two ways to control complexity: regularisation, which penalises large coefficients, and Gaussian processes, a Bayesian approach that also tells us how uncertain each prediction is.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Course goal. This chapter contributes to step 4 of the course goals: build and validate prediction and monitoring models.
Datasets in this chapter
Suppose the data are generated by \(y = f(x) + \varepsilon\) with an unknown function \(f\) and noise \(\varepsilon\) with variance \(\sigma^2\). We fit a model \(\hat f\) on a training set. Its error on the training data is always optimistic: the model was tuned to exactly these points. The relevant quantity is the expected error on new data from the same process – the generalisation error or test error.
The practical consequence: never judge a model by its training error. Set data aside for testing, or use cross-validation.
crumbs: 6  Model Selection, Regularisation and Gaussian Processes

title: 6  Model Selection, Regularisation and Gaussian Processes
text:
Figure 6.1: Under- and overfitting. A model that is too simple (left) misses the structure; a model that is too flexible (centre) follows the noise of the training data. The test error is U-shaped in model complexity (right), while the training error keeps decreasing.









Bias–variance decomposition



For squared error loss, the expected test error at a point \(x\) decomposes into \[\begin{aligned} E\big[(y - \hat f(x))^2\big] &= \underbrace{\big(E[\hat f(x)] - f(x)\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\text{Var}\big(\hat f(x)\big)}_{\text{variance}} \\ &\quad + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible noise}}. \end{aligned}\] Simple models have high bias (systematic error, underfitting); flexible models have high variance (they change strongly with the training sample, overfitting). The best model balances both. The noise \(\sigma^2\) cannot be reduced by any model.
crumbs: 6  Model Selection, Regularisation and Gaussian Processes

title: 6  Model Selection, Regularisation and Gaussian Processes
text:
6.2 Cross-validation






Definition: k-fold cross-validation



Split the data randomly into \(k\) parts (folds) of equal size. For each fold, train the model on the other \(k-1\) folds and compute the error on the held-out fold. The cross-validation error is the average over the \(k\) folds. Typical values are \(k = 5\) or \(k = 10\).








Figure 6.2: 5-fold cross-validation: each observation is used for testing exactly once and for training four times.



Cross-validation uses the data efficiently and gives, besides the mean, an idea of the variability of the error across folds. It is the standard tool to select a model or a hyperparameter (polynomial degree, regularisation strength). If the selected model’s performance must be reported, use a separate test set that was never touched during selection – otherwise the reported error is again optimistic.






Pitfall: data leakage



Any information from the test data that influences training makes the test error too optimistic. Typical leaks: scaling or imputing with statistics of the full dataset, selecting features by their correlation with the target on all data, random splits of time series (Chapter 11), or several rows of the same part/machine in both training and test set. In scikit-learn, putting all preprocessing steps into a Pipeline ensures that they are fitted inside each training fold only.








Engineering practice: one median for training and test data



In Chapter 2, the gaps in SECOM were filled with medians. Which median fills the gaps in the test data? The training median – not one computed from the test data. The median is a parameter of the model, just like a regression coefficient: it is estimated once from the training data and then applied unchanged to all new data. Three reasons:

In operation there is no “test median”: new data often arrive one observation at a time – a single production run, a single sensor reading – and a median cannot be computed from one value.
The model must always receive the same preprocessing. If a gap was filled with 52.3 during training but with 48.9 during testing, the model sees inputs it was not trained on.
A test median would itself be a small leak: the prediction for one test point would depend on the other test points.

The same holds for scaling, PCA and every other preprocessing step: fit on the training data, transform on training and test data – exactly what a Pipeline does. If the distribution of new data drifts away from the training data, the remedy is to monitor the drift and retrain – not to compute statistics on the test data. (One legitimate exception: if a whole batch – say all wafers of a lot – is always available at prediction time, statistics per batch may be used, but then in exactly the same way during training.)

title: 6  Model Selection, Regularisation and Gaussian Processes
text:
6.3 Regularisation: Ridge and Lasso
Instead of choosing between few and many features, we can keep a flexible model and penalise large coefficients:






Definition: Ridge and Lasso regression



\[\begin{aligned} \text{Ridge:}&\quad \min_\beta \sum_i (y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_j \beta_j^2, \\ \text{Lasso:}&\quad \min_\beta \sum_i (y_i - x_i^\top\beta)^2 + \lambda \sum_j |\beta_j|. \end{aligned}\] The hyperparameter \(\lambda \ge 0\) (in scikit-learn: alpha) controls the strength of the penalty: \(\lambda = 0\) gives ordinary least squares, large \(\lambda\) shrinks all coefficients towards zero.


Ridge shrinks coefficients smoothly and copes well with collinear inputs. Lasso can set coefficients exactly to zero and thus performs feature selection. Because the penalty depends on the size of the coefficients, the inputs must be standardised first – otherwise the penalty depends on the units. \(\lambda\) is chosen by cross-validation (RidgeCV, LassoCV).

6.4.1 How complex should the model be?
We fit polynomial models of increasing degree – with five inputs, degree 6 already produces several hundred terms – and compare training and cross-validation errors.

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, RidgeCV
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_validate

cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
rows = []
for degree in range(1, 7):
    pipe = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), StandardScaler(), LinearRegression())
    res = cross_validate(pipe, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error",
                         return_train_score=True)
    rows.append({"degree": degree, "terms": PolynomialFeatures(degree).fit(X).n_output_features_,
                 "train RMSE": -res["train_score"].mean(), "CV RMSE": -res["test_score"].mean()})
scores = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("degree")
ax = scores[["train RMSE", "CV RMSE"]].plot(marker="o")
ax.set(ylabel="RMSE (dB)", ylim=(0, None))

Discussion. The training error decreases steadily with the degree – more terms can always fit the training data better. The cross-validation error first decreases (less bias) and eventually increases again (more variance); its minimum indicates a good degree. The growing gap between training and CV error is the signature of overfitting. Note also the scale: a straight-line model leaves errors of several dB, which matters for acoustic requirements.


6.4.2 Regularisation in action
Instead of picking the degree exactly, we can use a rich model and let Ridge regression control its complexity. RidgeCV selects \(\lambda\) by internal cross-validation; the outer cross-validation evaluates the whole procedure.

alphas = np.logspace(-4, 3, 30)        # 30 candidate values from 10^-4 to 10^3, evenly spaced on a log scale
ridge = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(5), StandardScaler(), RidgeCV(alphas=alphas))
res_ridge = cross_validate(ridge, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
print(f"Ridge, degree 5: CV RMSE = {-res_ridge['test_score'].mean():.2f} dB")

Ridge, degree 5: CV RMSE = 3.14 dB








Engineering practice: nested model selection



Here, cross-validation happens at two levels: RidgeCV chooses \(\lambda\) on the training part of each outer fold, and the outer loop measures how well the whole procedure (including the choice of \(\lambda\)) generalises. This nested cross-validation gives an honest estimate. Choosing \(\lambda\) on the same folds used to report the error would again be optimistic.

title: 6  Model Selection, Regularisation and Gaussian Processes
section: 6.5 Gaussian process regression: predictions with uncertainty
text:
6.5 Gaussian process regression: predictions with uncertainty
Polynomial and linear models assume a fixed functional form. A Gaussian process (GP) assumes much less: only that the response changes smoothly with the inputs. It combines this assumption with the measurements by Bayes’ theorem (Section 3.5) and therefore delivers, for every input, a prediction and its uncertainty. We explain the idea first with a single measurement, using numbers of the power plant from Chapter 1; Figure 6.3 shows the two steps.
Prior: what we assume before measuring. The unknown quantity is the value \(f(x)\) of the response at every input \(x\) – here the output of the plant at the ambient temperature \(x\). Before any measurement, a GP assumes two things:

At every input, \(f(x)\) is normally distributed with the same mean \(m\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_f\). Here: the output lies around \(m = 455\) MW, give or take \(\sigma_f = 17\) MW.
The values at two inputs \(x\) and \(x'\) are correlated – the more strongly, the closer the inputs are. The kernel specifies this correlation; the most common choice is \[\rho(x, x') = \exp\left(-\frac{(x - x')^2}{2\ell^2}\right).\] The length scale \(\ell\) states how far the similarity reaches: at a distance of \(\ell\), the correlation is 0.61, at \(2\ell\) 0.14, at \(3\ell\) practically 0. Here we use \(\ell = 5\) °C.

Step 1 – Bayes at the measured input. At \(x_1 = 20\) °C we measure \(y_1 = 440\) MW; the measurement scatters with a standard deviation \(\sigma_n = 10\) MW around the true value. Prior and measurement are two pieces of information about the same value \(f(x_1)\). Bayes’ theorem for densities – posterior ∝ likelihood × prior – combines them. For two normal distributions, the posterior is again normal, with mean and standard deviation
\[\mu_1 = m + w\,(y_1 - m), \qquad \sigma_1 = \sigma_f\sqrt{1 - w}, \qquad w = \frac{\sigma_f^2}{\sigma_f^2 + \sigma_n^2}.\]
The weight \(w\) between 0 and 1 states how much the measurement counts compared with the prior. Here \(w = 17^2/(17^2 + 10^2) = 0.74\), so \(\mu_1 = 455 + 0.74 \cdot (440 - 455) = 443.9\) MW and \(\sigma_1 = 8.6\) MW – more precise than prior and measurement alone. A precise measurement (\(\sigma_n \ll \sigma_f\)) gives \(w \approx 1\): the GP follows the measurement. A noisy one pulls the result towards the prior mean.
Step 2 – transfer to other inputs. Nothing was measured at 22 °C, but the value there is correlated with the one at 20 °C, with \(\rho = 0.92\). Therefore the fraction \(\rho\) of the correction found at 20 °C carries over:
\[\mu(x) = m + \rho\,w\,(y_1 - m), \qquad \sigma(x) = \sigma_f\sqrt{1 - \rho^2 w}, \qquad \rho = \rho(x, x_1).\]
At 22 °C this gives 444.7 ± 10.3 MW, at 30 °C (\(\rho = 0.14\)) 453.5 ± 16.9 MW – almost the prior. At the measured input itself (\(\rho = 1\)), the formulas give step 1 again.






Figure 6.3: A Gaussian process with a single measurement. Left: Bayes at the measured input – prior and measurement combine into the posterior. Right: the correction carries over to other temperatures according to the correlation ρ; far from the measurement, prediction and uncertainty return to the prior.



Many measurements. With many measurements, every measurement pulls its neighbourhood, and the GP combines all of them at once; neighbouring measurements that carry the same information are not counted twice. The software evaluates the same logic in matrix form (extension box below). Figure 6.4 shows the result for five measurements:

Near the measurements, the uncertainty is small – it cannot become smaller than the measurement noise allows.
Between the measurements, it grows – the more, the farther apart they are compared with \(\ell\).
Beyond the data, the correlation carries the trend of the data on for about one length scale. Several length scales away, the prediction returns to the prior mean \(m\) and the uncertainty to \(\sigma_f\): a GP does not extrapolate a trend indefinitely.

Fitting. \(\sigma_f\), \(\ell\) and \(\sigma_n\) are the hyperparameters of the GP. The software fits them by maximum likelihood (Chapter 3): they are chosen such that the measured data become most plausible – no cross-validation needed.






Figure 6.4: A Gaussian process before and after observing data. Left: random functions that satisfy the prior assumptions – at every input, values around the mean with standard deviation \(\sigma_f\), and neighbouring values correlated as the kernel prescribes, hence smooth curves. Right: after five noisy measurements, the posterior mean passes close to the data; the uncertainty band is narrow near the measurements and wide in between and outside.









Extension: where do the formulas come from?





Step 1. Prior and likelihood are normal densities: \[p(f) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{(f - m)^2}{2\sigma_f^2}\right), \qquad p(y_1 \mid f) \propto \exp\left(-\frac{(y_1 - f)^2}{2\sigma_n^2}\right).\] Their product, the posterior, has an exponent that is quadratic in \(f\) – so the posterior is a normal density, too. Its variance \(\sigma_1^2\) follows from the factor of \(f^2\), \(1/\sigma_1^2 = 1/\sigma_f^2 + 1/\sigma_n^2\), and completing the square gives its mean \(\mu_1 = \sigma_1^2\,(m/\sigma_f^2 + y_1/\sigma_n^2)\). Rearranged, this is \(\mu_1 = m + w\,(y_1 - m)\) and \(\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_f^2\,(1 - w)\).
Step 2. \(f(x)\) and \(f(x_1)\) are normally distributed with the same mean \(m\), the same standard deviation \(\sigma_f\) and correlation \(\rho\). If \(f(x_1)\) were known exactly, the best prediction of \(f(x)\) would be the regression line \(m + \rho\,(f(x_1) - m)\) – with equal standard deviations, its slope is the correlation – and the share \(\rho^2\) of the variance would be explained, as \(R^2\) in a simple regression. The rest, \(\sigma_f^2(1 - \rho^2)\), would remain. Since \(f(x_1)\) is only known as \(\mu_1 \pm \sigma_1\), its uncertainty is passed on with the factor \(\rho^2\): \[\mu(x) = m + \rho\,(\mu_1 - m), \qquad \sigma^2(x) = \sigma_f^2\,(1 - \rho^2) + \rho^2\,\sigma_1^2 = \sigma_f^2\,(1 - \rho^2 w).\] The two parts of the variance have the same structure as the prediction interval in Chapter 5: scatter around the curve plus uncertainty of the curve.
Many measurements. With measurements \(y_1, \dots, y_n\) at \(x_1, \dots, x_n\), the matrix \(K\) contains the prior covariances \(\sigma_f^2\,\rho(x_i, x_j)\) between the measured inputs, and the vector \(k(x)\) the covariances \(\sigma_f^2\,\rho(x, x_i)\) between \(x\) and the measured inputs. Then \[\mu(x) = m + k(x)^\top (K + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1}(y - m), \qquad \sigma^2(x) = \sigma_f^2 - k(x)^\top (K + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1} k(x).\] For a single measurement, \(K = \sigma_f^2\) and \(k = \sigma_f^2 \rho\), and the formulas of step 2 follow.



GPs are popular as surrogate models for expensive simulations and experiments, where data are scarce and knowing the uncertainty matters. Their limitation: the computational cost grows with \(n^3\), so they suit datasets up to a few thousand points.






Engineering practice: Gaussian process or a fixed functional form?



A GP needs no functional form – but that is not always an advantage.

GP: few, expensive data points, a smooth response, and the uncertainty matters – surrogate models, design of experiments.
Physical or empirical model (Chapter 5): if its form is right, it extrapolates sensibly beyond the data, while a GP returns to the prior mean. Its parameters have a meaning, such as the final strength \(f_\infty\), and can be interpreted and compared.
Many inputs, thresholds, large datasets: with many inputs, distances lose their meaning; the smoothness assumption blurs steps and thresholds. Tree ensembles (Chapter 8) are usually the better choice for large tabular datasets.
Best of both: use the physical model as the prior mean and let the GP learn only the deviations from it.



We first look at a one-dimensional example: the power output of the combined cycle power plant as a function of ambient temperature, learned from only 15 measurements.

from sklearn.gaussian_process import GaussianProcessRegressor
from sklearn.gaussian_process.kernels import RBF, WhiteKernel, ConstantKernel as C

ccpp = fetch_ucirepo(id=294)
pp = pd.concat([ccpp.data.features, ccpp.data.targets], axis=1)
few = pp.sample(15, random_state=1)

# kernel = sigma_f² x correlation with length scale l + measurement noise sigma_n² (starting values)
kernel = C(100.0) * RBF(length_scale=10.0) + WhiteKernel(noise_level=10.0)
gp = GaussianProcessRegressor(kernel=kernel, normalize_y=True,   # normalize_y: standardised outputs, m = their mean
                              random_state=0)
gp.fit(few[["AT"]], few["PE"])
print("Fitted kernel:", gp.kernel_)

T = np.linspace(-5, 45, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
mean, std = gp.predict(pd.DataFrame(T, columns=["AT"]), return_std=True)
plt.scatter(pp["AT"], pp["PE"], s=2, c="lightgray", label="all data (unknown to the model)")
plt.scatter(few["AT"], few["PE"], c="C3", zorder=3, label="15 training points")
plt.plot(T, mean, label="GP mean")
plt.fill_between(T.ravel(), mean - 1.96 * std, mean + 1.96 * std, alpha=0.3, label="95 % interval")
plt.xlabel("Ambient temperature (°C)"); plt.ylabel("Power output (MW)"); plt.legend()
plt.show()

Fitted kernel: 2.27**2 * RBF(length_scale=29.5) + WhiteKernel(noise_level=0.118)









Discussion. With only 15 points, the GP recovers the almost linear trend. The printed kernel contains the three fitted hyperparameters. Because of normalize_y=True, the GP works with standardised outputs: the prior mean \(m\) is the mean of the 15 measured outputs, and \(\sigma_f\) and \(\sigma_n\) are measured in units of their standard deviation.

2.27**2 is \(\sigma_f^2\): before the data, the output may deviate from \(m\) by about 2.3 standard deviations.
RBF(length_scale=29.5): the length scale \(\ell = 29.5\) °C is large compared with the measured range. Even values 30 °C apart are correlated with \(\rho = 0.60\), so the curve can bend only gently.
WhiteKernel(noise_level=0.118) is \(\sigma_n^2\): the measurements scatter by \(\sigma_n = \sqrt{0.118} \approx 0.34\) standard deviations around the curve.

Outside the measured temperatures (about 6 to 30 °C), the band widens. The mean, however, continues the downward trend: with \(\ell = 29.5\) °C, the correlation carries it over the whole plotted range; only several length scales away would the prediction return to \(m\). Note also that the band describes single new measurements: with a WhiteKernel, predict(..., return_std=True) includes the measurement noise – like the prediction interval in Chapter 5. A polynomial would extrapolate without any warning.

# GP on the full airfoil problem (5 inputs), compared with the polynomial ridge model
gp_air = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), GaussianProcessRegressor(
    kernel=C(1.0) * RBF(length_scale=np.ones(5)) + WhiteKernel(0.1), normalize_y=True))
res_gp = cross_validate(gp_air, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error")
print(f"Gaussian process: CV RMSE = {-res_gp['test_score'].mean():.2f} dB")

Gaussian process: CV RMSE = 1.89 dB


Here the kernel has one length scale per input (length_scale=np.ones(5) sets their starting values). After fitting, a long length scale indicates that the output changes slowly with that input – a built-in measure of relevance.

title: 6  Model Selection, Regularisation and Gaussian Processes
text:
6.6 Back to the decision
The requirement refers to new conditions, so we compare the cross-validation errors – never the training errors. Among the models that meet the 2 dB requirement, we release the simplest one; if none meets it, the tunnel cannot yet be replaced.

cv_rmse = {
    "linear model": scores.loc[1, "CV RMSE"],
    f"polynomial (degree {scores['CV RMSE'].idxmin()})": scores["CV RMSE"].min(),
    "polynomial degree 5 + Ridge": -res_ridge["test_score"].mean(),
    "Gaussian process": -res_gp["test_score"].mean(),
}
for name, e in cv_rmse.items():
    print(f"{name:32s} CV RMSE = {e:.2f} dB {'✓' if e < 2.0 else '✗'}")
ok = [name for name, e in cv_rmse.items() if e < 2.0]
print("Decision:", f"release '{ok[0]}' for the screening." if ok else "no model is accurate enough – keep using the tunnel.")

linear model                     CV RMSE = 4.83 dB ✗
polynomial (degree 4)            CV RMSE = 3.19 dB ✗
polynomial degree 5 + Ridge      CV RMSE = 3.14 dB ✗
Gaussian process                 CV RMSE = 1.89 dB ✓
Decision: release 'Gaussian process' for the screening.


The models are listed from simple to complex, so the first model that meets the requirement is released. Two caveats belong in the recommendation: cross-validation estimates the error for conditions similar to the measured ones – for configurations outside the measured ranges (e.g. larger chords or higher speeds) the error can be much larger, and the Gaussian process at least signals this through its uncertainty. And the best candidates of the screening should still be confirmed in the tunnel.

title: 6  Model Selection, Regularisation and Gaussian Processes
section: 6.7 Extension: Bayesian optimisation – design of experiments with a GP
text:
6.7 Extension: Bayesian optimisation – design of experiments with a GP
Extension – optional material, not required for the exam.
When every experiment is expensive – a test bench run, a CFD simulation, a production trial – we want to find the optimum with as few runs as possible. Bayesian optimisation fits a GP to the runs so far and chooses the next run where an acquisition function is largest. The popular expected improvement (EI) is
\[\text{EI}(x) = (\mu(x) - y^*)\,\Phi(z) + \sigma(x)\,\varphi(z), \qquad z = \frac{\mu(x) - y^*}{\sigma(x)},\]
where \(\mu(x)\) and \(\sigma(x)\) are the GP’s predicted mean and standard deviation at \(x\), \(y^*\) is the best result so far and \(\Phi, \varphi\) are the standard normal CDF and PDF. EI is large where the predicted mean is high (exploitation) or the uncertainty is large (exploration).
The example uses a simulated “experiment”: the yield of a process as a function of temperature, which the algorithm does not know.

from scipy.stats import norm

def experiment(temp):                       # unknown to the optimiser
    return 40 + 45 * np.exp(-((temp - 172) / 25) ** 2) + 5 * np.sin(temp / 9)

grid = np.linspace(100, 250, 500).reshape(-1, 1)
X_runs = np.array([[110.0], [180.0], [240.0]])            # three initial runs
y_runs = experiment(X_runs.ravel())

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(14, 6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax in axes.ravel():
    gp_bo = GaussianProcessRegressor(C(1.0) * RBF(20.0), normalize_y=True, alpha=1e-6)
    gp_bo.fit(X_runs, y_runs)
    mu, sd = gp_bo.predict(grid, return_std=True)
    best = y_runs.max()
    z = (mu - best) / np.maximum(sd, 1e-9)
    ei = (mu - best) * norm.cdf(z) + sd * norm.pdf(z)       # expected improvement
    x_next = grid[np.argmax(ei)]

    ax.plot(grid, experiment(grid.ravel()), "k:", lw=1, label="true (unknown)")
    ax.plot(grid, mu, label="GP mean")
    ax.fill_between(grid.ravel(), mu - 1.96 * sd, mu + 1.96 * sd, alpha=0.25)
    ax.scatter(X_runs, y_runs, c="C3", zorder=3, label="runs")
    ax.axvline(x_next[0], c="C2", ls="--", label="next run")
    ax.set_title(f"{len(y_runs)} runs, best yield {best:.1f}")

    X_runs = np.vstack([X_runs, x_next])
    y_runs = np.append(y_runs, experiment(x_next[0]))
axes[0, 0].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.supxlabel("Temperature (°C)"); fig.supylabel("Yield (%)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Discussion. After a few iterations the algorithm concentrates its runs near the optimum, while regions that cannot contain a better result are not explored further. Compared with a classical grid (Chapter 5), Bayesian optimisation adapts the design sequentially to the results – very efficient when runs are expensive and can be done one after another. Once the optimum is found, EI becomes small everywhere and the proposals cluster; in practice one stops when the expected improvement falls below a threshold.

title: 6  Model Selection, Regularisation and Gaussian Processes
text:
6.8 Summary






Key takeaways




Test honestly: the training error is optimistic; judge models by their error on unseen data.
The test error is U-shaped in model complexity: too simple → bias, too flexible → variance.
k-fold cross-validation selects models and hyperparameters; preprocessing belongs inside the pipeline.
Ridge and Lasso control complexity by penalising coefficients (standardise first!).
Gaussian processes combine a smoothness assumption (prior) with the measurements by Bayes’ theorem. They give predictions with uncertainty – valuable for small data and expensive experiments – and return to the prior far from the data.

title: 6  Model Selection, Regularisation and Gaussian Processes
text:
6.9 Exercises


Repeat the degree study for the power plant data (pp, target PE). Why does the curve look so different from the airfoil case?
Why must the StandardScaler be part of the pipeline instead of being fitted on all data beforehand? Construct an example in which the difference becomes visible. Useful: a step that uses the target makes the effect large – SelectKBest(f_regression, k=20) from sklearn.feature_selection keeps the 20 features most correlated with the target; pure noise data come from rng.normal(size=(100, 2000)).
Plot predicted vs. measured sound pressure level for the Ridge model, using cross_val_predict. In which range does the model fail? Useful: cross_val_predict(ridge, X, y, cv=cv) from sklearn.model_selection returns for every observation the prediction of the fold model that did not see it.
GP: increase the number of training points from 15 to 50 and 200. How does the uncertainty band change? What happens outside the measured temperature range? Useful: pp.sample(n, random_state=1) and the kernel and plotting code of the live coding.
A GP for the plant output has the prior mean 455 MW, \(\sigma_f = 17\) MW and the length scale \(\ell = 5\) °C. A single measurement at 25 °C gives 450 MW, with a measurement scatter of \(\sigma_n = 5\) MW. Compute the prediction and its standard deviation by hand at 25, 27 and 35 °C, and explain the three results.
Replace Ridge by LassoCV (degree 3). How many of the polynomial features survive? Useful: make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(3), StandardScaler(), LassoCV(cv=5)); after fit, pipe[-1].coef_ contains the coefficients of the last step and pipe[0].get_feature_names_out(X.columns) the names of the polynomial terms.
(Extension) Bayesian optimisation: start with a different set of three runs. Does the algorithm still find the optimum? Compare with a regular grid of the same number of runs. Useful: change X_runs in the code of the extension.



6.9.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1






X_pp, y_pp = pp[["AT", "V", "AP", "RH"]], pp["PE"]
rows = []
for degree in range(1, 6):
    pipe = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), StandardScaler(), LinearRegression())
    res = cross_validate(pipe, X_pp, y_pp, cv=cv, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error",
                         return_train_score=True)
    rows.append({"degree": degree, "train RMSE": -res["train_score"].mean(),
                 "CV RMSE": -res["test_score"].mean()})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("degree").round(3)

The power plant relationship is nearly linear, there are only four inputs and almost 10,000 observations. Higher degrees improve the fit only slightly, and training and CV errors stay close together – with this much data relative to the number of parameters, overfitting hardly occurs. The remaining error is dominated by the irreducible noise. The airfoil problem is more nonlinear and has six times less data, so flexibility helps first and then overfits.









Solution to Exercise 2





Fitting the scaler on all data uses the means and standard deviations of the test folds – a (here mild) form of leakage. The effect is small for scaling with many observations but becomes large for steps that use the target, e.g. selecting the features most correlated with \(y\) before cross-validation:

from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_regression

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
noise = pd.DataFrame(rng.normal(size=(100, 2000)))          # pure noise features
target = pd.Series(rng.normal(size=100))                     # unrelated target

leaky_X = SelectKBest(f_regression, k=20).fit_transform(noise, target)   # selection on ALL data
leaky = cross_validate(LinearRegression(), leaky_X, target, cv=cv, scoring="r2")["test_score"].mean()
proper = cross_validate(make_pipeline(SelectKBest(f_regression, k=20), LinearRegression()),
                        noise, target, cv=cv, scoring="r2")["test_score"].mean()
print(f"CV R² with leaky selection: {leaky:.2f},  inside the pipeline: {proper:.2f}")

CV R² with leaky selection: 0.47,  inside the pipeline: -0.32


With selection outside the pipeline, the “model” appears to predict pure noise; inside the pipeline the CV R² is correctly around zero or negative.









Solution to Exercise 3






from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict

y_hat = cross_val_predict(ridge, X, y, cv=cv)
plt.scatter(y, y_hat, s=8, alpha=0.5)
lims = [y.min(), y.max()]
plt.plot(lims, lims, "k--")
plt.xlabel("Measured SPL (dB)"); plt.ylabel("Predicted SPL (dB)")
plt.show()








cross_val_predict returns for each observation the prediction of the model that did not see it during training. Deviations are typically largest at the extremes – the quietest and loudest conditions are underrepresented, and the model shrinks predictions towards the mean (a typical effect of regularisation). Plotting the residuals against frequency shows that some frequency ranges are captured less well than others.









Solution to Exercise 4






fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4), sharey=True)
for ax, n_train in zip(axes, [15, 50, 200]):
    sub = pp.sample(n_train, random_state=1)
    g = GaussianProcessRegressor(kernel=kernel, normalize_y=True, random_state=0).fit(sub[["AT"]], sub["PE"])
    m, s = g.predict(pd.DataFrame(T, columns=["AT"]), return_std=True)
    ax.scatter(sub["AT"], sub["PE"], s=8, c="C3")
    ax.plot(T, m); ax.fill_between(T.ravel(), m - 1.96 * s, m + 1.96 * s, alpha=0.3)
    ax.set(title=f"n = {n_train}", xlabel="AT (°C)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("PE (MW)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








With more data the band becomes narrower, but it does not shrink to zero: because the kernel contains a WhiteKernel, the predicted standard deviation includes the measurement noise, so the band approaches the scatter of individual observations (similar to a prediction interval). The uncertainty about the trend itself, however, decreases. Outside the data range the band still widens; with more points the trend is better determined, so the widening is less dramatic. Where there are no data at all, data elsewhere can only reduce the uncertainty as far as the kernel assumes smoothness.

Solution to Exercise 7





Change X_runs to, e.g., [[100.0], [130.0], [250.0]] and rerun the loop. Usually the algorithm still finds the region of the optimum, because the large uncertainty in unexplored regions makes EI large there. With an unlucky start and a misleading local maximum (the sine term), it may need more iterations. A regular grid of 8 runs over 100–250 °C has a spacing of about 21 °C; the best grid point can easily be several percent below the true optimum, and the grid cannot refine itself. Bayesian optimisation pays off when each run is expensive and runs can be performed one after another.

title: 7  Classification
text:
7.1 Three ways to classify
Many engineering decisions are categorical: a part is OK or not OK, a machine will fail within the next shift or not, a fault belongs to type A, B or C. Predicting such a category from measured data is called classification. It is the core of automated quality inspection, predictive maintenance and fault diagnosis.
Classification raises questions that regression does not. How do we measure the quality of a classifier when failures are rare? What is worse – a false alarm or a missed failure? And how do we choose the decision threshold that turns a predicted probability into an action? This chapter introduces three basic classifiers and, just as importantly, the metrics to evaluate them honestly.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Course goal. This chapter contributes to step 4 of the course goals: build and validate prediction and monitoring models.
Datasets in this chapter
In classification, the response \(y\) takes one of \(K\) classes; in the binary case \(y \in \{0, 1\}\) (e.g. 1 = failure). Most classifiers estimate the probability \(P(y = 1 \mid x)\) and predict class 1 if this probability exceeds a threshold, by default 0.5.

title: 7  Classification
text:
7.1.1 Logistic regression






Definition: Logistic regression



The probability of class 1 is modelled as \[P(y = 1 \mid x) = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta^\top x), \qquad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}.\] Equivalently, the log-odds are linear in the inputs: \(\ln\frac{P(y=1\mid x)}{1 - P(y=1\mid x)} = \beta_0 + \beta^\top x\). The parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood.


Logistic regression is the classification counterpart of linear regression: simple, fast, interpretable. A coefficient \(\beta_j\) means that one unit more of \(x_j\) multiplies the odds of failure by \(e^{\beta_j}\) (the odds ratio). Its decision boundary – the set of \(x\) where the probability equals the threshold – is a straight line (a hyperplane). Nonlinear boundaries require engineered features such as products or squares.
Fitting by maximum likelihood. Each record is a Bernoulli experiment, as in the inspection example of Chapter 3 – but now every record \(i\) has its own failure probability \(p_i = \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta^\top x_i)\), which depends on its inputs. The likelihood of the observed labels \(y_i\) is therefore a function of the coefficients: \[L(\beta) = \prod_i p_i^{\,y_i}\,(1 - p_i)^{1 - y_i}.\] Each factor is the probability that the model gave to what actually happened: \(p_i\) for a failure, \(1 - p_i\) for an OK record. The logarithm with reversed sign is the quantity that is minimised, the log-loss or cross-entropy: \[-\ln L(\beta) = -\sum_i \big[y_i \ln p_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - p_i)\big].\] In each term, only \(-\ln\)(probability of the true class) remains, so confident mistakes are expensive:



probability given to the true class
0.9
0.5
0.1
0.01




contribution to the log-loss
0.11
0.69
2.3
4.6



The squared error of linear regression arises in the same way, as the negative log-likelihood of normally distributed errors (Chapter 5). In general, a loss function is the negative log-likelihood of an assumed distribution of the data: choosing a loss means making an assumption about the data.
Unlike least squares, there is no closed-form solution: \(p_i\) depends nonlinearly on \(\beta\), so the software improves the coefficients step by step (max_iter limits the number of steps). The log-loss of logistic regression is convex – it has a single minimum, which the iteration finds from any starting point, unlike the nonlinear fits of Chapter 5. Note that scikit-learn’s LogisticRegression adds a Ridge penalty by default (C=1.0, Chapter 6; a larger C weakens it): it shrinks the coefficients slightly, which matters when they are read as odds ratios.


7.1.2 k-nearest neighbours (kNN)
kNN stores the training data and classifies a new point by majority vote of its \(k\) nearest training points. It makes no assumption about the shape of the boundary, but it depends entirely on the distance measure – inputs must be standardised, otherwise the input with the largest numerical range dominates. Small \(k\) gives ragged boundaries (high variance), large \(k\) smooth ones (high bias).


7.1.3 Decision trees
A decision tree splits the input space step by step with simple rules such as “torque > 55 Nm”. At each node, the split is chosen that makes the resulting groups as pure as possible, measured e.g. by the Gini impurity \(G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2\), where \(p_k\) is the share of class \(k\) in the node. A small example: ten milling operations, three of which failed.

Before any split, the failure share is 0.3, and \(G = 1 - (0.3^2 + 0.7^2) = 0.42\). The tree tries every possible threshold – one between each pair of neighbouring values – and computes the impurity of the two groups, weighted by their size:

torque > 50 Nm: left 6 operations without failure (\(G = 0\)), right 3 failures out of 4 (\(G = 1 - 0.75^2 - 0.25^2 = 0.375\)); weighted \(0.6 \cdot 0 + 0.4 \cdot 0.375 = 0.15\),
torque > 41 Nm: weighted 0.30; torque > 60 Nm: weighted 0.18; all other thresholds give between 0.24 and 0.40.

The tree takes the split with the smallest weighted impurity, “torque > 50 Nm”, and repeats the same search – over all inputs – in each of the two groups, until the groups are pure or the maximum depth is reached. For a numeric target (a regression tree), the same procedure uses the variance of the target in each group instead of the Gini impurity.
Figure 7.1 shows the same procedure with two inputs. Each split is a line parallel to one axis – vertical for a split on \(x_1\), horizontal for a split on \(x_2\) – and it divides only the rectangle in which it is made. For each rectangle, the tree chooses input and threshold anew: the same input can be used several times in a row, and an input that never helps is never used. Pure rectangles are not split further. Some splits do not change the predicted class but make one side purer: at depth 4, bottom right, an orange rectangle is split into two orange ones. Another split at depth 4 cuts off a sliver with a single point – too thin to see. Here the tree starts to follow single points.






Figure 7.1: A decision tree with two inputs, built level by level. Black: the splits added at each depth; grey: the splits of the levels above. The shading shows the predicted class.



Trees are easy to explain to colleagues and can capture interactions and thresholds, but a single deep tree overfits strongly; its depth must be limited. Chapter 8 shows how combining many trees fixes this.






Figure 7.2: Decision boundaries of the three classifiers on a two-dimensional toy problem. Logistic regression draws a straight line, kNN follows the local structure of the data, and a decision tree uses axis-parallel steps.

title: 7  Classification
text:
7.2 Evaluating classifiers






Definition: Confusion matrix and derived metrics












predicted OK (0)
predicted failure (1)




actual OK (0)
true negative (TN)
false positive (FP) – false alarm


actual failure (1)
false negative (FN) – missed failure
true positive (TP)




Accuracy = (TP + TN) / all
Precision = TP / (TP + FP): how many alarms are real?
Recall (sensitivity, detection rate) = TP / (TP + FN): how many failures are detected?
F1 score = harmonic mean of precision and recall
Balanced accuracy = mean of the recall of both classes









Pitfall: accuracy on imbalanced data



If 3 % of the records are failures, a “model” that always predicts “OK” reaches 97 % accuracy – and detects nothing. With rare events, accuracy is almost meaningless. Use precision, recall, F1 or balanced accuracy, and always look at the confusion matrix.



7.2.1 How much can we trust an alarm?
Precision answers the question the maintenance team asks first: if the alarm fires, how likely is a real failure? It is the conditional probability \(P(F \mid A)\) of a failure \(F\) given an alarm \(A\). Bayes’ theorem (Section 3.5) relates it to the properties of the detector: \(P(A \mid F)\) is the recall, \(P(A \mid \bar F) = \text{FP}/(\text{FP} + \text{TN})\) the false alarm rate, and \(P(F)\) the share of failures, the base rate: \[P(F \mid A) = \frac{P(A \mid F)\,P(F)}{P(A \mid F)\,P(F) + P(A \mid \bar F)\,P(\bar F)}.\] Chapter 3 computed an example: with a recall of 95 %, a false alarm rate of 5 % and a base rate of 1 %, only 16 % of the alarms are real. Five out of six alarms are false – not because the detector is bad, but because failures are rare.






Pitfall: base rate neglect



Intuition tends to confuse \(P(A \mid F)\) (“the alarm detects 95 % of all failures”) with \(P(F \mid A)\) (“95 % of all alarms are real”). When the base rate \(P(F)\) is small, the two differ dramatically: even a detector with high recall and a low false alarm rate can have a low precision.




7.2.2 Thresholds, ROC and precision–recall curves
Lowering the threshold produces more alarms: recall increases, precision usually decreases. Instead of judging a single threshold, we can look at all thresholds at once:

The ROC curve plots the true positive rate (recall) against the false positive rate FP/(FP + TN). The area under the curve (ROC AUC) is the probability that a randomly chosen failure gets a higher score than a randomly chosen OK record; 0.5 = random guessing, 1 = perfect ranking.
The precision–recall curve plots precision against recall. For rare events it is more informative than ROC, because the false positive rate stays small even when the false alarms far outnumber the true alarms.







Engineering practice: choose the threshold by costs



The threshold 0.5 is arbitrary. If a missed failure costs \(c_{FN}\) and a false alarm \(c_{FP}\), choose the threshold that minimises the total cost \(c_{FN} \cdot \text{FN} + c_{FP} \cdot \text{FP}\) – on validation data, not on the test data. For well-calibrated probabilities – among all records with a predicted probability of 5 %, about 5 % actually fail – the optimal threshold is \(c_{FP}/(c_{FP} + c_{FN})\): if a miss is 20 times as expensive as a false alarm, alarm already at a failure probability of about 5 %.




7.2.3 Strategies for imbalanced classes

Stratified splitting: keep the class proportions equal in training and test data (stratify=y).
Class weights: weight errors on the rare class more strongly during training (class_weight="balanced").
Resampling: undersample the majority class or oversample the minority class (only in the training data!).
Threshold adjustment as described above – often the simplest and most effective measure.

title: 7  Classification
text:
7.3 Live coding: predictive maintenance
The AI4I 2020 dataset is a synthetic dataset that reflects a real milling process. Each of the 10,000 records contains the product quality variant (L/M/H), air and process temperature, rotational speed, torque and tool wear, and the label Machine failure. The failures are generated by five documented mechanisms: tool wear failure (TWF), heat dissipation failure (HDF), power failure (PWF), overstrain failure (OSF) and random failures (RNF). Because the mechanisms are known, the dataset is ideal to check whether a model has learned something physically sensible.

from ucimlrepo import fetch_ucirepo

ai4i = fetch_ucirepo(id=601).data.original

# Some versions of the dataset have no units in the column names. We add them;
# names that already carry units stay unchanged.
units = {"Air temperature": "Air temperature [K]", "Process temperature": "Process temperature [K]",
         "Rotational speed": "Rotational speed [rpm]", "Torque": "Torque [Nm]", "Tool wear": "Tool wear [min]"}
ai4i = ai4i.rename(columns=units)
print("Columns:", ai4i.columns.tolist())

features = ["Type", "Air temperature [K]", "Process temperature [K]",
            "Rotational speed [rpm]", "Torque [Nm]", "Tool wear [min]"]
X = pd.get_dummies(ai4i[features], columns=["Type"], drop_first=True)
y = ai4i["Machine failure"]
print(f"Failure rate: {y.mean():.1%}")
# NOTE: the columns TWF, HDF, PWF, OSF, RNF describe the failure mode.
# Using them as features would be data leakage!

Columns: ['UID', 'Product ID', 'Type', 'Air temperature [K]', 'Process temperature [K]', 'Rotational speed [rpm]', 'Torque [Nm]', 'Tool wear [min]', 'Machine failure', 'TWF', 'HDF', 'PWF', 'OSF', 'RNF']
Failure rate: 3.4%




Code
sns.scatterplot(data=ai4i.sample(3000, random_state=0), x="Rotational speed [rpm]", y="Torque [Nm]",
                hue="Machine failure", s=10, alpha=0.6, palette=["lightgray", "C3"])
plt.show()









The failures are not spread randomly: they concentrate at very high torque with low speed and at very low torque with high speed – regions of high and low mechanical power. A linear boundary in this plane cannot separate them; this matters for the choice of model.

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)

models = {
    "logistic regression": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=1000)),
    "kNN (k=5)": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(5)),
    "decision tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, class_weight="balanced", random_state=0),
}
for name, m in models.items():
    m.fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(f"--- {name}")
    print(classification_report(y_test, m.predict(X_test), digits=3))

Discussion. Read the reports row by row: the line for class 1 (failure) is the interesting one. Typically, logistic regression with class weights detects many failures (high recall) but raises many false alarms (low precision), because its linear boundary cannot isolate the failure regions. kNN without class weights is conservative: few false alarms, but many missed failures. The decision tree can represent the thresholds in torque, speed and tool wear that generate the failures and usually achieves the best balance. The accuracy row is high for all models – and says little. support is the number of test records of each class (85 failures). The last two rows average over the classes: macro avg treats both classes equally, weighted avg weights them by their support – and is therefore dominated by the many OK records.


Code
from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay, PrecisionRecallDisplay, RocCurveDisplay

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.5))
ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_estimator(models["decision tree"], X_test, y_test, ax=axes[0], colorbar=False)
axes[0].set_title("Decision tree")
for name, m in models.items():
    RocCurveDisplay.from_estimator(m, X_test, y_test, ax=axes[1], name=name)
    PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_estimator(m, X_test, y_test, ax=axes[2], name=name)
axes[1].set_title("ROC curves"); axes[2].set_title("Precision–recall curves")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()









Discussion. The ROC curves may look reassuringly good for all models, while the precision–recall curves reveal clear differences – the typical picture for rare events. The precision–recall curve directly shows the trade-off an engineer faces: “If I want to catch 80 % of the failures, how many of my alarms will be false?”

title: 7  Classification
text:
7.4 Back to the decision
We compare the total cost per test period for the status quo (every failure is a missed failure) and for each model at its default threshold. A missed failure costs 10,000 €, a false alarm 500 €. Detected failures are assumed to be prevented and to cost only the inspection.

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

c_fn, c_fp = 10_000, 500
status_quo = c_fn * int(y_test.sum())
costs = {}
for name, m in models.items():
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_test, m.predict(X_test)).ravel()
    costs[name] = c_fn * fn + c_fp * (fp + tp)          # every alarm triggers an inspection
print(f"{'status quo (no alarm)':22s} {status_quo / 1000:8.1f} k€")
for name, c in costs.items():
    print(f"{name:22s} {c / 1000:8.1f} k€")
best = min(costs, key=costs.get)
if costs[best] < status_quo:
    print(f"Decision: install the alarm based on the {best} – saving {(status_quo - costs[best]) / 1000:.1f} k€ "
          f"({1 - costs[best] / status_quo:.0%}) per test period.")
else:
    print("Decision: no model beats the status quo – do not install.")

status quo (no alarm)     850.0 k€
logistic regression       441.5 k€
kNN (k=5)                 589.0 k€
decision tree             254.0 k€
Decision: install the alarm based on the decision tree – saving 596.0 k€ (70%) per test period.


The cost comparison translates the confusion matrix into the language of the plant manager. Strictly, choosing the cheapest of three models on the test set makes its cost slightly optimistic; the clean way chooses on a validation split – as Exercise 2 does for the threshold – and reports the cost of the chosen model on the test set. With differences this large, the choice of the decision tree would not change. Exercise 2 shows that choosing the threshold by cost improves the logistic regression (from 442 to 404 k€) – but not enough to catch up with the tree. Before the final decision, two things should be checked: the AI4I data are simulated, so the savings must be confirmed in a pilot on the real line; and the assumption that every detected failure can be prevented is optimistic.

title: 7  Classification
text:
7.5 Summary






Key takeaways




Start from the decision: classifiers estimate class probabilities, and a threshold turns them into decisions – choose it by the costs of errors.
Logistic regression: linear boundary, interpretable; kNN: local, needs scaling; trees: thresholds and interactions, must be kept shallow.
Every model rests on assumptions: logistic regression minimises the log-loss, the negative log-likelihood of Bernoulli-distributed labels.
With rare events, accuracy and ROC can look good while the model is useless – use precision, recall and precision–recall curves.
Bayes’ theorem: with rare events, even good detectors produce mostly false alarms – the precision depends on the base rate.
Features that encode the outcome (here: the failure mode columns) cause data leakage.

title: 7  Classification
text:
7.6 Exercises


Add the failure mode columns (TWF, HDF, PWF, OSF, RNF) as features and retrain the decision tree. What happens to the scores – and why is this result worthless? Useful: X.join(ai4i[["TWF", "HDF", "PWF", "OSF", "RNF"]]) adds the columns.
Assume a missed failure costs 10,000 € and a false alarm 500 €. Choose the decision threshold of the logistic regression that minimises the total cost. Use a validation split of the training data, not the test data. Useful: train_test_split(X_train, y_train, test_size=0.3, stratify=y_train) gives the validation split; predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1] the failure probabilities; np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 99) candidate thresholds.
Visualise the decision tree (sklearn.tree.plot_tree, depth 3). Do the rules make physical sense? Useful: plt.figure(figsize=(16, 7)) before plot_tree(tree, feature_names=X.columns, class_names=["OK", "failure"], filled=True).
Construct the feature power [W] = torque × angular velocity and the temperature difference between process and air. Do they improve the logistic regression? Why? Useful: angular velocity = rotational speed · 2π/60; compare with cross_val_score(..., scoring="average_precision") – the average precision summarises the precision–recall curve in one number (roughly the area under it; 1 = perfect).
A test set has TN = 950, FP = 30, FN = 5, TP = 15. Compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1 by hand. Is the model useful?
In a well-maintained plant, only 0.1 % of the operations end in a failure. How reliable is an alarm with a recall of 95 % and a false alarm rate of 5 %? Which false alarm rate would be needed for \(P(F \mid A) = 50\,\%\)?



7.6.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1






X_leak = X.join(ai4i[["TWF", "HDF", "PWF", "OSF", "RNF"]])
Xl_tr, Xl_te, yl_tr, yl_te = train_test_split(X_leak, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)
tree_leak = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=5, random_state=0).fit(Xl_tr, yl_tr)
print(classification_report(yl_te, tree_leak.predict(Xl_te), digits=3))

              precision    recall  f1-score   support

           0      0.998     1.000     0.999      2415
           1      1.000     0.941     0.970        85

    accuracy                          0.998      2500
   macro avg      0.999     0.971     0.984      2500
weighted avg      0.998     0.998     0.998      2500



Precision and recall jump to nearly 100 %. The failure mode columns are only known after a failure has been diagnosed – they essentially encode the label. In operation, at prediction time, they are not available. Such leakage produces impressive but completely useless models. Rule: for each feature, ask “Would I know this value at the moment I need the prediction?”









Solution to Exercise 2






X_fit, X_val, y_fit, y_val = train_test_split(X_train, y_train, test_size=0.3,
                                              stratify=y_train, random_state=1)
logreg = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=1000))
logreg.fit(X_fit, y_fit)
p_val = logreg.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]

c_fn, c_fp = 10_000, 500
thresholds = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 99)
cost = [c_fn * ((p_val < t) & (y_val == 1)).sum() + c_fp * ((p_val >= t) & (y_val == 0)).sum()
        for t in thresholds]
t_best = thresholds[np.argmin(cost)]
plt.plot(thresholds, np.array(cost) / 1000)
plt.axvline(t_best, ls="--", c="k")
plt.xlabel("Threshold"); plt.ylabel("Total cost on validation data (k€)")
plt.show()

p_test = logreg.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
cost_test = c_fn * ((p_test < t_best) & (y_test == 1)).sum() + c_fp * ((p_test >= t_best) & (y_test == 0)).sum()
print(f"best threshold {t_best:.2f}, cost on test data {cost_test / 1000:.0f} k€")








best threshold 0.72, cost on test data 404 k€


The cost curve typically has a broad minimum. Note that with class_weight="balanced" the predicted probabilities are no longer calibrated (the model behaves as if failures were as frequent as OK records), so the optimal threshold differs from the theoretical \(c_{FP}/(c_{FP}+c_{FN}) \approx 0.048\). Choosing the threshold on validation data and reporting the cost on the untouched test data keeps the evaluation honest.









Solution to Exercise 3






from sklearn.tree import plot_tree

tree3 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, class_weight="balanced", random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
plt.figure(figsize=(16, 7))
plot_tree(tree3, feature_names=X.columns, class_names=["OK", "failure"], filled=True,
          impurity=False, proportion=True, fontsize=9)
plt.show()








The top splits typically use torque, rotational speed and tool wear – exactly the quantities behind the documented failure mechanisms: overstrain (high torque × tool wear), power failure (power too low or too high, i.e. extreme torque–speed combinations) and tool wear failure (large tool wear). A tree that splits mainly on product ID or random variables would be suspicious. Checking learned rules against physics is one of the best plausibility tests for a model.









Solution to Exercise 4






X_eng = X.copy()
X_eng["power [W]"] = ai4i["Torque [Nm]"] * ai4i["Rotational speed [rpm]"] * 2 * np.pi / 60
X_eng["delta T [K]"] = ai4i["Process temperature [K]"] - ai4i["Air temperature [K]"]
X_eng["strain [min Nm]"] = ai4i["Tool wear [min]"] * ai4i["Torque [Nm]"]

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold
skf = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
for name, data in [("original features", X), ("with engineered features", X_eng)]:
    s = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=2000)),
                        data, y, cv=skf, scoring="average_precision")
    print(f"{name:26s} average precision = {s.mean():.3f}")

original features          average precision = 0.429
with engineered features   average precision = 0.453


Here the engineered features help only a little (average precision 0.43 → 0.45). Physics-based features can turn curved boundaries into simpler ones – but power failures occur for both too low and too high power, and a linear model in power can only represent one side. Squared or binned terms, or a tree-based model, are needed to capture both. This is a typical example of how domain knowledge and model choice interact.









Solution to Exercise 5





Total = 1000. Accuracy = (950 + 15)/1000 = 96.5 %. Precision = 15/(15 + 30) = 33 %. Recall = 15/(15 + 5) = 75 %. F1 = 2 · 0.33 · 0.75/(0.33 + 0.75) ≈ 0.46.
The accuracy is lower than that of the trivial model “always OK” (98 %)! Still, the model may be useful: it detects three of four failures, at the price of two false alarms per real one. Whether that is acceptable depends on the costs – if a missed failure is expensive and checking an alarm is cheap, this model is valuable despite its “bad” accuracy.









Solution to Exercise 6





With \(P(F) = 0.001\): \[P(F \mid A) = \frac{0.95 \cdot 0.001}{0.95 \cdot 0.001 + 0.05 \cdot 0.999} \approx 0.019,\] i.e. only about 2 % of the alarms are real. For \(P(F \mid A) = 0.5\) we need \(0.95 \cdot 0.001 = q \cdot 0.999\), where \(q = P(A \mid \bar F)\) is the false alarm rate, so \(q \approx 0.00095\) – roughly one false alarm per thousand healthy operations. The more reliable the plant, the more specific the alarm must be.

title: 8  Ensembles and Interpretability
text:
8.1 Why ensembles work
A single decision tree is easy to understand but a poor predictor: it overfits, and a small change in the data can produce a completely different tree. The remedy is surprisingly simple – combine many trees. Ensemble methods such as random forests and gradient boosting are, for tabular data, among the most accurate general-purpose methods available. In industrial practice they are often the first choice for quality prediction, fault classification and virtual sensors.
Their accuracy comes at a price: an ensemble of hundreds of trees is no longer transparent. Yet engineers need to know why a model predicts a defect – to trust it, to check it against physics and to derive process improvements. The second half of this chapter therefore introduces methods to interpret such models.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Course goal. This chapter contributes to step 4 of the course goals: build and validate prediction and monitoring models.
Datasets in this chapter
Recall the bias–variance decomposition from Chapter 6. A deep decision tree has low bias but high variance. If we could average many trees trained on different datasets from the same process, the variance would shrink while the bias stays low. Ensembles approximate this idea in two different ways.

title: 8  Ensembles and Interpretability
text:
Figure 8.1: Bagging and boosting. Bagging trains many deep trees independently on bootstrap samples and averages them (variance reduction). Boosting trains shallow trees one after another, each one correcting the remaining errors of the ensemble so far (bias reduction).




8.1.1 Bagging and random forests






Definition: Bagging and random forest



Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) trains \(B\) models on \(B\) bootstrap samples of the training data and averages their predictions (regression) or takes a majority vote (classification). A random forest is bagging with decision trees plus one additional trick: at each split, only a random subset of the features (e.g. \(\sqrt{p}\) of \(p\) features) is considered. This decorrelates the trees and makes the averaging more effective.


Why the extra randomness helps: averaging \(B\) predictions with variance \(\sigma^2\) and pairwise correlation \(\rho\) gives a variance of \(\rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2\). More trees reduce only the second term; reducing the correlation \(\rho\) between the trees reduces the first. Random forests have few critical hyperparameters, rarely overfit when more trees are added, and provide a free validation estimate: each tree did not see about a third of the data (out-of-bag samples), on which it can be evaluated.


8.1.2 Boosting






Definition: Gradient boosting



Gradient boosting builds the model step by step: \[F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \nu\, h_m(x),\] where each new tree \(h_m\) is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions \(F_{m-1}(x_i)\): for each training point, it states in which direction and how strongly the prediction must change to reduce the loss. For the squared error \(\frac12 (y_i - F)^2\), the negative gradient is simply the residual \(y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)\). The learning rate \(0 < \nu \le 1\) shrinks each step.


Boosting uses shallow trees (depth 3–8) that individually are weak, and reduces mainly the bias. Unlike random forests, boosting can overfit if too many trees are added; the number of trees, the learning rate and the tree depth must be tuned together, typically with early stopping: part of the training data is held out as validation data, and no more trees are added once the validation score stops improving. Modern implementations (scikit-learn’s HistGradientBoostingClassifier, XGBoost, LightGBM) are very fast and handle missing values natively.






Engineering practice: which method first?



For a new tabular problem, a random forest with default settings is a robust first model that needs almost no tuning. Gradient boosting is often a few percent more accurate but requires tuning. A linear or logistic model remains the essential baseline – if the ensemble is only marginally better, the simpler model may be preferable for transparency.

title: 8  Ensembles and Interpretability
text:
8.2 Multi-class problems
Many classifiers handle several classes directly. Logistic regression generalises with the softmax function: each class \(k\) gets its own linear score \(z_k = \beta_{k0} + \beta_k^\top x\), and \[p_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}}\] turns the scores into probabilities that are positive and add up to 1; for \(K = 2\), this is the logistic function of Chapter 7. The coefficients are again fitted by maximum likelihood, and the loss is the cross-entropy \(-\sum_i \ln p_{i,\,\text{true class}}\) – the log-loss of Chapter 7 for \(K\) classes. Decision trees need no change: the Gini impurity is defined for any number of classes.
With \(K > 2\) classes, the confusion matrix becomes \(K \times K\), and precision and recall are computed per class. They can be averaged in two ways: the macro average treats every class equally (important if rare classes matter), the weighted average weights them by their frequency. Balanced accuracy is the macro average of the recalls.

title: 8  Ensembles and Interpretability
text:
8.3 Interpreting models






Definition: Permutation importance



The importance of feature \(j\) is the decrease in a performance score (on validation or test data) when the values of feature \(j\) are randomly shuffled, which destroys its relationship with the target while keeping its distribution.


Permutation importance works for any model. The impurity-based feature_importances_ of tree models are cheaper but biased towards features with many distinct values and computed on training data.






Pitfall: importance is not causality – and correlated features share importance



A high importance means that the model relies on a feature, not that the feature causes the defect. If two features are strongly correlated (e.g. two dimensions of a defect), shuffling one of them hurts little because the other still carries the information – both may appear unimportant although the information is essential.


A partial dependence plot (PDP) shows how the predicted probability changes on average when one feature is varied over its range while the others keep their observed values. It answers the engineering question “in which direction and how strongly does this measurement influence the prediction?” and reveals thresholds and nonlinearities.
