title: 8  Ensembles and Interpretability
text:
8.4 Live coding: steel plate faults
The dataset comes from the automatic inspection of steel plates. For 1,941 detected surface defects, 27 features were extracted from the inspection images and the production data: position and size of the defect (X_Minimum, Pixels_Areas, Length_of_Conveyer, …), luminosity statistics, shape indices, the steel type and the plate thickness. Each defect belongs to one of seven classes: Pastry, Z_Scratch, K_Scratch, Stains, Dirtiness, Bumps and Other_Faults.

from ucimlrepo import fetch_ucirepo

steel = fetch_ucirepo(id=198)
X = steel.data.features
y = steel.data.targets.idxmax(axis=1)      # 7 one-hot columns -> one label
y.value_counts()

Other_Faults    673
Bumps           402
K_Scratch       391
Z_Scratch       190
Pastry          158
Stains           72
Dirtiness        55
Name: count, dtype: int64


The classes are imbalanced: Other_Faults is by far the largest class, while Dirtiness and Stains are rare. “Other faults” is a heterogeneous rest category – we must expect it to be hard to classify.

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=0)
cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)

candidates = {
    "logistic regression (baseline)": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=3000)),
    "random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0, n_jobs=-1),
    "gradient boosting": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
}
for name, m in candidates.items():
    s = cross_val_score(m, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="balanced_accuracy")
    print(f"{name:32s} balanced accuracy = {s.mean():.3f} ± {s.std():.3f}")

logistic regression (baseline)   balanced accuracy = 0.717 ± 0.019
random forest                    balanced accuracy = 0.750 ± 0.019
gradient boosting                balanced accuracy = 0.785 ± 0.022


Discussion. Both ensembles clearly outperform the logistic regression baseline. The standard deviation across folds indicates how much of the difference between the ensembles is real – differences smaller than this spread should not be over-interpreted. With seven classes, guessing would reach a balanced accuracy of about 1/7 ≈ 0.14. Gradient boosting reaches the highest score, about 3.5 percentage points ahead of the random forest – more than the fold-to-fold spread, so probably a real but small advantage. We nevertheless continue with the random forest, the robust default that needs no tuning; Exercise 1 checks whether gradient boosting would change the decision.

from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, ConfusionMatrixDisplay

rf = candidates["random forest"].fit(X_train, y_train)
print(classification_report(y_test, rf.predict(X_test), digits=3))
disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_estimator(rf, X_test, y_test, xticks_rotation=45, colorbar=False,
                                             normalize="true", values_format=".2f")
disp.ax_.grid(False)                                   # no grid lines across the matrix
plt.show()

              precision    recall  f1-score   support

       Bumps      0.771     0.733     0.751       101
   Dirtiness      0.833     0.714     0.769        14
   K_Scratch      0.967     0.908     0.937        98
Other_Faults      0.692     0.804     0.744       168
      Pastry      0.656     0.538     0.592        39
      Stains      1.000     0.944     0.971        18
   Z_Scratch      0.929     0.812     0.867        48

    accuracy                          0.792       486
   macro avg      0.836     0.779     0.804       486
weighted avg      0.800     0.792     0.793       486










The row-normalised confusion matrix shows for each true class where its defects end up. Scratches and stains are recognised well. Most errors end up in the column Other_Faults: many Pastry, Dirtiness, Bumps and Z_Scratch defects are classified as “other” – the heterogeneous rest category attracts the uncertain cases. Bumps and Other_Faults are also confused with each other.

from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

pi = permutation_importance(rf, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=10, random_state=0,
                            scoring="balanced_accuracy")
imp = pd.Series(pi.importances_mean, index=X.columns).sort_values()
imp.tail(10).plot.barh(xlabel="Drop in balanced accuracy when shuffled")
plt.show()









from sklearn.inspection import PartialDependenceDisplay

# The most important feature with a continuous range of values (binary features such as
# the steel type have no meaningful curve). Partial dependence needs floating-point data.
continuous = [c for c in imp.index[::-1] if X_test[c].nunique() > 10]   # most important first
top = continuous[0]
print("Feature:", top)
PartialDependenceDisplay.from_estimator(rf, X_test.astype(float), [top], target=rf.classes_[0], kind="average")
plt.title(f"Partial dependence for class '{rf.classes_[0]}'")
plt.show()

Feature: Length_of_Conveyer









Discussion. The importance ranking tells us which measurements the model relies on – for steel defects typically luminosity and geometry features as well as the steel type and plate thickness. The partial dependence plot shows how the predicted probability of one class changes along the most important continuous feature. Look for thresholds: a steep step suggests a physical limit or a property of the inspection system worth discussing with the process engineers.

title: 8  Ensembles and Interpretability
text:
8.5 Back to the decision
For each class we need both high precision (when the model says “scratch”, it really is one) and high recall (it finds the scratches). We read both from the test set and apply the 90 % criterion.

from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_fscore_support

prec, rec, _, support = precision_recall_fscore_support(y_test, rf.predict(X_test), labels=rf.classes_, zero_division=0)
per_class = pd.DataFrame({"precision": prec, "recall": rec, "test cases": support}, index=rf.classes_)
per_class["automate"] = (per_class["precision"] >= 0.9) & (per_class["recall"] >= 0.9)
print(per_class.round(2))
share = per_class.loc[per_class["automate"], "test cases"].sum() / per_class["test cases"].sum()
auto = list(per_class.index[per_class["automate"]])
print(f"Decision: automate {auto if auto else 'no class yet'} – about {share:.0%} of the defects would no longer need an inspector.")

              precision  recall  test cases  automate
Bumps              0.77    0.73         101     False
Dirtiness          0.83    0.71          14     False
K_Scratch          0.97    0.91          98      True
Other_Faults       0.69    0.80         168     False
Pastry             0.66    0.54          39     False
Stains             1.00    0.94          18      True
Z_Scratch          0.93    0.81          48     False
Decision: automate ['K_Scratch', 'Stains'] – about 24% of the defects would no longer need an inspector.


With only a few dozen test cases per class, precision and recall are themselves uncertain – a class that just passes the 90 % mark should be monitored closely after go-live, for example by having inspectors check a random sample of automatically classified plates. Classes that fail the criterion are good candidates for better labels or additional features.

title: 8  Ensembles and Interpretability
text:
8.6 Extension: SHAP values
Extension – optional material, not required for the exam.
SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) distributes a single prediction among the features, based on the Shapley value from cooperative game theory: each feature receives its average marginal contribution over all possible orders in which features could be added. The contributions add up exactly to the difference between the prediction and the average prediction. SHAP answers the question: why did the model classify this plate as K_Scratch?


Code
import shap

explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(rf)
sv = explainer(X_test.iloc[:200])
cls = list(rf.classes_).index("K_Scratch")      # position of the class K_Scratch in the model
print("SHAP values for class:", rf.classes_[cls])
shap.plots.beeswarm(sv[:, :, cls], max_display=10)


SHAP values for class: K_Scratch









Each dot is one plate; its horizontal position is the contribution of the feature to the K_Scratch score, its colour the feature value. Features at the top have the largest overall influence. Unlike permutation importance, the beeswarm plot also shows the direction of the effect.

title: 8  Ensembles and Interpretability
text:
8.7 Summary






Key takeaways




Bagging/random forests reduce variance by averaging decorrelated deep trees; boosting reduces bias by adding shallow trees sequentially.
Random forests are robust defaults; gradient boosting needs tuning but is often slightly more accurate.
In multi-class problems, use per-class metrics and the confusion matrix; macro averages protect rare classes.
Associations are not causes: permutation importance and partial dependence show what a model uses, not what causes a defect – but they make black-box models inspectable.

title: 8  Ensembles and Interpretability
text:
8.8 Exercises


Tune max_depth, learning_rate and max_iter of the gradient boosting model with RandomizedSearchCV. How much does the tuning gain compared with the default? Then repeat the decision of the live coding with the tuned model: which classes could be automated now? Useful: search.best_estimator_ is the tuned model, refitted on all training data; precision_recall_fscore_support from the live coding.
Which fault classes are confused most often? Look at the row-normalised confusion matrix and discuss whether the confusions are plausible. Useful: the confusion matrix of the live coding.
Compare impurity-based importance (rf.feature_importances_) with permutation importance. Why can they differ? Useful: pd.DataFrame({...}).rank(ascending=False) ranks both importances.
Train the random forest with class_weight="balanced". How do the recalls of the rare classes Dirtiness and Stains change? Useful: recall_score(y_test, y_pred, average=None, labels=rf.classes_) (sklearn.metrics) gives one recall per class.
(Extension) Explain one single prediction with a SHAP waterfall plot, as you would to a quality engineer. Useful: shap.plots.waterfall(sv[i, :, k]) for plate i and class number k, with sv from the extension.



8.8.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1

Random search samples hyperparameter combinations instead of trying a full grid – usually more efficient when only a few parameters matter. Here, tuning gains nothing: the tuned CV score is no better than that of the default settings in the live coding – the defaults of HistGradientBoostingClassifier already suit this problem. i = 0
pred_class = rf.predict(X_test.iloc[[i]])[0]
k = list(rf.classes_).index(pred_class)
print("predicted class:", pred_class, " true class:", y_test.iloc[i])
shap.plots.waterfall(sv[i, :, k], max_display=8)

predicted class: Stains  true class: Stains









The waterfall plot starts at the average model output for this class and adds the contribution of each feature until the prediction for this plate is reached. A good explanation for a quality engineer names the two or three largest contributions in physical terms – for a scratch, for example: “The model considers this a scratch mainly because the defect is long and narrow and its luminosity is low – typical for K_Scratch.” It should also state what the explanation is not: a causal statement about the production process.

title: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection
text:
9.1 Principal component analysis
In the previous chapters every training example came with a label: the strength of the concrete, the failure of the machine, the type of defect. In engineering, labels are often the scarcest resource. Failures are rare, new fault types appear that nobody has seen before, and expert labelling is slow and expensive. Yet we usually have plenty of data from normal operation.
Unsupervised learning finds structure in data without labels. In this chapter we use it for three purposes: to compress hundreds of correlated sensor signals into a few meaningful components (PCA), to monitor a process by detecting deviations from its normal behaviour, and to group operating states or products into clusters.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Course goal. This chapter contributes to step 4 of the course goals: build and validate prediction and monitoring models.
Datasets in this chapter
Process data are highly redundant: dozens of temperatures in the same furnace, pressures along the same line, currents of coupled drives all move together. PCA exploits this redundancy.
Keeping the first \(k\) components gives the best possible approximation of the data by a \(k\)-dimensional plane (in the least-squares sense). The scree plot (explained variance per component) and the cumulative explained variance help to choose \(k\).
crumbs: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection

title: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection
text:
Definition: Principal component analysis (PCA)



Given standardised data \(Z \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\) (each column with mean 0 and standard deviation 1), PCA finds orthogonal directions \(v_1, v_2, \dots\) (the loadings) such that the projection of the data onto \(v_1\) has maximal variance, the projection onto \(v_2\) has maximal variance among all directions orthogonal to \(v_1\), and so on. The projections \(Z v_j\) of the data onto the loadings are the scores of component \(j\). The variance \(\lambda_j\) of the scores is the variance explained by component \(j\). The \(\lambda_j\) of all components add up to the total variance of the standardised data, \(p\), so \(\lambda_j / p\) is the share of the variance explained by component \(j\).









Pitfall: standardise before PCA



PCA maximises variance, and variance depends on units. Without standardisation, a pressure in Pa (values around \(10^5\)) dominates a temperature in °C. Standardise unless all variables share a unit and their natural variances are meaningful.
crumbs: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection

title: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection
text:
9.2 Process monitoring with PCA
The idea of multivariate statistical process control: build a PCA model from data of normal operation (phase I) and then check every new observation against it (phase II). Two complementary statistics measure the deviation:






Figure 9.1: Geometry of PCA monitoring, shown for two correlated sensors and a one-component model (in practice: many sensors and a model plane of several components). Hotelling’s T² measures how unusual an observation is within the model (an extreme value along the known pattern); the squared prediction error SPE measures its distance from the model (a new kind of variation the model has never seen).









Definition: Hotelling’s T² and SPE



Let \(V_k = [v_1, \dots, v_k]\) contain the first \(k\) loadings and \(\lambda_j\) be the explained variance of component \(j\) in the normal-operation data. For a new standardised observation \(z\) with scores \(t = V_k^\top z = (t_1, \dots, t_k)^\top\): \[T^2 = \sum_{j=1}^k \frac{t_j^2}{\lambda_j}, \qquad \text{SPE} = \|z - V_k t\|^2 .\] Control limits are derived from the normal-operation data, e.g. as the 99 % quantile of each statistic.


When an alarm occurs, contribution plots show which original variables contribute most to the large T² or SPE value – a first hint for the operator where to look.
crumbs: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection

title: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection
text:
9.3 Clustering
Clustering groups observations so that members of a group are similar and different groups are dissimilar. Engineering uses: identifying operating modes of a machine (idle, part load, full load), grouping products or customers, finding families of similar faults.






Definition: k-means



k-means partitions the data into \(k\) clusters by minimising the within-cluster sum of squared distances to the cluster centres. The algorithm alternates two steps until convergence: (1) assign each point to the nearest centre, (2) move each centre to the mean of its points. The result depends on the starting centres, so the algorithm is run several times.


k-means assumes roughly spherical clusters of similar size, and \(k\) must be chosen: the elbow of the within-cluster sum of squares or the silhouette score (how much closer a point is to its own cluster than to the next one, between −1 and 1) help. DBSCAN instead defines clusters as dense regions: it finds clusters of arbitrary shape, determines their number itself and labels points in sparse regions as noise – a natural link to anomaly detection.
crumbs: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection

title: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection
text:
9.4 Anomaly detection






Definition: Isolation Forest



An Isolation Forest builds random trees that split the data at random features and random thresholds. Anomalies are “few and different”: they are isolated after few splits. The anomaly score is derived from the average path length needed to isolate a point – short paths mean anomalous.








Engineering practice: evaluating unsupervised detectors



Even if the detector is trained without labels, a few labelled faults are invaluable for evaluating it. Use them only for evaluation and threshold selection, never for training – and fit the model on normal data that is separate from the normal data used for evaluation.

        subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", pkg], check=True)

import warnings

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

title: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection
section: 9.5 Live coding: PCA monitoring of semiconductor production
text:
9.5 Live coding: PCA monitoring of semiconductor production
We use the SECOM data introduced in Chapter 2: 1,567 production runs, 590 process measurements, and a pass/fail label. Following the findings of Chapter 2, we remove sparse and constant features, impute the remaining gaps with the median and standardise. All preprocessing steps and the PCA model are fitted on passed runs only – this is our model of normal operation.

from ucimlrepo import fetch_ucirepo
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.feature_selection import VarianceThreshold
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

secom = fetch_ucirepo(id=179).data.original    # as in Chapter 2
y = secom["class"].astype(int)                  # the label: -1 = pass, 1 = fail
X = secom.drop(columns=["timestamp", "class"])  # the 590 measurements
X = X.loc[:, X.isna().mean() < 0.5]             # drop features with > 50 % missing

prep = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), VarianceThreshold(1e-8), StandardScaler())
Z = prep.fit_transform(X[y == -1])           # model of normal operation
pca = PCA().fit(Z)
cum = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
k = int((cum < 0.80).sum()) + 1                # components needed for 80 %
plt.plot(np.arange(1, 101), cum[:100]); plt.axhline(0.8, ls="--", c="k")
plt.xlabel("Number of components"); plt.ylabel("Cumulative explained variance")
plt.show()
print("Components for 80 % variance:", k)








Components for 80 % variance: 87


Discussion. The cumulative explained variance rises steeply for the first components and then slowly. For SECOM, many components are needed to reach 80 % – the process has many partly independent sources of variation, and much of the variance is noise. The choice of 80 % is a convention; in monitoring, the number of components is often chosen by cross-validation of the reconstruction error or by the scree plot’s elbow.

pca_k = PCA(k).fit(Z)

def t2_spe(Zx):
    scores = pca_k.transform(Zx)
    t2 = np.sum(scores**2 / pca_k.explained_variance_, axis=1)
    spe = np.sum((Zx - pca_k.inverse_transform(scores))**2, axis=1)
    return t2, spe

t2, spe = t2_spe(prep.transform(X))
t2_lim, spe_lim = np.percentile(t2[y == -1], 99), np.percentile(spe[y == -1], 99)

plt.scatter(t2, spe, c=(y == 1), cmap="coolwarm", s=8, alpha=0.6)
plt.axvline(t2_lim, c="k", ls="--"); plt.axhline(spe_lim, c="k", ls="--")
plt.xscale("log"); plt.yscale("log"); plt.xlabel("Hotelling T²"); plt.ylabel("SPE")
plt.title("Red: failed runs, dashed: 99 % limits of normal runs")
plt.show()








Discussion. The dashed lines are the 99 % limits of the normal runs, so about 1 % of normal runs exceed each limit by construction (false alarms). Failed runs that exceed a limit are detected; those inside the limits look normal to the model. If most failures lie inside the limits, the measured variables may not contain the cause of the failure, or the failure manifests itself in variables that were removed, or in a way that PCA does not capture.

from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

iso = IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(Z)
score = -iso.score_samples(prep.transform(X))
print(f"ROC AUC  Isolation Forest: {roc_auc_score(y == 1, score):.3f}")
print(f"ROC AUC  T²:               {roc_auc_score(y == 1, t2):.3f}")
print(f"ROC AUC  SPE:              {roc_auc_score(y == 1, spe):.3f}")

ROC AUC  Isolation Forest: 0.571
ROC AUC  T²:               0.541
ROC AUC  SPE:              0.726








Pitfall: evaluating on the training data



In this quick comparison, the normal runs used to fit the models are also part of the evaluation. They naturally look “very normal” to the models, which makes the result optimistic. Exercise 1 repeats the evaluation properly with separate normal runs.


For SECOM, expect modest AUC values: fault detection in semiconductor manufacturing from summary process data is known to be hard. This is a realistic lesson – many sensors do not guarantee that the relevant information is in the data.

title: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection
text:
9.6 Back to the decision
The requirement fixes the false alarm rate at 5 %, so we set the alarm limit at the 95 % quantile of the statistic on good runs and then measure which share of the failed runs exceeds it. To avoid the optimism discussed above, we fit preprocessing and PCA on 70 % of the good runs and evaluate on the remaining good runs plus all failed runs.

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_good_fit, X_good_eval = train_test_split(X[y == -1], test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
prep_d = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), VarianceThreshold(1e-8), StandardScaler())
Z_fit = prep_d.fit_transform(X_good_fit)
pca_d = PCA(k).fit(Z_fit)

def spe_of(Zx):
    return np.sum((Zx - pca_d.inverse_transform(pca_d.transform(Zx)))**2, axis=1)

limit = np.percentile(spe_of(prep_d.transform(X_good_eval)), 95)
detection = (spe_of(prep_d.transform(X[y == 1])) > limit).mean()
print(f"False alarm rate on good runs: 5 % (by construction), detection rate of failed runs: {detection:.0%}")
print("Decision:", "install the alarm." if detection >= 0.5 else "do not install – the alarm would miss too many failures.")

False alarm rate on good runs: 5 % (by construction), detection rate of failed runs: 11%
Decision: do not install – the alarm would miss too many failures.


(Strictly, the limit should be set on one part of the held-out good runs and the false alarm rate checked on another; with a few hundred good runs we accept this simplification.) If the detection rate falls short, the result is still valuable: it tells the fab that the summary data do not contain enough information about the failures – and that investing in different measurements is more promising than tuning the algorithm.

text:
9.7 Live coding: operating states of a hydraulic test rig
The hydraulic dataset was recorded on a test rig in which the condition of four components – cooler, valve, pump and accumulator – was varied deliberately. Each of the 2,205 load cycles lasts 60 seconds; 17 sensors were recorded at up to 100 Hz. The file profile.txt contains the component conditions, e.g. the cooler efficiency (3 %, 20 % or 100 %). The archive contains one text file per sensor, with one row per load cycle and the values of the cycle separated by tabs. We compute simple features per cycle from the temperature sensors and the cooling efficiency and see whether PCA and k-means recover the cooler condition without using the labels.

# Download helper, as in Chapter 3
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path
import requests

DATA = Path("data")
DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)                         # create the folder ./data if it does not exist

def download(url, fname=None):
    """Download a file once and cache it in ./data."""
    if fname is None:                             # no file name given:
        fname = url.split("/")[-1]                # use the last part of the URL
    path = DATA / fname                           # "/" joins folder and file name
    if not path.exists():                         # download only if not cached yet
        r = requests.get(url, timeout=300)        # give up after 300 s without response
        r.raise_for_status()                      # stop with an error if the download failed
        path.write_bytes(r.content)               # open, write and close the file in one step
    return path

hz = download("https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/447/condition+monitoring+of+hydraulic+systems.zip",
              "hydraulic.zip")

def read_sensor(z, name):
    """Read one file of the archive: one row per load cycle."""
    return pd.read_csv(z.open(name), sep="\t", header=None).values

with zipfile.ZipFile(hz) as z:
    sensors = {s: read_sensor(z, f"{s}.txt") for s in ["TS1", "TS2", "TS3", "TS4", "CE", "CP"]}
    profile = pd.DataFrame(read_sensor(z, "profile.txt"),
                           columns=["cooler", "valve", "pump_leak", "accumulator", "stable"])

feat = pd.DataFrame()
for s, v in sensors.items():                     # v: one row per cycle, one column per time step
    feat[f"{s}_mean"] = v.mean(axis=1)           # mean of each cycle
    feat[f"{s}_std"] = v.std(axis=1)             # standard deviation of each cycle
feat.shape

(2205, 12)



from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

Zh = StandardScaler().fit_transform(feat)
scores_h = PCA(2).fit_transform(Zh)

for k_ in range(2, 7):                           # silhouette score for 2 to 6 clusters
    labels_k = KMeans(k_, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Zh)
    print(f"k = {k_}: silhouette score {silhouette_score(Zh, labels_k):.3f}")
clusters = KMeans(3, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Zh)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
sns.scatterplot(x=scores_h[:, 0], y=scores_h[:, 1], hue=profile["cooler"].astype(int).astype(str),
                ax=axes[0], s=12).set(title="Coloured by true cooler condition (%)", xlabel="PC 1", ylabel="PC 2")
sns.scatterplot(x=scores_h[:, 0], y=scores_h[:, 1], hue=clusters.astype(str), ax=axes[1], s=12,
                palette="Set2").set(title="Coloured by k-means cluster", xlabel="PC 1", ylabel="PC 2")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
pd.crosstab(profile["cooler"], clusters, rownames=["cooler %"], colnames=["cluster"])

Discussion. Temperatures and cooling efficiency depend directly on the cooler condition, so the operating states form well-separated groups in the score plot, and k-means finds them without ever seeing the labels. The cross-table compares clusters and true conditions. This is the ideal case for unsupervised learning: the dominant source of variation in the chosen features is the condition of interest. With features dominated by other influences, clusters would reflect those instead – feature choice is decisive.
The silhouette scores, however, hardly differ between 2 and 6 clusters (0.54 to 0.56): here they give no clear answer to the question of how many clusters there are. We used \(k = 3\) because the test rig was run with three cooler conditions. Without such knowledge, a flat silhouette curve is a warning that the data do not determine the number of clusters – the choice then has to be justified by the purpose of the analysis.

title: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection
text:
9.8 Summary






Key takeaways




Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels: compression (PCA), grouping (clustering), deviations (anomaly detection).
PCA on standardised data summarises correlated sensors; T² and SPE monitor a process against its normal behaviour.
k-means needs a chosen \(k\) and assumes roughly spherical clusters; the silhouette score can help to choose \(k\), but often the purpose of the analysis decides.
Test honestly: fit detectors on normal data, evaluate them with held-out normal data and a few labelled faults.

title: 9  Unsupervised Learning and Anomaly Detection
text:
9.9 Exercises


Split the passed SECOM runs into a training part (70 %) and a test part (30 %). Fit preprocessing, PCA and Isolation Forest on the training part only and evaluate on the test part plus all failed runs. How much does the AUC change compared with the optimistic evaluation? Useful: train_test_split(X[y == -1], test_size=0.3, random_state=0) splits the passed runs; pd.concat([a, b]) stacks two tables; roc_auc_score as in the live coding.
Plot the first two principal component scores of SECOM coloured by pass/fail. Then run k-means with 2–6 clusters. Do clusters correspond to failures? Useful: pca_k.transform(prep.transform(X))[:, :2] gives the first two scores; KMeans(k, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Z) the cluster of every run.
Hydraulic system: repeat the analysis with the pressure sensors PS1–PS6 instead of the temperatures. Which component condition (cooler, valve, pump, accumulator) do the clusters now reflect best? Useful: read_sensor and the feature loop of the live coding; adjusted_rand_score(a, b) (sklearn.metrics) measures the agreement of two groupings – 1 for identical groupings, about 0 for random agreement.
Discuss: why is failure detection in SECOM so hard, even though there are almost 600 sensors?



9.9.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1






from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_pass, X_fail = X[y == -1], X[y == 1]
X_pass_tr, X_pass_te = train_test_split(X_pass, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

prep2 = make_pipeline(SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), VarianceThreshold(1e-8), StandardScaler())
Z_tr = prep2.fit_transform(X_pass_tr)
X_eval = pd.concat([X_pass_te, X_fail])
y_eval = np.r_[np.zeros(len(X_pass_te)), np.ones(len(X_fail))]
Z_eval = prep2.transform(X_eval)

iso2 = IsolationForest(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(Z_tr)
pca2 = PCA(k).fit(Z_tr)
spe2 = np.sum((Z_eval - pca2.inverse_transform(pca2.transform(Z_eval)))**2, axis=1)
print(f"ROC AUC Isolation Forest (proper): {roc_auc_score(y_eval, -iso2.score_samples(Z_eval)):.3f}")
print(f"ROC AUC SPE (proper):              {roc_auc_score(y_eval, spe2):.3f}")

ROC AUC Isolation Forest (proper): 0.577
ROC AUC SPE (proper):              0.594


The SPE in particular drops when evaluated properly: the PCA model reconstructs its own training runs better than new runs, so in the optimistic evaluation the normal runs looked “too normal” compared with the failed ones. Proper separation of training and evaluation data is just as important in unsupervised as in supervised learning.









Solution to Exercise 2






scores_s = pca_k.transform(prep.transform(X))[:, :2]
plt.scatter(scores_s[:, 0], scores_s[:, 1], c=(y == 1), cmap="coolwarm", s=8, alpha=0.6)
plt.xlabel("PC 1"); plt.ylabel("PC 2"); plt.title("SECOM scores, red = fail")
plt.show()

Zall = prep.transform(X)
for k_ in range(2, 7):
    lab = KMeans(k_, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Zall)
    runs = pd.DataFrame({"cluster": lab, "fail": (y == 1).values})
    per_cluster = runs.groupby("cluster")["fail"].agg(["size", "mean"])   # runs and failure rate
    print(f"k = {k_}: runs per cluster {per_cluster['size'].tolist()}, "
          f"failure rate {per_cluster['mean'].round(3).tolist()}")








k = 2: runs per cluster [5, 1562], failure rate [0.2, 0.066]
k = 3: runs per cluster [813, 750, 4], failure rate [0.049, 0.084, 0.25]
k = 4: runs per cluster [725, 4, 805, 33], failure rate [0.08, 0.25, 0.047, 0.212]
k = 5: runs per cluster [467, 664, 400, 4, 32], failure rate [0.06, 0.072, 0.05, 0.25, 0.219]
k = 6: runs per cluster [241, 459, 439, 32, 392, 4], failure rate [0.137, 0.041, 0.055, 0.219, 0.051, 0.25]


The failed runs are scattered among the passed ones in the first two components. Most clusters have failure rates close to the overall rate of about 7 %. Always check the number of runs before interpreting a higher rate: the clusters of four or five unusual runs reach 20–25 % with a single failure. More interesting is a group of about 32 runs that appears from \(k = 4\) on, with 7 failures (22 %), and for \(k = 6\) a cluster of 241 runs with 14 %. Such groups are worth a closer look with the process engineers – for example, whether they belong to one period of production (Chapter 2: the failure rate fell from September on). Still, most failed runs lie in clusters with ordinary failure rates: the clustering does not separate failed from passed runs. The dominant sources of variation in SECOM (e.g. tool or recipe changes) are largely unrelated to the pass/fail outcome. Clustering finds the largest structure in the data – which need not be the structure we are interested in.









Solution to Exercise 3






with zipfile.ZipFile(hz) as z:
    ps = {s: read_sensor(z, f"{s}.txt") for s in ["PS1", "PS2", "PS3", "PS4", "PS5", "PS6"]}
feat_ps = pd.DataFrame()
for s, v in ps.items():
    feat_ps[f"{s}_mean"] = v.mean(axis=1)
    feat_ps[f"{s}_std"] = v.std(axis=1)
    feat_ps[f"{s}_max"] = v.max(axis=1)
Zp = StandardScaler().fit_transform(feat_ps)
lab_ps = KMeans(4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Zp)

from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score
for c in ["cooler", "valve", "pump_leak", "accumulator"]:
    print(f"{c:12s}: adjusted Rand index {adjusted_rand_score(profile[c], lab_ps):.3f}")

cooler      : adjusted Rand index 0.584
valve       : adjusted Rand index 0.033
pump_leak   : adjusted Rand index 0.094
accumulator : adjusted Rand index 0.039


The adjusted Rand index (0 = random agreement, 1 = identical grouping) shows which component condition the clusters reflect. Perhaps surprisingly, the clusters of the pressure features again reflect mainly the cooler and hardly the valve, pump or accumulator. The cooler condition changes the oil temperature and thus, probably through the viscosity of the oil, the pressures in the whole system – it is the dominant source of variation in these features. The valve condition is nevertheless contained in the pressure features: a supervised model predicts it with about 99 % accuracy (Chapter 10, Exercise 4). Clustering, however, finds only the largest structure in the data – as in Exercise 2. For a weaker effect, labels and a supervised model are needed.









Solution to Exercise 4





Possible reasons: (1) the measurements are summary values per run and may not capture the physical cause of the failure; (2) the failures may have several different causes, so there is no single “failure direction”; (3) many features are noise, and in high dimensions the distance to normal data grows for every point, which dilutes anomaly scores; (4) only about 100 failures are available, and labels may be noisy; (5) part of the failures may originate in later process steps that are not measured at all. More sensors do not help if they do not measure the right thing.

title: 10  Signals and Feature Engineering
text:
10.1 Sampling and aliasing
Condition monitoring systems record vibration, current, pressure or acoustic signals at sampling rates of several kilohertz. A single minute of vibration data from one accelerometer at 12 kHz contains 720,000 numbers. Machine learning models cannot – and should not – work on such raw data directly. They need a small set of features that capture the information relevant for the question at hand.
This chapter shows how to get from a raw signal to meaningful features. We look at signals in the time and in the frequency domain, use the physics of rolling bearings to know where in the spectrum a fault should appear, and compute statistical features that summarise a signal window. Feature engineering is where engineering knowledge pays off most in data science.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Datasets in this chapter
A sensor signal is continuous; the data acquisition system samples it at discrete times \(t_n = n/f_s\) with the sampling rate \(f_s\).
A component at frequency \(f\) with \(f_N < f < f_s\) appears at \(|f - f_s|\). This is why data acquisition systems use an analogue anti-aliasing filter before the A/D converter. Once aliasing has happened, no digital processing can undo it.
crumbs: Part D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning

title: 10  Signals and Feature Engineering
text:
Sampling theorem (Nyquist–Shannon)



A signal can be reconstructed from its samples if it contains no frequencies at or above half the sampling rate, the Nyquist frequency \(f_N = f_s/2\). Frequencies above \(f_N\) are not lost silently – they are folded back and appear as false lower frequencies (aliasing).








Figure 10.1: Aliasing. A 9 Hz sine sampled at 10 Hz (dots) produces exactly the same samples as a 1 Hz sine. After sampling, the two cannot be distinguished.
crumbs: Part D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning

title: 10  Signals and Feature Engineering
text:
10.2 The frequency domain
Rotating machines produce periodic excitations: imbalance at the shaft frequency, gear meshing at the tooth frequency, bearing defects at characteristic frequencies. In the time domain these components overlap; in the frequency domain they separate into peaks.






Definition: Discrete Fourier transform and amplitude spectrum



For \(N\) samples \(x_0, \dots, x_{N-1}\), the discrete Fourier transform is \[X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n\, e^{-2\pi i\,kn/N}, \qquad k = 0, \dots, N-1,\] computed efficiently by the fast Fourier transform (FFT). Bin \(k\) corresponds to the frequency \(f_k = k\,f_s/N\). The single-sided amplitude spectrum \(A_k = 2|X_k|/N\) (for \(0 < k < N/2\)) gives the amplitude of a sine component at \(f_k\).


Two practical facts:

Frequency resolution \(\Delta f = f_s/N = 1/T\): it depends only on the measurement duration \(T\). To separate two peaks 1 Hz apart, you need at least one second of data.
Leakage: the FFT assumes the signal window repeats periodically. If a component does not complete an integer number of periods in the window, its energy “leaks” into neighbouring bins. Multiplying the window by a smooth window function (e.g. Hann) reduces leakage at the price of slightly wider peaks.

title: 10  Signals and Feature Engineering
text:
10.3 Bearing fault frequencies
When a rolling element passes a local defect on a raceway, it produces a short impact. These impacts repeat at frequencies that follow from the bearing geometry: with shaft frequency \(f_r\), number of rolling elements \(n_b\), rolling element diameter \(d\), pitch diameter \(D\) and contact angle \(\phi\),
\[\text{BPFO} = \frac{n_b f_r}{2}\left(1 - \frac{d}{D}\cos\phi\right), \qquad \text{BPFI} = \frac{n_b f_r}{2}\left(1 + \frac{d}{D}\cos\phi\right).\]
BPFO and BPFI are the ball pass frequencies of the outer and inner race. For the drive-end bearing of the CWRU test rig (SKF 6205), the CWRU documentation gives BPFI = 5.4152 \(f_r\) and BPFO = 3.5848 \(f_r\).






Engineering practice: let physics tell you where to look



Knowing the fault frequencies turns a vague search (“is the spectrum different?”) into a targeted test (“is there a peak at BPFI and its harmonics?”). Features built from physics – the amplitude at BPFI, the energy in a resonance band – are more robust and easier to explain than features found by blind search.

title: 10  Signals and Feature Engineering
section: 10.4 Statistical features of a signal window
text:
10.4 Statistical features of a signal window






Definition: Common time-domain features



For a window \(x_1, \dots, x_N\):

RMS \(= \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum x_i^2}\) – overall vibration energy,
peak \(= \max |x_i|\),
crest factor \(=\) peak / RMS – impulsiveness,
kurtosis \(= m_4/m_2^2 - 3\) (excess kurtosis), with the central moments \(m_r = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N (x_i - \bar x)^r\) – “spikiness”; 0 for a normal distribution, large for signals with short impacts,
skewness – asymmetry of the amplitude distribution.



Early bearing damage produces short impacts: kurtosis and crest factor rise while the RMS hardly changes. As damage progresses and spreads, the impacts become less distinct, kurtosis may fall again and RMS rises – a reason to use several features together.






Pitfall: splitting windows of the same recording



When a long recording is cut into windows, neighbouring windows are almost identical. If windows of the same recording end up in both training and test set, the model recognises the recording, not the fault – the test accuracy is meaningless. Split by recording, machine or time period (e.g. with GroupKFold), never randomly by window.

def download(url, fname=None):

text:
10.5 Live coding: healthy vs. inner-race fault
The Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) bearing data are a widely used benchmark. Faults of defined size were introduced into the bearings of a 2 hp motor test rig by electro-discharge machining; vibration was measured with accelerometers at the drive end and fan end. We use two files: normal baseline (97.mat) and a 0.007-inch inner race fault at the drive end (105.mat), both at 0 hp motor load (approx. 1797 rpm).
The fault recording was sampled at 12 kHz, the normal recording only at 48 kHz. A fair comparison needs the same sampling rate, because features such as RMS and peak depend on the frequency range the signal contains. We therefore bring the normal recording to 12 kHz with signal.decimate(x, 4): it first removes all components above the new Nyquist frequency of 6 kHz with a low-pass filter – a digital anti-aliasing filter – and then keeps every fourth sample.

FILES = {"normal": ("97.mat", 48_000), "inner race": ("105.mat", 12_000)}   # file, sampling rate (Hz)
BASE_URL = "https://engineering.case.edu/sites/default/files/"

signals = {}
for label, (fname, fs) in FILES.items():
    mat = loadmat(download(BASE_URL + fname))
    key = [k for k in mat if k.endswith("_DE_time")][0]     # drive-end accelerometer
    x = mat[key].ravel()
    if fs == 48_000:                                         # bring the normal recording to 12 kHz
        x, fs = signal.decimate(x, 4), 12_000
    signals[label] = (x, fs)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 5), sharex=True)
for ax, (label, (x, fs)) in zip(axes, signals.items()):
    t = np.arange(len(x)) / fs
    ax.plot(t, x, lw=0.5); ax.set(title=label, ylabel="Acceleration (g)")
axes[1].set(xlim=(0, 0.2), xlabel="Time (s)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Discussion. Already in the time domain the faulty bearing looks different: short, regularly spaced impacts are visible on top of the background vibration. Count the impacts in 0.1 s – their rate should match the BPFI of about 5.4 × 30 Hz ≈ 162 Hz.

text:
10.6 Live coding: amplitude spectrum

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
for label, (x, fs) in signals.items():
    f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x), 1 / fs)
    A = 2 * np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) / len(x)
    ax.plot(f, A, label=label, lw=0.6)
ax.set(xlim=(0, 6000), xlabel="Frequency (Hz)", ylabel="Amplitude (g)",
       title="Amplitude spectrum of the raw signals")
ax.legend(); plt.show()








Discussion. The faulty bearing shows much more energy at high frequencies, in the range of several kilohertz. These are structural resonances of the bearing and housing, excited by the impacts – not the fault frequency itself. The impact rate of about 162 Hz modulates these resonances but is hard to see directly in this spectrum. Envelope analysis makes it visible.

title: 10  Signals and Feature Engineering
text:
10.7 Extension: envelope analysis
Extension – optional material, not required for the exam.






Figure 10.2: Envelope analysis. Periodic impacts excite a high-frequency resonance (1). A band-pass filter isolates the resonance band (2). The envelope – the magnitude of the analytic signal from the Hilbert transform – recovers the impact pattern (3). Its spectrum shows peaks at the impact frequency and its harmonics (4).



The plain spectrum shows that the faulty bearing excites high-frequency resonances, but not why. The envelope spectrum reveals the repetition rate of the impacts – and thus the damaged component.

f_r = 1797 / 60          # shaft frequency (Hz)
bpfi = 5.4152 * f_r

def envelope_spectrum(x, fs, band=(2000, 5000)):
    b, a = signal.butter(4, band, btype="bandpass", fs=fs)
    env = np.abs(signal.hilbert(signal.filtfilt(b, a, x)))
    env -= env.mean()
    f = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(env), 1 / fs)
    return f, np.abs(np.fft.rfft(env)) / len(env)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
for label, (x, fs) in signals.items():
    f, A = envelope_spectrum(x, fs)
    ax.plot(f, A, label=label, lw=0.8)
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    ax.axvline(k * bpfi, c="k", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set(xlim=(0, 600), xlabel="Frequency (Hz)", ylabel="Envelope amplitude",
       title="Envelope spectrum, dotted: BPFI harmonics")
ax.legend(); plt.show()








For the inner race fault, peaks appear at BPFI and its harmonics; often there are also sidebands spaced at the shaft frequency, because the defect on the rotating inner ring moves in and out of the load zone once per revolution. The choice of the band (here 2–5 kHz) matters: it should contain the resonance excited by the impacts. Methods such as the kurtogram select it automatically.

            "kurtosis": stats.kurtosis(x), "skewness": stats.skew(x)}

# features on 1-second windows
rows = []
for label, (x, fs) in signals.items():
    for start in range(0, len(x) - fs, fs):
        rows.append({"condition": label, **features(x[start:start + fs])})

title: 10  Signals and Feature Engineering
text:
10.9 Back to the decision
A single-feature threshold works if the feature values of healthy and faulty windows do not overlap. We check kurtosis and crest factor and, if they separate, place the threshold in the middle of the gap.

for f_name in ["kurtosis", "crest"]:
    healthy_max = feat.loc[feat.condition == "normal", f_name].max()
    faulty_min = feat.loc[feat.condition == "inner race", f_name].min()
    if faulty_min > healthy_max:
        print(f"{f_name:9s}: separates (healthy max {healthy_max:.2f} < faulty min {faulty_min:.2f}) "
              f"-> threshold {(healthy_max + faulty_min) / 2:.2f}")
    else:
        print(f"{f_name:9s}: overlap (healthy max {healthy_max:.2f} >= faulty min {faulty_min:.2f})")

kurtosis : separates (healthy max -0.19 < faulty min 2.05) -> threshold 0.93
crest    : separates (healthy max 4.00 < faulty min 5.15) -> threshold 4.58


If a feature separates the two recordings, the decision looks easy – but it rests on one healthy and one faulty recording at one load – only 5 and 10 windows of one second. Before ordering sensors for dozens of pumps, the threshold must be checked on other loads, other fault types and sizes, and above all on healthy pumps in the field, whose kurtosis can be raised by cavitation or electrical interference. The recommendation is therefore: a pilot on a few pumps with the chosen feature, logging the values for some months before alarms are switched on.

title: 10  Signals and Feature Engineering
text:
10.10 Summary






Key takeaways




Sample at more than twice the highest relevant frequency and filter before sampling – aliasing cannot be undone.
The FFT reveals periodic components; frequency resolution is \(1/T\), leakage is reduced by window functions.
Bearing geometry determines where fault frequencies appear; physics-based features are robust and explainable.
RMS, crest factor and kurtosis summarise signal windows.
Test honestly: split windows by recording, not randomly – neighbouring windows are almost identical.

title: 10  Signals and Feature Engineering
text:
10.11 Exercises


A vibration signal contains a component at 7 kHz. It is sampled at 10 kHz without anti-aliasing filter. At which frequency does the component appear in the spectrum? What sampling rate would be needed?
You record 0.5 s of vibration data at 12 kHz. What is the frequency resolution? Can you separate the BPFI (≈ 162.3 Hz) from its sideband at BPFI + \(f_r\)?
Build a classifier for normal / inner race / ball / outer race faults on the statistical window features. Split each recording in time (first 70 % of the windows for training, last 30 % for testing). Why is a random split of the windows wrong? Useful: the function features and the dictionary FILES from the live coding (ball fault: 118.mat, outer race fault: 130.mat, both 12 kHz); signal.decimate; RandomForestClassifier, classification_report.
Hydraulic system: compute features per cycle (mean, std, max) for the 100 Hz pressure sensors and predict the valve condition with a random forest. Use stratified cross-validation. Useful: the data are a zip file with one text file per sensor (one row per cycle, tab-separated); zipfile.ZipFile, pd.read_csv(..., sep="\t", header=None), cross_val_score with StratifiedKFold.
(Extension) Compare the plain amplitude spectrum with the envelope spectrum around BPFI. Then download an outer race fault file and check whether a peak appears at BPFO. Useful: the function envelope_spectrum from the extension, the file 130.mat.



10.11.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1





The Nyquist frequency is 5 kHz. The 7 kHz component is folded back to \(|7 - 10| = 3\) kHz – it appears as a false peak at 3 kHz. To capture 7 kHz correctly, the sampling rate must exceed 14 kHz; in practice one chooses about 2.5 times the highest frequency of interest (≥ 17.5 kHz) and uses an anti-aliasing filter with its cut-off below the Nyquist frequency.









Solution to Exercise 2





\(\Delta f = 1/T = 1/0.5\,\text{s} = 2\) Hz. The sideband lies \(f_r \approx 30\) Hz from the BPFI peak, i.e. 15 bins away – easily separable. Peaks closer than about 2–3 bins (here 4–6 Hz) could not be separated, especially with a window function that widens the peaks. Note that the sampling rate does not affect the resolution; only the duration does.









Solution to Exercise 3






from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report

FILES4 = {"normal": ("97.mat", 48_000), "inner race": ("105.mat", 12_000),
          "ball": ("118.mat", 12_000), "outer race": ("130.mat", 12_000)}
rows = []
for label, (fname, fs) in FILES4.items():
    mat = loadmat(download(BASE_URL + fname))
    key = [k for k in mat if k.endswith("_DE_time")][0]   # drive-end accelerometer
    x = mat[key].ravel()
    if fs == 48_000:                                   # bring all signals to 12 kHz
        x, fs = signal.decimate(x, 4), 12_000
    win = fs // 4                                      # 0.25 s windows
    starts = range(0, len(x) - win, win)
    n_train = int(0.7 * len(starts))
    for i, s in enumerate(starts):
        rows.append({"condition": label, "train": i < n_train, **features(x[s:s + win])})
fw = pd.DataFrame(rows)
feat_cols = ["rms", "peak", "crest", "kurtosis", "skewness"]
clf = RandomForestClassifier(300, random_state=0).fit(fw.loc[fw.train, feat_cols], fw.loc[fw.train, "condition"])
print(classification_report(fw.loc[~fw.train, "condition"], clf.predict(fw.loc[~fw.train, feat_cols])))

        ball       1.00      1.00      1.00        12
  inner race       1.00      1.00      1.00        12
      normal       1.00      1.00      1.00         6
  outer race       1.00      1.00      1.00        12

    accuracy                           1.00        42
   macro avg       1.00      1.00      1.00        42
weighted avg       1.00      1.00      1.00        42



As in the live coding, all signals are first brought to 12 kHz, because features such as peak and RMS depend on the frequency range of the signal. A random split would put neighbouring, nearly identical windows into training and test, so the test accuracy would measure memorisation. The time split is better, but still optimistic: there is only one recording per condition, so the model may learn properties of the individual test run (sensor mounting, load) rather than the fault. A convincing evaluation needs several recordings per class – e.g. train on 0 and 1 hp, test on 2 and 3 hp.









Solution to Exercise 4






import zipfile
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold

hz = download("https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/447/condition+monitoring+of+hydraulic+systems.zip",
              "hydraulic.zip")

def read_sensor(z, name):
    """Read one file of the archive: one row per load cycle."""
    return pd.read_csv(z.open(name), sep="\t", header=None).values

with zipfile.ZipFile(hz) as z:
    ps = {s: read_sensor(z, f"{s}.txt") for s in ["PS1", "PS2", "PS3", "PS4", "PS5", "PS6"]}
    profile = pd.DataFrame(read_sensor(z, "profile.txt"),
                           columns=["cooler", "valve", "pump_leak", "accumulator", "stable"])
feat_ps = pd.DataFrame()
for s, v in ps.items():                            # v: one row per cycle
    feat_ps[f"{s}_mean"] = v.mean(axis=1)
    feat_ps[f"{s}_std"] = v.std(axis=1)
    feat_ps[f"{s}_max"] = v.max(axis=1)
acc = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(300, random_state=0), feat_ps, profile["valve"].astype(int),
                      cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0))
print(f"Valve condition accuracy: {acc.mean():.3f} ± {acc.std():.3f}")

Valve condition accuracy: 0.986 ± 0.008


Simple pressure statistics per cycle usually predict the valve condition well, because a degraded valve changes the switching behaviour and thus the pressure curves. Caution: the conditions were changed in blocks over the duration of the experiment, so neighbouring cycles share conditions and drifting factors such as oil temperature. A time-based split would give a more conservative estimate than the shuffled cross-validation used here.









Solution to Exercise 5

f_plain = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(x_ir), 1 / fs_ir)
A_plain = 2 * np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x_ir)) / len(x_ir)
f_env, A_env = envelope_spectrum(x_ir, fs_ir)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
axes[0].plot(f_plain, A_plain); axes[0].set(xlim=(0, 600), title="Plain spectrum", xlabel="Hz")
axes[1].plot(f_env, A_env); axes[1].set(xlim=(0, 600), title="Envelope spectrum", xlabel="Hz")
for ax in axes:
    ax.axvline(bpfi, c="k", ls=":")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

mat = loadmat(download(BASE_URL + "130.mat"))                 # outer race fault, 12 kHz
key = [k for k in mat if k.endswith("_DE_time")][0]
x_or = mat[key].ravel()
f_o, A_o = envelope_spectrum(x_or, 12_000)
bpfo = 3.5848 * f_r
plt.plot(f_o, A_o); plt.xlim(0, 600)
for k in (1, 2, 3):
    plt.axvline(k * bpfo, c="k", ls=":")
plt.title("Outer race fault: envelope spectrum, dotted: BPFO harmonics"); plt.xlabel("Hz")
plt.show()















In the plain spectrum, the low-frequency range is dominated by shaft harmonics and noise, and the impact rate hardly shows, because the impacts carry their energy at the resonance frequencies. The envelope spectrum demodulates the resonance and reveals BPFI clearly. For the outer race fault, the peaks appear at BPFO; since the outer ring is stationary, the defect stays in the same position relative to the load zone, and shaft-frequency sidebands are typically weaker than for inner race faults.

title: 11  Time Series Forecasting
text:
11.1 Components and autocorrelation
Grid operators must know tomorrow’s electricity demand to schedule power plants; a factory plans shifts based on forecast orders; an energy manager wants to know the peak load of next week. All of these are forecasting problems on time series – sequences of measurements ordered in time.
Time series differ from the tabular data of the previous chapters in one fundamental way: the observations are not independent. Today’s load is strongly related to yesterday’s and to the load one week ago. This dependence is what makes forecasting possible – and it changes the rules for model validation. The single most common mistake in practical forecasting is to evaluate a model with information it would not have had at forecast time.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Datasets in this chapter
A time series \(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_T\) is often thought of as a combination of
Many classical models assume stationarity: mean, variance and autocorrelation do not change over time. Trends and seasonal patterns violate this; differencing (\(y_t - y_{t-1}\), or \(y_t - y_{t-7}\) for a weekly season) removes them.
crumbs: Part D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning

title: 11  Time Series Forecasting
text:
a trend (slow change of the level, e.g. growing electrification),
one or several seasonal patterns (daily, weekly, yearly cycles),
exogenous influences (temperature, holidays, production plans),
and an irregular noise component.







Definition: Autocorrelation function (ACF)



The autocorrelation at lag \(h\) is the correlation of the series with itself shifted by \(h\) time steps: \[\rho(h) = \frac{\text{Cov}(y_t, y_{t-h})}{\text{Var}(y_t)}.\] Peaks of the ACF at lags 7, 14, 21 (for daily data) indicate a weekly cycle; a slow decay indicates a trend or strong persistence.
crumbs: Part D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning

title: 11  Time Series Forecasting
text:
11.2 Defining the forecasting task
Before choosing a model, answer three questions:

Horizon: how far ahead must we forecast – one hour, one day, one week?
Information set: which data are available at the time the forecast is made? Yesterday’s load is known for a day-ahead forecast; today’s load is not.
Granularity and metric: hourly or daily values? Which error matters – average error, peaks, under- or overestimation?







Definition: Forecast error metrics



For forecasts \(\hat y_t\) and actual values \(y_t\) over a test period: \[\begin{aligned} \text{MAE} &= \frac1n\sum_{t}|y_t - \hat y_t|, \\ \text{RMSE} &= \sqrt{\frac1n\sum_{t}(y_t - \hat y_t)^2}, \\ \text{MAPE} &= \frac1n\sum_{t}\left|\frac{y_t - \hat y_t}{y_t}\right|, \end{aligned}\] where the sums run over the \(n\) time steps of the test period. RMSE penalises large errors more strongly; MAPE is scale-free but undefined for \(y_t = 0\).








Engineering practice: always compare with naive forecasts



The naive forecast predicts the last observed value; the seasonal naive forecast predicts the value one season ago (e.g. the same weekday last week). They are free, robust and surprisingly hard to beat. A sophisticated model that does not clearly outperform the seasonal naive forecast is not worth its complexity.
crumbs: Part D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning

title: 11  Time Series Forecasting
text:
11.3 Forecasting as regression
The most flexible approach in practice: build a table in which each row is one time step and the columns contain information available at forecast time – lagged values (\(y_{t-1}\), \(y_{t-7}\), …), rolling statistics (mean of the last 7 days), calendar features (weekday, month, holiday) and exogenous variables (temperature forecast). Any regression method from the previous chapters can then be used; gradient boosting is a strong default.






Pitfall: information from the future




Random splits put future observations into the training set and past observations into the test set. The model then “interpolates” instead of forecasting, and the error is unrealistically small.
Lags shorter than the horizon: for a forecast 24 hours ahead, the lag 1 hour is not available at forecast time.
Measured instead of forecast exogenous data: training with the measured temperature of tomorrow overstates the accuracy – in operation only a weather forecast is available.









Figure 11.1: Time series cross-validation with an expanding window. The model is always trained on the past (blue) and tested on the period that immediately follows (orange). In a random split (bottom), test observations are surrounded by training observations from before and after.

title: 11  Time Series Forecasting
text:
11.4 Live coding: German electricity load
The Open Power System Data (OPSD) time series package collects load, wind and solar generation and prices for 32 European countries from the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform and other sources. We use version 2020-10-06 (2015 to mid-2020) and only the column with the actual German load. The full CSV file is about 124 MB; we read only the two columns we need.

url = ("https://data.open-power-system-data.org/time_series/2020-10-06/"
       "time_series_60min_singleindex.csv")
load = pd.read_csv(download(url), usecols=["utc_timestamp", "DE_load_actual_entsoe_transparency"],
                   parse_dates=["utc_timestamp"], index_col="utc_timestamp")
load = load.rename(columns={"DE_load_actual_entsoe_transparency": "load_MW"})["load_MW"]
daily = load.resample("D").mean().loc["2015-01-01":"2019-12-31"] / 1000   # GW
ax = daily.plot(figsize=(10, 3), ylabel="Mean load (GW)")
plt.show()








Discussion. The daily mean load shows a yearly cycle (higher in winter: lighting, heating), a strong weekly cycle (lower on weekends) and sharp drops around Christmas and public holidays. We restrict ourselves to 2015–2019 to avoid the exceptional Covid-19 period of 2020 – a reminder that structural breaks can make historical data unrepresentative.


Code
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf
plot_acf(daily, lags=40); plt.show()









The ACF has pronounced peaks at lags 7, 14, 21, … – the weekly cycle – and decays slowly overall, reflecting the yearly cycle and persistence.

11.4.1 Baselines
The forecast for a day \(D\) is made at noon of the day before. At that time, the load of that day is only half known, so the most recent complete day is \(D - 2\). The last year serves as test period.

test_start = "2019-01-01"
y_test = daily[test_start:]
naive = daily.shift(2)[test_start:]                 # last complete day: two days before
seasonal_naive = daily.shift(7)[test_start:]        # same weekday last week

def report(name, pred):
    err = y_test - pred
    print(f"{name:22s} MAE = {err.abs().mean():.2f} GW,  MAPE = {(err.abs() / y_test).mean():.1%}")

report("naive (day D-2)", naive)
report("seasonal naive (t-7)", seasonal_naive)

naive (day D-2)        MAE = 7.15 GW,  MAPE = 13.4%
seasonal naive (t-7)   MAE = 2.30 GW,  MAPE = 4.3%


The naive forecast fails at every weekday/weekend transition; the seasonal naive forecast handles these well and fails mainly on holidays and around them.


11.4.2 Feature-based forecasting with gradient boosting

import holidays
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, cross_val_score

df = daily.to_frame("load")
for lag in (2, 7, 14):                             # lag 1 is not complete at noon of the day before
    df[f"lag_{lag}"] = df["load"].shift(lag)
df["dow"] = df.index.dayofweek
df["doy"] = df.index.dayofyear
de_holidays = holidays.Germany(years=range(2015, 2021))
df["holiday"] = [d.date() in de_holidays for d in df.index]
df = df.dropna()

X, y = df.drop(columns="load"), df["load"]
gbr = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0)
scores = cross_val_score(gbr, X, y, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(5), scoring="neg_mean_absolute_percentage_error")
print("MAPE per fold (time series CV):", np.round(-scores, 3))

gbr.fit(X[:"2018-12-31"], y[:"2018-12-31"])         # train on 2015-2018, test on 2019
report("gradient boosting", pd.Series(gbr.predict(X[test_start:]), index=X[test_start:].index))

MAPE per fold (time series CV): [0.035 0.035 0.022 0.023 0.021]
gradient boosting      MAE = 1.09 GW,  MAPE = 2.0%


Discussion. All features are available at forecast time: lags of 2, 7 and 14 days – at noon, the load of the day before the target day is not yet complete –, the calendar and the holiday calendar, which is known in advance. TimeSeriesSplit trains on an expanding window and always tests on the following block; the error per fold shows how stable the model is over time. The comparison with the baselines on the same test year shows how much the model really adds.
Weather as an input. Temperature drives heating and cooling demand. Historical hourly temperatures are available from the DWD (reading the raw files: Chapter 2, Exercise 1; temperature as a feature: Exercise 2 below). For a real day-ahead forecast, the model must be trained and operated with temperature forecasts – using measured temperatures overstates the accuracy.

title: 11  Time Series Forecasting
text:
11.5 Back to the decision
We compare both methods on the test year 2019, which was not used for training. The model must reduce the MAE by at least 10 %.

pred_gb = pd.Series(gbr.predict(X[test_start:]), index=X[test_start:].index)
mae_naive = (y_test - seasonal_naive).abs().mean()         # both methods on all days of 2019
mae_model = (y_test - pred_gb).abs().mean()
gain = 1 - mae_model / mae_naive
print(f"MAE seasonal naive: {mae_naive:.2f} GW,  MAE gradient boosting: {mae_model:.2f} GW,  improvement: {gain:.0%}")
print("Decision:", "replace the seasonal naive forecast." if gain >= 0.10 else "keep the seasonal naive forecast.")

MAE seasonal naive: 2.30 GW,  MAE gradient boosting: 1.09 GW,  improvement: 52%
Decision: replace the seasonal naive forecast.


A one-year test is a good basis, but the recommendation should add: about half of the improvement comes from the nine public holidays of the test year and the days one week after them (16 days in total), where the seasonal naive forecast misses or copies the holiday dip, and half from ordinary days – check the error on such special days separately; the model should be monitored after go-live, because structural changes (such as the drop in demand in 2020) can make it worse than the simple method; and the temperature of a single station did not help (Exercise 2) – better weather data, such as a weighted average of many stations, could be tested next.

title: 11  Time Series Forecasting
text:
11.6 Extension: seasonal ARIMA
Extension – optional material, not required for the exam.
ARIMA models describe a series by its own past values (AR, autoregressive part), past forecast errors (MA, moving average part) after differencing \(d\) times (I, integrated). The seasonal extension SARIMA\((p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_s\) adds the same terms at the seasonal lag \(s\) (here \(s = 7\) days). ARIMA models are the classical statistical approach: compact, with well-founded prediction intervals, but harder to extend with many exogenous variables than the regression approach.

from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX

train, test = daily[:"2019-10-31"], daily["2019-11-01":"2019-11-30"]
sarima = SARIMAX(train, order=(1, 0, 1), seasonal_order=(1, 1, 1, 7)).fit(disp=False)
fc = sarima.get_forecast(len(test))
ax = train["2019-09-01":].plot(label="train", figsize=(10, 3))
test.plot(ax=ax, label="actual")
fc.predicted_mean.plot(ax=ax, label="SARIMA forecast")
ci = fc.conf_int()
ax.fill_between(ci.index, ci.iloc[:, 0], ci.iloc[:, 1], alpha=0.2)
ax.legend(); plt.show()
mape = (abs(fc.predicted_mean - test) / test).mean()
print(f"MAPE November 2019 (forecast up to 30 days ahead): {mape:.1%}")








MAPE November 2019 (forecast up to 30 days ahead): 6.1%


Note that this is a multi-step forecast: all 30 days are forecast at once from the end of October, so the horizon grows from 1 to 30 days, and the prediction interval widens accordingly. It is therefore not directly comparable with the one-day-ahead forecasts above.

title: 11  Time Series Forecasting
text:
11.7 Summary






Key takeaways




Define horizon and information set first; they determine which features are legal.
Lag, calendar and exogenous features turn forecasting into regression; gradient boosting is a strong default.
Test honestly: validate in time order (TimeSeriesSplit) and compare with naive and seasonal naive baselines; random splits and future information produce misleadingly small errors.

title: 11  Time Series Forecasting
text:
11.8 Exercises


Use a random 5-fold KFold with shuffling instead of TimeSeriesSplit for the gradient boosting model. Why does the error look better – and why is that wrong?
Add the daily mean temperature of the DWD station Trier-Petrisberg (historical hourly data) as a feature. How much does the error improve? Why is this improvement optimistic for real operation?
Remove the holiday feature. On which days does the error increase most?
Build a forecast for 7 days ahead (e.g. for weekly planning). Which lag features may you still use? How does the error compare with the 1-day-ahead forecast?
You want to forecast hourly load one day ahead. Which seasonal periods and which lags are relevant now?



11.8.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1






from sklearn.model_selection import KFold

random_scores = cross_val_score(gbr, X, y, cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0),
                                scoring="neg_mean_absolute_percentage_error")
print("MAPE random KFold:      ", np.round(-random_scores, 3))
print("MAPE TimeSeriesSplit:   ", np.round(-scores, 3))

MAPE random KFold:       [0.02  0.02  0.019 0.02  0.018]
MAPE TimeSeriesSplit:    [0.035 0.035 0.022 0.023 0.021]


With random folds, every test day is surrounded by training days from just before and just after. The model effectively interpolates within known periods – it has, for instance, seen the Christmas holidays of the same year. In operation, the future is never available for training. The time-ordered split measures what we need: the error on a period that lies entirely after the training data.









Solution to Exercise 2






import re, zipfile

hist_dir = ("https://opendata.dwd.de/climate_environment/CDC/observations_germany/"
            "climate/hourly/air_temperature/historical/")
listing = download(hist_dir, "dwd_hist_index.html").read_text()
# the file name contains the period covered, so we look it up in the directory listing
fname = re.search(r"stundenwerte_TU_05100_\d+_\d+_hist\.zip", listing).group(0)
with zipfile.ZipFile(download(hist_dir + fname)) as z:
    name = [n for n in z.namelist() if n.startswith("produkt")][0]   # the data file, as in Chapter 2
    dwd = pd.read_csv(z.open(name), sep=";", na_values=[-999], skipinitialspace=True)
dwd.columns = dwd.columns.str.strip()
dwd["time"] = pd.to_datetime(dwd["MESS_DATUM"].astype(str), format="%Y%m%d%H")
temp = dwd.set_index("time")["TT_TU"].resample("D").mean().rename("temp")
temp.index = temp.index.tz_localize("UTC")          # DWD time stamps are UTC, like the OPSD index

df_t = df.join(temp, how="inner").dropna()
X_t, y_t = df_t.drop(columns="load"), df_t["load"]
s_t = cross_val_score(gbr, X_t, y_t, cv=TimeSeriesSplit(5), scoring="neg_mean_absolute_percentage_error")
print(f"MAPE without temperature: {-scores.mean():.3f},  with temperature: {-s_t.mean():.3f}")

MAPE without temperature: 0.027,  with temperature: 0.027


Here, the temperature hardly changes the error: the lags and the calendar already contain the seasonal pattern that the temperature would explain, and one station is a rough proxy. Any improvement would also be optimistic, for two reasons: we use the measured temperature of the forecast day, which is not known one day in advance (in operation one would use a weather forecast with its own error), and one station represents the temperature relevant to German demand only roughly – a population-weighted average of many stations would be better.









Solution to Exercise 3






X_nh = X.drop(columns="holiday")
m_h = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(X[:"2018-12-31"], y[:"2018-12-31"])
m_nh = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(X_nh[:"2018-12-31"], y[:"2018-12-31"])
err_h = (y[test_start:] - m_h.predict(X[test_start:])).abs()

(err_nh - err_h).sort_values(ascending=False).head(10).round(2)

The largest increases occur on public holidays (Labour Day, Good Friday, Whit Monday, German Unity Day, New Year, Easter Monday, Ascension Day, Christmas) and on some days after them, because the lag features of 2 and 7 days then contain the unusual holiday load. A “bridge day” feature or a feature “holiday 7 days ago” can reduce these after-effects.









Solution to Exercise 4






h = 7
df7 = daily.to_frame("load")
for lag in (h + 1, 14, 364):                       # most recent complete day: h + 1 days before
    df7[f"lag_{lag}"] = df7["load"].shift(lag)
df7["dow"], df7["doy"] = df7.index.dayofweek, df7.index.dayofyear
df7["holiday"] = [d.date() in de_holidays for d in df7.index]
df7 = df7.dropna()
s7 = cross_val_score(HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0), df7.drop(columns="load"), df7["load"],
                     cv=TimeSeriesSplit(5), scoring="neg_mean_absolute_percentage_error")
print(f"MAPE 1 day ahead: {-scores.mean():.3f},  7 days ahead: {-s7.mean():.3f}")

MAPE 1 day ahead: 0.027,  7 days ahead: 0.034


For a forecast made at noon seven days ahead, the most recent complete day lies 8 days before the target day, so lags 1 to 7 are forbidden. Lags 8, 14 and the same day one year ago (lag 364, which keeps the weekday) remain. The error typically increases because recent changes – a cold spell, a holiday period – are not yet visible in the data.









Solution to Exercise 5





Hourly load has a daily cycle (period 24 h), a weekly cycle (168 h) and a yearly cycle (8760 h), and the daily profile itself differs between weekdays and weekends and between summer and winter (interaction of calendar features). For a day-ahead forecast made at noon for all 24 hours of the next day, the most recent known hour is noon of the day before: hour \(h\) of the next day lies \(12 + h\) hours ahead. Even the lag of 24 hours is therefore unknown for the afternoon hours; safe lags are 36 hours and more – e.g. 48 hours and 168 hours (same hour last week). Useful features: hour of day, weekday, holiday, these lags and temperature forecasts. Also note daylight saving time: in local time, one day per year has 23 and one 25 hours – working in UTC and adding local-time calendar features avoids errors.

title: 12  Deep Learning in Engineering
text:
12.1 From linear regression to neural networks
Neural networks are behind most of the recent headlines about artificial intelligence: image recognition, speech assistants, large language models. In engineering, they are used for visual quality inspection, for virtual sensors, for surrogate models of simulations and for predicting the remaining useful life of machines. Their strength is that they can learn suitable features from raw data – pixels, signal samples, sequences – by themselves, where the methods of the previous chapters needed hand-crafted features.
This chapter gives a compact, application-oriented introduction. We build a neural network from its smallest unit, the neuron, train it with gradient descent and apply it to predict the remaining useful life of jet engines. An extension section shows how pretrained networks detect defects on images. Neural networks in depth are the subject of a separate course; here the goal is to understand the principles and to judge when deep learning is worth its cost.
Learning goals. After this chapter you can
Datasets in this chapter
A linear regression computes a weighted sum of its inputs. A neuron does the same and then applies a nonlinear activation function:

title: 12  Deep Learning in Engineering
text:
Definition: Neuron, layer, multilayer perceptron



A neuron computes \(a = \sigma(w^\top x + b)\) with weights \(w\), bias \(b\) and activation function \(\sigma\). A layer applies many neurons to the same input: \(a = \sigma(Wx + b)\). A multilayer perceptron (MLP) stacks layers: \[\hat y = W_3\,\sigma\big(W_2\,\sigma(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2\big) + b_3.\] Common activations are ReLU, \(\sigma(z) = \max(0, z)\), and the sigmoid \(1/(1+e^{-z})\).








Figure 12.1: A multilayer perceptron with two hidden layers. Each arrow carries a weight; each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs and applies an activation function. Without the nonlinear activations, the whole network would collapse into a single linear model.









Universal approximation



An MLP with one hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region arbitrarily well. The theorem guarantees that a suitable network exists – not that training will find it, nor how much data is needed. In practice, deeper networks with fewer neurons per layer often learn more efficiently.
crumbs: Part D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning

title: 12  Deep Learning in Engineering
text:
12.2 Training: loss, gradients and backpropagation
The network’s weights and biases, collected in a parameter vector \(\theta\), are found by minimising a loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) on the training data, e.g. the mean squared error for regression or the cross-entropy for classification (Chapters 7 and 8). Since the loss is a nonconvex function of possibly millions of weights, we use gradient descent:
\[\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta),\]
with the learning rate \(\eta\). The gradient is computed by backpropagation – the chain rule of calculus applied layer by layer from the output back to the input. Frameworks like PyTorch do this automatically (automatic differentiation).
Practical ingredients:

Mini-batches: each step uses a small random subset of the data (e.g. 256 examples) – stochastic gradient descent. One pass through all data is an epoch.
Optimisers like Adam adapt the step size per weight and usually work well with default settings.
Scaling: inputs should be standardised; otherwise training is slow or unstable.
Validation and early stopping: monitor the loss on a validation set during training and stop when it no longer improves – the most important protection against overfitting.







Engineering practice: when is deep learning worth it?




Raw, high-dimensional data (images, spectrograms, long signals, text): yes – neural networks learn the features.
Tabular data with meaningful engineered features: usually no – gradient boosting is typically as good or better, faster to train and easier to explain.
Little data: usually no, unless a pretrained network can be reused (transfer learning).
Always compare with a classical baseline and consider the costs: training time, hardware, expertise, explainability, certification.
