title: 12  Deep Learning in Engineering
section: 12.3 Remaining useful life from sensor sequences
text:
12.3 Remaining useful life from sensor sequences
The remaining useful life (RUL) of a machine is the time it can still operate before failure. Predicting it is the core of predictive maintenance: replace parts shortly before they fail, not too early (wasted life) and not too late (unplanned failure).
Two modelling choices are typical for RUL prediction:

Sliding windows: the input for a prediction at cycle \(t\) is the sensor history of the last \(L\) cycles, an \(L \times p\) matrix (\(p\) sensors). Each trajectory provides many overlapping windows for training.
Piecewise linear target: early in life, degradation is not observable in the sensors – a new engine with 300 remaining cycles looks like one with 200. The RUL target is therefore capped at a constant (commonly 125 cycles) and decreases linearly afterwards.







Figure 12.2: Sliding windows and capped RUL target. From each engine’s sensor history, windows of L cycles are cut; the target of a window is the RUL at its last cycle. The RUL is capped at 125 cycles because early degradation is invisible in the data.



Windows of the same engine are highly correlated – exactly like signal windows in Chapter 10. Training and validation data must be split by engine.

title: 12  Deep Learning in Engineering
text:
12.4 Live coding: remaining useful life
The data are downloaded automatically as in Chapter 3. Subset FD001 has one operating condition and one fault mode (degradation of the high-pressure compressor). The test file contains trajectories that end some time before failure; RUL_FD001.txt gives the true RUL at the end of each test trajectory.

# Download helper, as in Chapter 3
from pathlib import Path
import zipfile
import requests

DATA = Path("data")
DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)                         # create the folder ./data if it does not exist

def download(url, fname=None):
    """Download a file once and cache it in ./data."""
    if fname is None:                             # no file name given:
        fname = url.split("/")[-1]                # use the last part of the URL
    path = DATA / fname                           # "/" joins folder and file name
    if not path.exists():                         # download only if not cached yet
        r = requests.get(url, timeout=300)        # give up after 300 s without response
        r.raise_for_status()                      # stop with an error if the download failed
        path.write_bytes(r.content)               # open, write and close the file in one step
    return path

url = "https://data.nasa.gov/docs/legacy/CMAPSSData.zip"
cols = ["unit", "cycle", "op1", "op2", "op3"] + [f"s{i}" for i in range(1, 22)]
with zipfile.ZipFile(download(url)) as z:         # read the three files directly from the archive
    train = pd.read_csv(z.open("train_FD001.txt"), sep=r"\s+", header=None, names=cols)
    test = pd.read_csv(z.open("test_FD001.txt"), sep=r"\s+", header=None, names=cols)
    rul_test = pd.read_csv(z.open("RUL_FD001.txt"), header=None)[0].values   # true RUL at the end of each test engine

train["rul"] = (train.groupby("unit")["cycle"].transform("max") - train["cycle"]).clip(upper=125)
sensors = [c for c in cols[5:] if train[c].std() > 1e-3]       # drop constant sensors
mu, sd = train[sensors].mean(), train[sensors].std()
train[sensors] = (train[sensors] - mu) / sd
test[sensors] = (test[sensors] - mu) / sd
print("Sensors used:", sensors)

Sensors used: ['s2', 's3', 's4', 's6', 's7', 's8', 's9', 's11', 's12', 's13', 's14', 's15', 's17', 's20', 's21']




Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 3.5))
for ax, s in zip(axes, sensors[:3]):
    for u in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]:
        g = train[train.unit == u]
        ax.plot(g["cycle"] - g["cycle"].max(), g[s], lw=0.8)
    ax.set(title=s, xlabel="Cycles before failure", ylabel="standardised value")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()









Plotted against the cycles before failure, several sensors show a clear trend that accelerates towards the end of life – the degradation signature the network must learn. Some sensors are constant in FD001 and were removed.
We cut each engine’s history into windows of \(L = 30\) cycles. For early stopping, 20 of the 100 training engines are held out as validation engines – split by engine, not by window.

L = 30   # window length (cycles)

def windows(df, with_target=True):
    X, y = [], []
    for _, g in df.groupby("unit"):
        v = g[sensors].values
        if len(v) < L:                                   # pad short test series
            v = np.vstack([np.repeat(v[:1], L - len(v), axis=0), v])
        if with_target:
            r = g["rul"].values
            for end in range(L, len(v) + 1):
                X.append(v[end - L:end]); y.append(r[end - 1])
        else:
            X.append(v[-L:])
    return np.array(X, dtype=np.float32), np.array(y, dtype=np.float32)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
val_units = rng.choice(train["unit"].unique(), size=20, replace=False)   # 20 validation engines
X_fit, y_fit = windows(train[~train.unit.isin(val_units)])               # 80 engines for fitting
X_val, y_val = windows(train[train.unit.isin(val_units)])
X_te, _ = windows(test, with_target=False)                                # last window of each test engine
X_fit.shape, X_val.shape, X_te.shape

((13980, 30, 15), (3751, 30, 15), (100, 30, 15))



import copy

def fit(model, X_fit, y_fit, X_val, y_val, loss_fn=nn.MSELoss(), patience=5, max_epochs=100):
    """Train with mini-batches and Adam; stop early when the validation loss no longer improves."""
    Xf, yf = torch.tensor(X_fit), torch.tensor(y_fit).unsqueeze(1)
    Xv, yv = torch.tensor(X_val), torch.tensor(y_val).unsqueeze(1)
    loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(torch.utils.data.TensorDataset(Xf, yf),
                                         batch_size=256, shuffle=True)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    train_loss, val_loss = [], []
    best_loss, best_weights, wait = np.inf, None, 0
    for epoch in range(max_epochs):
        model.train()
        for xb, yb in loader:                            # one epoch = one pass through all batches
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)                # forward pass and loss
            loss.backward()                              # gradients by backpropagation
            opt.step()                                   # update the weights
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():                            # evaluate after each epoch
            train_loss.append(loss_fn(model(Xf), yf).item())
            val_loss.append(loss_fn(model(Xv), yv).item())
        if val_loss[-1] < best_loss:                     # new best epoch: keep a copy of the weights
            best_loss, best_weights, wait = val_loss[-1], copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()), 0
        else:
            wait += 1
            if wait == patience:                         # no improvement for `patience` epochs: stop
                break
    model.load_state_dict(best_weights)                  # go back to the best epoch
    return train_loss, val_loss

torch.manual_seed(0)                                     # reproducible initial weights
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Flatten(),
    nn.Linear(L * len(sensors), 64), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(32, 1),
)
train_loss, val_loss = fit(model, X_fit, y_fit, X_val, y_val)

with torch.no_grad():
    pred = model(torch.tensor(X_te)).squeeze().numpy()
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((pred - np.minimum(rul_test, 125))**2))
print(f"Stopped after {len(val_loss)} epochs, best validation RMSE {np.sqrt(min(val_loss)):.1f} cycles")
print(f"Test RMSE: {rmse:.1f} cycles")

Stopped after 44 epochs, best validation RMSE 15.6 cycles
Test RMSE: 13.9 cycles


The function fit contains the training loop, which is the same in every PyTorch project: for each mini-batch a forward pass, the loss, backward() to compute the gradients and step() to update the weights. model.train() and model.eval() switch between training and evaluation mode, and torch.no_grad() switches off the gradient computation, which is not needed for evaluation. After each epoch, fit computes the loss on the training and on the validation engines. If the validation loss has not improved for patience = 5 epochs, training stops and the weights of the best epoch are restored; copy.deepcopy keeps a copy of them that further training does not change. The network has about 31,000 weights – small by deep learning standards.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
axes[0].plot(train_loss, label="training engines")
axes[0].plot(val_loss, label="validation engines")
axes[0].set(xlabel="Epoch", ylabel="Loss (MSE)", yscale="log"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].scatter(np.minimum(rul_test, 125), pred, s=12)
axes[1].plot([0, 125], [0, 125], "k--")
axes[1].set(xlabel="True RUL (cycles, capped)", ylabel="Predicted RUL (cycles)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()









Discussion. At first, the training and the validation loss fall together. Later, the validation loss falls more and more slowly while the training loss keeps falling, and the gap grows: the network starts to learn properties of the individual training engines that do not carry over to new engines – overfitting. Early stopping ends the training when the validation loss has not improved for five epochs. The predictions follow the diagonal, with larger scatter at high RUL, where degradation is barely visible, and smaller scatter near the end of life – fortunately the region where accurate predictions matter most. Note that the test RMSE is computed on only 100 engines and therefore has considerable uncertainty itself. Whether the network beats a gradient boosting model on window statistics is an open question – Exercise 1.
crumbs: Part D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning

title: 12  Deep Learning in Engineering
text:
12.5 Back to the decision
An engine is scheduled too late if the model overestimates its RUL at the moment of the decision. We schedule an overhaul when predicted RUL − margin falls below the planning horizon of 20 cycles, so the decision is made for engines close to the end of life. Only the errors in this range matter; the large errors at high RUL, where degradation is not yet visible, do not. We therefore use the test engines with a true RUL of at most 60 cycles (20 cycles horizon plus a margin of a few tens of cycles). The margin must cover the overestimates of 95 % of these engines – i.e. it must equal the 95 % quantile of their prediction error \(\hat y - y\).

true_rul = np.minimum(rul_test, 125)
err = pred - true_rul                                   # > 0: overestimate (dangerous)
near = rul_test <= 60                                   # engines in the range where the decision is made
margin = max(0.0, float(np.quantile(err[near], 0.95)))
print(f"Test engines with true RUL <= 60: {near.sum()}, of which overestimated: {(err[near] > 0).mean():.0%}")
print(f"95 % quantile of their error: {np.quantile(err[near], 0.95):.1f} cycles")
print(f"Decision: schedule an overhaul when the predicted RUL falls below 20 + {margin:.0f} = {20 + margin:.0f} cycles.")

Test engines with true RUL <= 60: 39, of which overestimated: 72%
95 % quantile of their error: 18.7 cycles
Decision: schedule an overhaul when the predicted RUL falls below 20 + 19 = 39 cycles.


Near the end of life, the network overestimates most engines – a systematic error that the margin must absorb (Exercise 3 shows how to reduce it). The margin is the price of the model’s uncertainty: the more accurate the model, the smaller the margin and the more useful life is used. Note that the quantile is estimated from only about 40 engines – it is roughly their second-largest error and correspondingly uncertain. The fleet manager should add a reserve and refine the margin with field experience. And as in Chapter 3: C-MAPSS is a simulation, so the procedure must be validated on real engine data before it replaces the fixed interval.
crumbs: Part D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning

title: 12  Deep Learning in Engineering
section: 12.6 Extension: CNNs and transfer learning for visual inspection
text:
12.6 Extension: CNNs and transfer learning for visual inspection
Extension – optional material, not required for the exam.
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) process images with small learnable filters (e.g. 3 × 3 pixels) that slide across the image. Early layers detect edges and simple textures, deeper layers combine them into complex patterns. Because the same filter is applied everywhere, CNNs need far fewer weights than an MLP on raw pixels.
Training a CNN from scratch requires many thousands of labelled images. Transfer learning avoids this: a network pretrained on millions of everyday images (ImageNet) already provides general visual features that transfer surprisingly well to industrial images. For anomaly detection, a simple but strong approach is: embed all good training images with the pretrained CNN and score a test image by its distance to the nearest good image in this feature space. No defective images are needed for training.

12.6.1 Live coding: anomaly detection on one MVTec category
Data access. MVTec AD is free for non-commercial use (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) and is downloaded from the MVTec website after accepting the license. Download one category (e.g. bottle, a few hundred MB) and extract it to data/mvtec/bottle/. A GPU (Colab: Runtime → Change runtime type) speeds things up but is not required. Because of the manual download, the two MVTec cells are not executed when the script is built – run them yourself after downloading the data.

from pathlib import Path
from torchvision import models
from PIL import Image

ROOT = Path("data/mvtec/bottle")
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

weights = models.ResNet18_Weights.DEFAULT
backbone = models.resnet18(weights=weights)
backbone.fc = torch.nn.Identity()           # use the 512-d feature vector
backbone.eval().to(device)
tf = weights.transforms()

@torch.no_grad()
def embed(paths):
    feats = []
    for p in paths:
        x = tf(Image.open(p).convert("RGB")).unsqueeze(0).to(device)
        feats.append(backbone(x).cpu().numpy()[0])
    return np.array(feats)

train_paths = sorted((ROOT / "train" / "good").glob("*.png"))
test_paths = sorted((ROOT / "test").glob("*/*.png"))
labels = np.array([p.parent.name != "good" for p in test_paths])
F_train, F_test = embed(train_paths), embed(test_paths)


from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

nn_model = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1).fit(F_train)
score = nn_model.kneighbors(F_test)[0][:, 0]
print(f"Image-level ROC AUC: {roc_auc_score(labels, score):.3f}")

order = np.argsort(score)[::-1][:5]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(15, 3))
for ax, i in zip(axes, order):
    ax.imshow(Image.open(test_paths[i])); ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(f"{test_paths[i].parent.name}\nscore {score[i]:.1f}")
plt.show()

The five most anomalous test images should mostly be defective bottles. State-of-the-art methods (e.g. PatchCore) refine this idea by comparing local image patches instead of whole images, which also localises the defect.

title: 12  Deep Learning in Engineering
text:
12.7 Outlook

Physics-informed machine learning: physical laws enter the model as constraints or as terms of the loss function – useful when data are scarce and extrapolation matters.
Surrogate models: neural networks or Gaussian processes replace expensive FEM or CFD simulations in optimisation loops.
Foundation models: large pretrained models for time series, images and text, adapted to specific tasks with little data; large language models as assistants for coding and documentation.
Deployment and MLOps: models in production must be monitored for data drift (the input data change, e.g. a new sensor or a new product), retrained, versioned and – in safety-relevant applications – validated and certified.
crumbs: Part D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning

title: 12  Deep Learning in Engineering
text:
12.8 Summary






Key takeaways




A neural network is a stack of linear maps and nonlinear activations, trained by gradient descent with backpropagation.
Test honestly: monitor a validation set and stop early; split by unit (engine, machine), not by window.
For RUL prediction, sliding windows and a capped target are standard; errors near end of life matter most.
Deep learning shines on raw images, signals and text; for tabular features, compare with gradient boosting first.
crumbs: Part D – Signals, Time Series and Deep Learning

title: 12  Deep Learning in Engineering
text:
12.9 Exercises


Build a baseline: gradient boosting on features of each window (last value, mean and slope of each sensor). Is the neural network better? Useful: HistGradientBoostingRegressor (Chapter 8); for an array of windows with the shape (windows, cycles, sensors), X[:, -1, :] gives the last values and X.mean(axis=1) the means of all sensors.
Choose the window length: train the network with \(L\) = 10, 20, 30 and 50 cycles and compare the validation RMSE. Which window length do you choose? Why must this choice be made on the validation engines and not on the test engines? Useful: the functions windows and fit from the live coding; windows uses the variable L.
Why is an underestimate of the RUL less critical than an overestimate? Design an asymmetric loss function, train the network with it and compare the safety margin with the one from the live coding. Useful: torch.where(condition, a, b); the argument loss_fn of fit.
(Extension) Replace the MLP by a 1D convolutional network (nn.Conv1d). Mind the tensor shape (batch, channels, time). Useful: nn.AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1) averages over time; the function fit.
(Extension) MVTec: repeat the anomaly detection for a texture category (e.g. carpet) and an object category (e.g. screw). Where does the method work better? Choose a threshold so that no defective part passes – what fraction of good parts is rejected?



12.9.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1






from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingRegressor

def window_features(Xw):
    t = np.arange(L) - (L - 1) / 2
    slope = (Xw * t[None, :, None]).sum(axis=1) / (t**2).sum()
    return np.hstack([Xw[:, -1, :], Xw.mean(axis=1), slope])

gb = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(window_features(X_fit), y_fit)
pred_gb = gb.predict(window_features(X_te))
rmse_gb = np.sqrt(np.mean((pred_gb - np.minimum(rul_test, 125))**2))
print(f"Test RMSE: MLP {rmse:.1f} cycles, gradient boosting {rmse_gb:.1f} cycles")

Test RMSE: MLP 13.9 cycles, gradient boosting 12.6 cycles


With well-chosen window features (level, mean and trend per sensor), gradient boosting is on par with or even better than a small MLP on FD001 – a reminder that deep learning is not automatically better on sensor data with few channels. Neural networks gain an advantage on the more complex subsets (FD002/FD004 with six operating conditions) and with architectures that exploit the sequence structure, such as 1D CNNs or LSTMs.









Solution to Exercise 2






for L in (10, 20, 30, 50):                       # windows() and the network use L
    Xf, yf = windows(train[~train.unit.isin(val_units)])
    Xv, yv = windows(train[train.unit.isin(val_units)])
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    net = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(L * len(sensors), 64), nn.ReLU(),
                        nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 1))
    train_loss_L, val_loss_L = fit(net, Xf, yf, Xv, yv)
    print(f"L = {L:2d}: validation RMSE {np.sqrt(min(val_loss_L)):.1f} cycles")
L = 30                                           # back to the window length of the live coding

L = 10: validation RMSE 21.0 cycles
L = 20: validation RMSE 19.2 cycles
L = 30: validation RMSE 15.6 cycles
L = 50: validation RMSE 15.8 cycles


Short windows contain too little of the degradation trend. Beyond about 30 cycles, the validation RMSE hardly improves any more, while a longer window needs more weights, and more test engines are shorter than the window and must be padded. A window length of about 30 cycles is therefore a good choice. The choice must be made on the validation engines: if we chose the window length with the best test RMSE, the test engines would have been used for a decision and their RMSE would no longer be an honest estimate for new engines.









Solution to Exercise 3





Two different things are called loss here: the real loss caused by a wrong decision, and the loss function that training minimises. The asymmetric loss function brings the ratio of the real losses into the training.
An underestimate leads to maintenance too early: some useful life is wasted, a cost that can be planned. An overestimate means the machine may fail before maintenance: unplanned downtime, secondary damage, possibly a safety risk. An asymmetric loss penalises late predictions (predicted RUL > true RUL) more strongly, e.g. the score of the PHM 2008 challenge with \(d = \hat y - y\): \[s(d) = \begin{cases} e^{-d/13} - 1, & d < 0 \\ e^{d/10} - 1, & d \ge 0. \end{cases}\] This score is used to evaluate models; for training, its exponential growth makes single large errors dominate. A simpler variant for training is a weighted squared error:

def asymmetric_mse(pred, target, w_late=4.0):
    d = pred - target
    return torch.mean(torch.where(d > 0, w_late * d**2, d**2))   # overestimates count 4 times

torch.manual_seed(0)
model_asym = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(L * len(sensors), 64), nn.ReLU(),
                           nn.Linear(64, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 1))
train_loss_a, val_loss_a = fit(model_asym, X_fit, y_fit, X_val, y_val, loss_fn=asymmetric_mse)
with torch.no_grad():
    err_asym = model_asym(torch.tensor(X_te)).squeeze().numpy() - true_rul
for name, e in [("squared error", err), ("asymmetric", err_asym)]:
    print(f"{name:14s}: overestimated {(e[near] > 0).mean():.0%}, margin {np.quantile(e[near], 0.95):.1f} cycles")

squared error : overestimated 72%, margin 18.7 cycles
asymmetric    : overestimated 44%, margin 10.1 cycles


Training with the asymmetric loss shifts the predictions towards lower RUL values – the model becomes deliberately conservative, and the margin needed for the safety requirement shrinks. The safety requirement itself is still checked with the margin; the asymmetric loss only moves part of the caution into the model. The weight should reflect the real cost ratio of late and early maintenance.









Solution to Exercise 4






class CNN1D(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_sensors):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv1d(n_sensors, 32, kernel_size=5, padding=2), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv1d(32, 32, kernel_size=5, padding=2), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.AdaptiveAvgPool1d(1), nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(32, 1))

    def forward(self, x):                  # x: (batch, time, sensors)
        return self.net(x.transpose(1, 2))  # Conv1d expects (batch, channels, time)

torch.manual_seed(0)
cnn = CNN1D(len(sensors))
train_loss_c, val_loss_c = fit(cnn, X_fit, y_fit, X_val, y_val)
with torch.no_grad():
    pred_cnn = cnn(torch.tensor(X_te)).squeeze().numpy()
print(f"Test RMSE 1D CNN: {np.sqrt(np.mean((pred_cnn - np.minimum(rul_test, 125))**2)):.1f} cycles")

Test RMSE 1D CNN: 16.5 cycles


The convolution filters slide along the time axis and share their weights over time, so the network detects local patterns (e.g. a steepening trend) wherever they occur in the window. The sensors are the input channels – hence the transposition from (batch, time, sensors) to (batch, sensors, time).









Solution to Exercise 5





Change ROOT to the new category and rerun the two cells. Image-level anomaly detection with global features typically works very well for objects with consistent appearance (bottle) and for many textures, but less well for categories with small, local defects on objects with varying pose (screw), because a global feature vector averages over the whole image. For a threshold that lets no defective part pass:

thr = score[labels].min()                          # lowest score among defective images
false_reject = (score[~labels] >= thr).mean()
print(f"threshold {thr:.2f}: {false_reject:.0%} of good parts rejected")

The resulting false reject rate shows the price of zero slip. Note that this threshold was chosen on the test set itself and is therefore optimistic; in practice it must be set on separate validation images.

title: 13  Review and Exam Preparation
text:
13.2 Core concepts at a glance








Concept
In one sentence
Chapter




CRISP-DM
Process model: understanding → data → preparation → modelling → evaluation → deployment, iterated.
1


Statistics vs. ML
Statistics focuses on understanding and uncertainty, ML on prediction for new data; they overlap in statistical learning.
1


Robust statistics
Median, IQR and MAD are barely affected by outliers, mean and standard deviation are.
2


MCAR / MAR / MNAR
Whether missingness is random, depends on observed data, or on the missing value itself.
2


Central limit theorem
Means of many independent observations are approximately normal, with standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\).
3


Weibull shape \(\beta\)
\(<1\) early failures, \(=1\) random failures, \(>1\) wear-out.
3


Confidence interval
A procedure that captures the true parameter in 95 % of repetitions.
3


p-value
Probability of data at least as extreme as observed, assuming \(H_0\).
4


Effect size
Size of a difference in physical units or standard deviations; decides relevance.
4


Prediction interval
Interval for a single new observation; wider than the confidence interval of the mean.
5


Bias–variance trade-off
Too simple models underfit, too flexible models overfit; the test error is U-shaped.
6


Cross-validation
Estimate of the test error by rotating held-out folds.
6


Precision / recall
Share of alarms that are real / share of failures that are detected.
7


Bagging / boosting
Averaging decorrelated deep trees / adding shallow trees that correct errors.
8


T² / SPE
Unusual within the PCA model plane / distance from the plane.
9


Nyquist frequency
Half the sampling rate; higher frequencies alias.
10


Time series validation
Train on the past, test on the following period.
11


Backpropagation
Chain rule to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to all weights.
12

title: 13  Review and Exam Preparation
text:
13.3 Checklist: typical pitfalls






Before you trust a result, check …




Data leakage: features that contain the answer, preprocessing fitted on all data, random splits of time series, windows or parts of the same unit in training and test.
Wrong metric: accuracy or ROC on imbalanced data; MAPE near zero values.
Significance without relevance: tiny effects with huge \(n\); dependent observations treated as independent.
Extrapolation: predictions outside the range (or the combinations) of the training data.
Missing baseline: no comparison with the mean, the seasonal naive forecast or a simple linear model.
Correlation vs. causation: importance and correlation do not prove that a factor causes the effect.

title: 13  Review and Exam Preparation
text:
13.4 Typical exam question types

Method choice: given a scenario, choose and justify a method and an evaluation metric.
Interpretation: read a regression table, a confusion matrix, a scree plot, a probability plot or a residual plot.
Calculation by hand: confidence interval, test statistic, Bayes’ theorem, precision/recall from a confusion matrix, aliasing frequency.
Code reading: find the error in a short Python snippet.
Analysis design: for a new scenario, sketch a complete analysis plan – from the engineering question to the decision criterion. There is usually more than one good plan; what counts is a consistent and justified one.
Recommendation: judge or improve a recommendation – does it state the uncertainty, the assumptions and the limits of data and model?

title: 13  Review and Exam Preparation
text:
13.5 Seven lessons from this course
The chapters of this course treat very different methods, but the same few ideas return in all of them. They do not replace the learning goals of the chapters – the exam covers those, with their methods and calculations. The lessons are what connects the chapters – and what remains useful long after the details have faded.








Lesson
What it means
Chapters




1. Start from the decision.
Fix the question, the criterion and the cost of an error before looking at results. The data determine how a model is fitted; the costs determine how it is used – thresholds, safety margins, intervals.
1, 7, 12 and every Back to the decision


2. Know your data before you model them.
Units, gaps, outliers and the way the data were produced decide what any model can learn.
1, 2, 9


3. Every estimate has an uncertainty.
A number without its uncertainty cannot support a decision. Quantify it – and say when it is too optimistic.
3, 4, 5, 6, 12


4. Significant is not the same as relevant.
With enough data, every difference becomes significant. What counts is its size compared with what matters in practice.
2, 4, 5


5. Every model rests on assumptions.
A loss function is the negative log-likelihood of an assumed distribution of the data; residuals and plots check the assumptions.
3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 12


6. Test honestly.
Judge a model on data it has not seen, using only the information available at decision time – for time series, only the past – and always against a simple baseline.
1, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12


7. Associations are not causes.
Observational data show which quantities move together, not why. Causes need designed experiments or physical understanding.
1, 4, 5, 8



In the key takeaways of the chapters, the lessons appear with exactly these words.

title: 13  Review and Exam Preparation
text:
13.6 Practice questions


A confusion matrix shows TN = 950, FP = 30, FN = 5, TP = 15. Compute accuracy, precision and recall. Is the model useful for failure detection?
A sensor detects 99 % of all leaks and raises a false alarm in 2 % of the leak-free tests; 0.5 % of all parts leak. What is the probability that a part with an alarm really leaks?
Find the error: X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X); X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y).
A t-test on 50,000 parts shows p < 0.001 for a 0.2 µm difference in mean diameter, tolerance ±20 µm. What do you tell the production manager?
Explain to a colleague, in five sentences, why a random train/test split is wrong for load forecasting.
Ten measurements of a shaft diameter give \(\bar x = 25.012\) mm and \(s = 0.004\) mm. Compute a 95 % confidence interval for the mean diameter (\(t_{9,\,0.975} = 2.262\)).
A Weibull analysis of pump seals gives \(\beta = 0.8\). The maintenance manager wants to replace all seals preventively after 2,000 hours. What do you advise?
A regression of tool wear on cutting speed gives \(R^2 = 0.95\) on the training data. The CV error is three times the training error. What do you conclude, and what do you do?
A vibration signal is sampled at 2 kHz. A gear mesh frequency of 1.6 kHz is present. Where does it appear in the spectrum?
In a PCA monitoring chart, a new production run exceeds the SPE limit but not the T² limit. How do you interpret this?
Analysis design. An injection moulding plant inspects the warpage of every part by hand. The plant manager asks whether a prediction from the machine data could replace most of this inspection. For every shot of the last six months, the machine logged temperatures, pressures and times (120,000 shots). For 3,000 of these parts, the warpage was measured; about 2 % of them exceed the limit. Sketch an analysis plan: target and inputs, data checks, method, validation, metric and decision criterion. Name the main risks.
Recommendation. A colleague summarises an analysis for the plant manager: “Our new alarm model detected 9 of the 10 failures in the test month, i.e. 90 %. We recommend installing it.” What is missing for a well-founded recommendation? Rewrite it.



13.6.1 Solutions






Solution to Question 1





Accuracy = 965/1000 = 96.5 %, precision = 15/45 = 33 %, recall = 15/20 = 75 %. The trivial model “always OK” would reach 98 % accuracy, so accuracy is misleading here. The model detects three out of four failures with two false alarms per real alarm. Whether it is useful depends on the cost ratio of missed failures and false alarms – often yes.









Solution to Question 2





\[\begin{aligned} P(\text{leak} \mid \text{alarm}) &= \frac{0.99 \cdot 0.005}{0.99 \cdot 0.005 + 0.02 \cdot 0.995} \\ &= \frac{0.00495}{0.00495 + 0.0199} \approx 0.20. \end{aligned}\] Only about one in five alarms is a real leak – the base rate effect. Alarmed parts should be re-tested before scrapping.









Solution to Question 3





The scaler is fitted on all data before the split, so means and standard deviations of the test data leak into the preprocessing. Correct: split first, then fit the scaler on the training data only – best by putting scaler and model into a Pipeline. (For time series, additionally shuffle=False or a time-based split.)









Solution to Question 4





The difference is statistically significant but practically irrelevant: 0.2 µm is 1 % of the tolerance half-width. With 50,000 parts, the test detects even tiny differences. No action is needed because of this difference; what matters is whether the process stays within tolerance (process capability).









Solution to Question 5





Neighbouring hours and days are strongly correlated. With a random split, the test days are surrounded by training days from before and after, so the model only interpolates. In operation, a forecast must be made without knowing the future. The random split therefore underestimates the real forecast error. A time-based split – train on the past, test on the following period – reproduces the real situation.









Solution to Question 6





\[\begin{aligned} 25.012 \pm 2.262 \cdot \frac{0.004}{\sqrt{10}} &= 25.012 \pm 0.0029\ \text{mm} \\ &\Rightarrow\; [25.0091,\ 25.0149]\ \text{mm}. \end{aligned}\] The interval describes the uncertainty of the mean diameter, not the spread of individual shafts (about ±2s = ±0.008 mm).









Solution to Question 7





\(\beta < 1\) means a decreasing failure rate – early failures dominate (e.g. installation errors, defective batches). A new seal is then more likely to fail soon than an old one, so preventive replacement at 2,000 hours would increase the number of failures and costs. Better: investigate the cause of the early failures (installation, quality of supply) and possibly run-in tests.









Solution to Question 8





The large gap between training and cross-validation error indicates overfitting: the model is too flexible for the amount of data, and the high training \(R^2\) is misleading. Actions: simpler model (fewer terms, lower polynomial degree), regularisation, more data; select the complexity by cross-validation and report the CV or test error, not the training \(R^2\).









Solution to Question 9





The Nyquist frequency is 1 kHz. The 1.6 kHz component aliases to \(|1.6 - 2.0| = 0.4\) kHz = 400 Hz. The spectrum shows a false peak at 400 Hz. A sampling rate above 3.2 kHz (in practice ≥ 4 kHz) with an anti-aliasing filter is needed.









Solution to Question 10





A high SPE with normal T² means that the run shows a pattern of variation that the PCA model of normal operation does not contain – a new kind of deviation, e.g. a sensor fault, a broken correlation between variables or a new fault type. The contribution plot of the SPE shows which variables cause the deviation and is the starting point for the root-cause analysis.









Solution to Question 11





One possible plan – other choices are fine if they are justified:

Decision and requirement: First agree on a requirement with production and quality, e.g. “at most 5 % of the parts outside the limit may pass without inspection”. Only then can the model be judged.
Target: Predict the measured warpage (regression) and compare the prediction with the limit, rather than training a classifier on 60 out-of-limit parts – the continuous target uses the information of all 3,000 measurements.
Inputs: Only machine data that are available before the inspection decision; nothing that is recorded during or after inspection or rework (data leakage).
Data checks: Were the 3,000 measured parts selected at random or because they looked suspicious (selection bias)? Do the time stamps of shots and measurements match? Missing values, sensor outliers, changes of mould or material batch.
Method: Baselines first (mean, simple linear model), then e.g. regularised regression or gradient boosting.
Validation: Time-based split – train on the first months, test on the last one – because tool wear and material batches change over time; a random split would be too optimistic.
Metric and decision criterion: On the test period, choose the threshold for “inspect” so that the requirement is met, and report the share of parts that still need inspection – that is the saving.
Uncertainty and risks: With 2 % defects, the last month contains only about ten out-of-limit parts. A measured recall of 9 of 10 is compatible with a true recall of only about 55 % (95 % confidence interval). Therefore: start with a pilot phase in which all parts are still inspected and the model runs in parallel; monitor the model in operation and retrain after changes of mould or material.










Solution to Question 12





The statement gives a single number – without its uncertainty, without the false alarms and without assumptions. A well-founded recommendation adds:

Uncertainty: 9 of 10 detected failures are compatible with a true detection rate between about 55 % and almost 100 % (95 % confidence interval).
False alarms and base rate: how many alarms were false? When failures are rare, even a low false alarm rate can mean that most alarms are false (Bayes’ theorem, precision).
Costs: what a missed failure and a false alarm cost – only then can the benefit and the threshold be judged.
Assumptions: the test month is representative, the model was tested on data after its training period, and there was no data leakage.
Limits: new failure types or changed operating conditions are not covered by the test.

A better version: “In the test month, the model detected 9 of 10 failures. With so few failures, the true detection rate could be as low as about 55 %; in addition, we have to check how many of its alarms are false. We recommend a pilot phase of three months in which the model runs alongside the current procedure, so that detection and false alarm rate can be confirmed before the plant relies on it.”

loc or iloc?



Every row has a label – the index shown on the left – and a position: first row, second row, … loc selects by label, iloc by integer position (memory aid: i for integer). As long as the index is 0, 1, 2, …, both give the same result. After sorting or filtering, they no longer do:

s.iloc[0]    # FIRST row            → T = 18
Ranges differ, too: df.loc[0:2] includes the end (labels 0, 1 and 2), df.iloc[0:2] does not (positions 0 and 1, as for Python lists). For time series, including the end is convenient: s.loc["2015-01-01":"2019-12-31"] contains 31 December.

Ch. 11









Method chaining – and why pandas makes it possible



In energy.set_index("date").sort_index(), the second method is applied directly to the result of the first. This works because of three design decisions in pandas:

Methods return a new object and leave the original unchanged. df.sort_values("a") returns a sorted copy; df stays as it is. Plain Python does the opposite for lists: values.sort() sorts the list itself and returns None – so values.sort().reverse() fails, while df.sort_values("a").head() works.
The type stays the same. A table becomes a table, a column a column – so the next method always fits. .str and .dt also return a column.
Methods instead of statements. An assignment such as df["temp_K"] = df["temp_C"] + 273.15 cannot be chained; df.assign(temp_K=df["temp_C"] + 273.15) returns a new table with the additional column. For the same reason, avoid the older option inplace=True: it changes the table itself and returns None, which breaks the chain.

Returning new tables might sound expensive. Since pandas 3.0 (“copy-on-write”), however, data are only copied when they are actually changed.
Many NumPy functions also exist as pandas methods – s.abs(), s.median(), s.std(). For pandas data, prefer the methods: they fit into a chain, and they skip missing values, which NumPy functions do not:
s = pd.Series([1, -4, np.nan, 3])
s.abs().median()            # 3.0 – pandas skips the missing value
np.median(np.abs(s))        # nan – one missing value makes the result missing
The standard deviation differs, too: s.std() divides by \(n-1\) (sample standard deviation, Chapter 2), np.std(...) by \(n\) unless you write ddof=1.
For longer chains, put the whole expression in brackets – inside brackets, Python continues on the next line – and write one step per line:
daily = (weather
         .dropna()            # remove rows with missing values
         .resample("D")       # group by day
         .mean())             # one mean per day
Chains are compact; separate steps are easier to check. A good habit: build a chain step by step, and if it fails, remove the last steps until it works again – this shows which step causes the error.

pandas, seaborn and Matplotlib



pandas and seaborn do not draw themselves – they call Matplotlib. These three lines produce essentially the same line plot:
ax.plot(df.index, df["Appliances"], lw=0.3)        # Matplotlib
df["Appliances"].plot(ax=ax, lw=0.3)                # pandas
sns.lineplot(x=df.index, y=df["Appliances"], ax=ax) # seaborn
pandas takes the x-axis from the index (a time index gives a date axis) and draws one line per column, labelled with its name. Matplotlib options such as lw, alpha, color or label are passed on. With ax=..., pandas and seaborn draw into an existing field created by plt.subplots; without it, they create a new figure. Both return this field (ax), so you can continue with the usual Matplotlib commands, e.g. ax.set(ylabel="...").
Rule of thumb: pandas for quick plots directly from a table, seaborn for statistical plots (histogram, box plot, heatmap), Matplotlib via ax for fine-tuning.

title: Appendix B — Formula Collection
text:
B.1 Describing data
This appendix collects the formulas of the script, ordered by task. It contains no explanations: what a formula means and when it applies is explained in the chapter named in the last column.
Notation: \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) are observations, \(n\) is the sample size, \(\bar x\) the mean, \(\tilde x\) the median and \(s\) the sample standard deviation. \(\sum_i\) runs over all observations.

Quantity
Formula
Used in




Mean
\(\bar x = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i\)
Ch. 2


Sample standard deviation
\(s = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}\)
Ch. 2

\(\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\) (quartiles: 25 % and 75 % quantiles)
Ch. 2


Median absolute deviation
\(\text{MAD} = \operatorname{median}\big(\lvert x_1 - \tilde x \rvert, \dots, \lvert x_n - \tilde x \rvert\big)\)

flag \(x_i\) if \(x_i < Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR}\) or \(x_i > Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}\)

\(z_i = \dfrac{x_i - \tilde x}{1.4826 \cdot \text{MAD}}\), flag \(x_i\) if \(\lvert z_i \rvert > 3.5\)

title: Appendix C — Data from Databases
text:
C.1 Tables, keys and relations
In the chapters of this script, data arrive as files: a table from a repository, a raw text file from a weather service. In a company, engineering data usually live somewhere else – in databases:
If you start a data science project in a company, you will therefore often get access to a database rather than a file. To find, combine and extract the data you need, you have to speak the language of databases: SQL (Structured Query Language). This appendix teaches the small part of SQL that covers most everyday needs – reading data – and shows how SQL and pandas fit together. No previous knowledge of databases is required.
Learning goals. After this appendix you can
A relational database stores data in tables. Each table follows the rules of tidy data from Chapter 1: one row per observation, one column per variable, one value per cell. The key idea is to use one table per kind of observational unit and to link the tables instead of repeating information.
Our production database has four tables:
Instead of writing the machine’s line and year into every one of thousands of inspection rows, each inspection only stores its order_id, and each order stores its machine_id. If a machine is moved to another line, one row has to be changed – not thousands.
We use SQLite, a database that consists of a single file, needs no server and is part of every Python installation. It works locally and in Google Colab. The following cell creates the example database; how it is created is not important here – in practice, the database already exists and you only read from it.
Code
# Create the example database production.db (simulated data; in practice the database exists already)
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def create_production_db(path="data/production.db", seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    Path(path).parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    Path(path).unlink(missing_ok=True)
    machines = pd.DataFrame({
        "machine_id": ["M1", "M2", "M3", "M4", "M5", "M6"],
        "line": ["A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B"],
        "year_built": [2019, 2019, 2015, 2008, 2021, 2015],
    })
    base_scrap = {"M1": 0.02, "M2": 0.025, "M3": 0.03, "M4": 0.07, "M5": 0.015, "M6": 0.03}
    shift_factor = {"early": 1.0, "late": 1.1, "night": 1.5}
    # orders start at 06:00, 14:00 and 22:00 local time (05:00, 13:00, 21:00 UTC in winter)
    starts = pd.date_range("2025-01-06 05:00", "2025-03-28 21:00", freq="8h", tz="UTC")
    shift_of = {5: "early", 13: "late", 21: "night"}
    orders, parts = [], []
    order_id, part_id = 1000, 1
    for t in starts:
        shift = shift_of[t.hour]
        for m in machines["machine_id"]:
            if rng.random() < 0.15:                      # machine idle in this shift
                continue
            material = str(rng.choice(["C45", "42CrMo4"], p=[0.7, 0.3]))
            n = int(rng.integers(20, 60))
            orders.append((order_id, m, t.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), shift, material, n))
            p = base_scrap[m] * shift_factor[shift] * (1.3 if material == "42CrMo4" else 1.0)
            if rng.random() > 0.03:                      # a few orders were never inspected
                for _ in range(n):
                    scrap = rng.random() < p
                    diam = rng.normal(25.0, 0.04 if scrap else 0.01)
                    if rng.random() < 0.02:
                        diam = None                      # diameter not recorded
                    parts.append((part_id, order_id, diam, "scrap" if scrap else "OK"))
                    part_id += 1
            order_id += 1
    maintenance = pd.DataFrame({
        "machine_id": ["M1", "M3", "M4", "M4", "M4", "M6"],
        "date": ["2025-01-20", "2025-02-03", "2025-01-13", "2025-02-10", "2025-03-10", "2025-03-03"],
        "kind": ["inspection", "repair", "repair", "repair", "inspection", "inspection"],
    })
    with sqlite3.connect(path) as con:
        con.execute("CREATE TABLE machines (machine_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, line TEXT, year_built INTEGER)")
        con.execute("""CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, machine_id TEXT REFERENCES machines,
                       start_time TEXT, shift TEXT, material TEXT, quantity INTEGER)""")
        con.execute("""CREATE TABLE inspections (part_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER REFERENCES orders,
                       diameter_mm REAL, result TEXT)""")
        con.execute("CREATE TABLE maintenance (machine_id TEXT REFERENCES machines, date TEXT, kind TEXT)")
        con.executemany("INSERT INTO machines VALUES (?, ?, ?)", machines.itertuples(index=False))
        con.executemany("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", orders)
        con.executemany("INSERT INTO inspections VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)", parts)
        con.executemany("INSERT INTO maintenance VALUES (?, ?, ?)", maintenance.itertuples(index=False))
    return path

db_path = create_production_db()

Definition: Primary key and foreign key



A primary key identifies each row of a table uniquely, e.g. machine_id in machines. A foreign key is a column that refers to the primary key of another table, e.g. machine_id in orders. Foreign keys are the links along which tables are combined.








Figure C.1: Tables of the production database and their links. Each arrow points from a foreign key to the primary key it refers to.

title: Appendix C — Data from Databases
text:
C.5 Combining tables: JOIN
JOIN puts rows of two tables side by side wherever the keys match. We link each inspected part to its order (via order_id) and each order to its machine (via machine_id):

query = """
SELECT m.machine_id, m.year_built,
       COUNT(*)                AS n_parts,
       AVG(i.result = 'scrap') AS scrap_rate
FROM inspections AS i
JOIN orders   AS o ON i.order_id   = o.order_id
JOIN machines AS m ON o.machine_id = m.machine_id
GROUP BY m.machine_id, m.year_built
ORDER BY scrap_rate DESC
"""

Engineering practice: filter and aggregate in the database



Let the database do what it is good at – selecting, joining and aggregating large tables – and load only the result into Python. Use pandas for everything that comes afterwards: plots, statistics, models. On a company database, also make sure that you only read: ask for a read-only account, and never run commands such as DELETE or UPDATE on a production system.

title: Appendix C — Data from Databases
text:
C.6 Pitfalls

C.6.1 A join can multiply rows
A join creates one output row for every matching pair. If a key appears several times in both tables, rows are multiplied. The table maintenance lists maintenance events – machine M4 has three of them. What happens if we join it to the orders?

query = """
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_rows
FROM orders AS o
JOIN maintenance AS mt ON o.machine_id = mt.machine_id
WHERE o.machine_id = 'M4'
"""
print("orders of M4:            ", pd.read_sql("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE machine_id = 'M4'", con).iloc[0, 0])
print("rows after joining with maintenance:", pd.read_sql(query, con).iloc[0, 0])

orders of M4:             209
rows after joining with maintenance: 627


Every order of M4 now appears three times – once per maintenance event. Sums and counts computed after such a join are three times too large, and nothing warns you. Always check the number of rows before and after a join, and be sure what one row of the result means.


C.6.2 Inner and left join
A plain JOIN (an inner join) keeps only rows that have a partner in both tables. Orders without any inspection therefore disappear silently. A LEFT JOIN keeps all rows of the left table and fills the missing columns with NULL:

query = """
SELECT o.order_id, o.machine_id, o.start_time
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN inspections AS i ON o.order_id = i.order_id
WHERE i.part_id IS NULL
"""
not_inspected = pd.read_sql(query, con)
print(len(not_inspected), "orders without any inspection record")
not_inspected.head()

C.6.3 NULL is a missing value
NULL is SQL’s missing value; pandas turns it into NaN or None. Aggregates such as AVG and COUNT(column) ignore NULL values silently, COUNT(*) counts all rows. A comparison with NULL is never true – use IS NULL instead of = NULL.

query = """
SELECT COUNT(*)            AS all_rows,
       COUNT(diameter_mm)  AS with_diameter,
       AVG(diameter_mm)    AS mean_diameter
FROM inspections
"""

C.6.4 Time stamps are often text
SQLite has no separate type for time stamps; here they are stored as text in UTC. After loading, convert them explicitly, as for the weather data in Chapter 2:
orders = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM orders", con)
orders["start_time"] = pd.to_datetime(orders["start_time"], format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", utc=True)
Other databases have proper date types, but the question “UTC or local time?” remains – check the documentation of the database.

title: Appendix C — Data from Databases
text:
C.7 Outlook
The commands of this appendix work with every relational database – SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle – with only small differences in dialect. To connect to a server database, you need a driver and the connection details (server, database, user name, password); the package SQLAlchemy offers a uniform interface for this. Process historians often have their own query interfaces, but usually also offer an SQL-like access or an export to tables.

title: Appendix C — Data from Databases
text:
C.8 Summary






Key takeaways




Relational databases store tidy tables – one per kind of observational unit – linked by primary and foreign keys.
Four SQL commands cover most reading tasks: SELECT (columns), WHERE (rows), GROUP BY (summaries) and JOIN (combining tables). Each has a pandas counterpart.
Filter and aggregate in the database, analyse in pandas.
Check the number of rows after every join, know the difference between inner and left join, and treat NULL as a missing value.

title: Appendix C — Data from Databases
text:
C.9 Exercises


Write a query that returns, for each material, the number of inspected parts and the scrap rate. Is one material more difficult to machine?
The production manager suspects that scrap increases towards the end of the week. Compute the scrap rate per weekday. (Hint: load the joined table with start_time, convert it as shown above and use the pandas attribute .dt.day_name().)
Determine the mean diameter and its standard deviation for OK parts and for scrap parts. What does the result tell you about the cause of the scrap? Useful: SQLite has no standard deviation – compute the variance as AVG(x * x) - AVG(x) * AVG(x) and take the square root in pandas.
Compute the scrap rate of M4 in the two weeks before and the two weeks after the repair on 2025-02-10. Can you see an effect of the repair? (Use WHERE with a condition on start_time; text in the format YYYY-MM-DD can be compared like dates.)



C.9.1 Solutions






Solution to Exercise 1

SELECT o.material, COUNT(*) AS n_parts, AVG(i.result = 'scrap') AS scrap_rate
FROM inspections AS i
JOIN orders AS o ON i.order_id = o.order_id
GROUP BY o.material
"""

Solution to Exercise 2






query = """
SELECT o.start_time, i.result
FROM inspections AS i
JOIN orders AS o ON i.order_id = o.order_id
"""
parts = pd.read_sql(query, con)
parts["start_time"] = pd.to_datetime(parts["start_time"], format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", utc=True)
weekday = parts["start_time"].dt.tz_convert("Europe/Berlin").dt.day_name()

The differences between the weekdays are small (between about 4 and 5 %) and show no trend towards the end of the week – the suspicion is not confirmed. Note the conversion to local time: here, orders start at 06:00, 14:00 and 22:00 local time, so the conversion does not change the weekday. For an order starting at 00:30 local time it would, because in UTC that is still the previous day.









Solution to Exercise 3

SELECT result, COUNT(diameter_mm) AS n, AVG(diameter_mm) AS mean_mm,
       AVG(diameter_mm * diameter_mm) - AVG(diameter_mm) * AVG(diameter_mm) AS var_mm2
FROM inspections
GROUP BY result
"""
diam = pd.read_sql(query, con)

       COUNT(*) AS n_parts, AVG(i.result = 'scrap') AS scrap_rate

JOIN orders AS o ON i.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.machine_id = 'M4' AND o.start_time >= '2025-01-27' AND o.start_time < '2025-02-24'
